Colombo 12.
Respondents
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL: Kasun Liyanage for the Petitioner.
Oswald Perera, SC for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON: 19.11.2024
DECIDED ON: 06.12.2024
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J.
1. This application is made under Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs Ordinance seeking bail for the 2nd suspect, Thisaru
Eranda. According to the Petitioner the 2nd suspect was arrested on
18.02.2023 with 100.69g of pure Methamphetamine. The grounds urged
are the relative weakness of the case and the unusual delay in concluding
the pre-trial conference.
2. It is common ground that the indictment has been filed on 12.02.2024,
within one year of the arrest and detection. The main grievance and
complaint of the petitioner is the unusual delay in concluding the pre-trial
proceedings in the Galle High Court. It is argued that provisions of Section

--- Page 3 ---
195A. (5) requires the pre-trial conference to be concluded within 3 months.
Section 195A. (5) reads thus;
195A. (5) Every endeavor shall be made to conclude a pre-trial
conference as expeditiously as possible:
Provided however, a pre-trial conference shall be concluded
within a period not exceeding three months from the date on
which the accused appeared before the court or was
required to appear before the court.
3. Of course, on the face of it the proviso to section 195A. (5) does require the
pre-trial proceeding to be concluded within three months from the date on
which the accused appeared before the court. It is couched in the
mandatory form. However, this matter is now set to be mentioned on
30.01.2025. Two previous scheduled pre-trial conference dates have been
cancelled. The petitioner tendered a certified copy of the journal entries of
HC/5963/23 of the High Court of Galle. According to which the indictment
was served on 12.02.2024 and this matter was set for pre-trial on
25.04.2024and mentioned 19.06.2024 and now it is to be mentioned again
on 30.01.2025. Accordingly, from the point of serving the indictment it has
now taken almost ten months and the trial date is yet to be fixed. The matter
for determination and consideration is, whether this delay in these
circumstances will be exceptional for the purposes of considering bail under
Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The
mere delay or the lapse of time does not amount to being exceptional unless
such delay is excessive or oppressive. Pre-trial conference is a joint exercise
with the participation of the prosecuting counsel, defence counsel and the
aggrieved party or the counsel if any, appearing on behalf of the aggrieved
party, of course presided over by the High Court Judge or the Recorder
Judge. Thus, it is the obligation of all the parties to endeavour to conclude
the same within the prescribed 3 month period though presided over by the
High Court Judge. In the present instance it appears from the journal
entries that the Accused himself has acquiesced and at least passively

--- Page 4 ---
participated in the cancellation of the pre-trial conference and the in the
postponement beyond 3 months without any objection.
4. Of course, the procedure prescribed by section 195A of the Code of Criminal
procedure Act does require a pre-trial conference to be concluded within a
period not exceeding three months from the date on which the accused
appeared before the court and it is primarily the duty of the presiding judge
to ensure the adherence to the said mandatory time frames. However, in
the circumstances of this matter the petitioner is not entitled take
advantage of and cannot be heard to say that the said delay is excessive or
oppressive.
5. The prosecution has expeditiously filed the indictment within a reasonable
time. However, the pre-trial proceedings appear to have taken time initially
due to not providing all the documents. Then, as to the delay in calling and
receiving certain items of productions and the other delay in this instance
cannot entirety or primarily be attributed to conduct of an oppressive or
excessive nature on the part of the prosecution. It may appear to be
excessive in the context of section 195A (5), but it is the Judge who had
granted these dates and certain steps to obtain the productions have taken
some time. Upon the consideration of the totality of the facts and
circumstances it appears that the time taken is not unusual and unique to
this matter alone and this appears to be the usual lapse of time that is
common to all similar cases pending before the said High Court. No doubt,
the 2nd suspect is said to have no previous convictions. However, since the
lapse of time in context cannot be singularly considered as being oppressive
or excessive, this cannot be considered as being exceptional.
6. The next argument advanced is the apparent improbability in the
prosecution version as to the manner of recovery and arrest. It was
submitted that this suspect along with another is alleged to has been
arrested while in room of a hotel at Baddegama. According to the notes of
investigation at pages 16 and 17 of the certified copy annexed, when the
police officers arrived at the hotel two suspects were in the room of which

--- Page 6 ---
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for Bail
under and in terms of Section 83(2) of
the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance No. as
amended by Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Narcotics Bureau,
Colombo 01.
Court of Appeal Case No.
CA/BAL/0706/2023 2. The Officer-in-Charge,
Magistrate Court of Police Station,
Kuliyapitiya Pannala.
Case No. B 38805/2023 Complainants
Vs.
Gamaralalage Lanisha Rashani
Wikummala,
Thalammahera,
Pannala.
Suspect
AND NOW BETWEEN

--- Page 2 ---
Gamaralalage Indra Kumara,
No. 25/1,
Pamunuwatta,
Meerigama.
Petitioner
Vs.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Narcotics Bureau,
Colombo 01.
2. The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station,
Pannala.
3. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
Complainants-Respondents
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL: M.C.M. Imtiaz instructed by Anuradi Nakandala for the
Petitioner.
Malik Azeez, SC, for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON: 03.12.2024
DECIDED ON: 19.12.2024

--- Page 3 ---
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J.
1. This application for bail is preferred by the Petitioner on behalf of the
Accused Respondent under the provisions of Section 83(2) of the
Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. According to the
Petitioner, the suspect was arrested at her house on 07.10.2023. When
the Police arrived, another person (male) had escaped from the house.
It is common ground that the person who so left the house is Loku
Pathiranage Lahiru Rukshan the husband of the suspect. (vide-the B
report marked X-5) When he so retreated he has left behind his mobile
phone a jeep was also found in the compound of the house which
belongs to him. Therefore, it appears that the suspects husband had
in fact taken to his heels and escaped when the Police team approached
the house.
2. The suspect denies being in possession of any narcotics. However,
according to the Respondents, as depicted in the B Reports, the suspect
was having a parcel of heroin in a plastic bag in her hand when the
raiding team approached the house. It is also common ground that the
husband who escaped had been apprehended several days after whilst
being in possession of heroin. The portion marked X-10 of the B Report
X-5 also states that the said Loku Pathiranage Lahiru Rukshan has
previously been apprehended by several police stations in that area for
similar offences.
3. It was further submitted that the suspect has a child of three years,
who is said to be now cared for and looked after by her aging parents.
4. The learned State Counsel vehemently objected to this application, but
conceded that the indictment is yet to be forwarded as the Attorney
General is awaiting the IB Extracts.
5. The crux of the Petitioners submission is that it is improbable to expect
any ordinary person to hold a parcel containing 310 grammes of heroin
in her hand when a Police team is seen approaching the house. Her

--- Page 4 ---
husband who was there, appears to have taken to his heels just as the
raiding party was approached. In these circumstances, if the suspect
was conscious and knew that the parcel contained narcotics, it is highly
unlikely and improbable for her to have held on to it and keep it in her
hand. Therefore, the suspect was either unaware and ignorant as to the
contents of the bag or the B Reports do not narrate correctly the manner
of arrest and how she possessed the substance.
6. Secondly, the petitioner relies on the delay without instituting criminal
proceedings which is submitted to be excessive and oppressive. The
indictment or charges are yet to be preferred.
7. The arrest has taken place in October 2023. A period of one year and
two months has lapsed as at the date of the inquiry. The State Counsel
concedes the indictment is yet to be considered as the Attorney General
is yet to receive the IB extracts. The learned State Counsel is unable to
inform this Court as the present status of the IB extracts or of any
reason for the delay. This application for bail had been filed on
13.12.2023. The state had appeared on notice on 22.10.2024 on which
day this was fixed for the objections on 04.03.2024. However, in the
interim this was fixed for inquiry on 03.12.2024 and by letter dated
06.11.2024 the Hon. Attorney General was informed by the Registrar of
this Court that this will be taken up for inquiry on 03.12.2024 and has
also informed that objections if any be filed on or before 25.11.2024.
Accordingly, the matter was taken up for inquiry on 03.12.2024 on
which day, the State Counsel was heard. However, there was no
statement of objection filed of record. The State Counsel is unable to
inform as to a date or at least a probable time frame as to when charges
may be filed.
8. As such it is the opinion of this Court that the delay of one year and
two months considered in conjunctions with the said failure to explain
may be considered has been exceptional. It is well to remember that

--- Page 5 ---
when a person is denied of his liberty and held in detention those who
are responsible for the said deprivation should consciously and
diligently take necessary steps to diligently pursue with, finalize and
institute legal action. If a reasonable explanation for any delay is not
forthcoming such delay will be considered as being excessive or
oppressive. As held in Attorney General v. Ediriweera (S.C. Appeal
No. 100/2005), Delay is always a relative term and the question to be
considered is not whether there was mere explicable delay, as when
there is a backlog of cases, but whether there has been excessive or
oppressive delay and this always depends on the facts and
circumstances of the case.
9. Under section 83(2) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs
Ordinance bail may be considered only on exceptional circumstances.
However, to my mind this extremely stringent provision of section 83
on granting of bail certainly cannot become or be allowed to be used as
a means to incarcerate an accused person without instituting action or
concluding the trial for an indefinite and unreasonably long time
without a just cause. Thus, time in remand when considered in
conjunction with the failure to take meaningful steps to institute action
and diligently prosecute to a finality in context may create the
circumstances that can be considered exceptional. The time spent in
remand cannot be considered in the abstract to determine if its
exceptional. Similarly, the normal delay which occurs between the
arrest and trial, cannot by itself amount to an exceptional
circumstance. I do not say that delay per se may not amount to an
exceptional circumstance. If there is inordinate and unexplained delay,
it may very well be.
10. It is common ground that the suspects estranged husband was present
and did escape and retreat when the police party was approaching. He
said to be a person with a previous history of drug related offences.
Then, on the other hand, there is an apparent improbability of the

--- Page 6 ---
suspect keeping in her hand a parcel with heroine when the police are
seen approaching and her husband retreats. As stated above, either she
may have been unaware as to the content or the version of the police
may be incorrect. Whatever be the reason this circumstance considered
with the unexplained delay in our view amounts to a circumstance that
can be considered exceptional. Accordingly, we are inclined to grant bail
to the suspect on the following conditions.
1. cash bail in a sum of Rs. 100,000.00;
2. to provide two sureties who should execute bonds to the value of
Rs. 500,000.00 each;
3. the sureties should provide certificates from the Grama Sevaka
and police reports from respective residential areas of such
sureties;
4. to surrender the passport or any travel document of the suspect,
if she has any, to the Registrar of the Magistrates Court of
Kuliyapitiya; and
5. report to the Officer-in-Charge of the Pannala Police Station on
every last Sunday of the month before 12 noon.
This Application is accordingly allowed and the Registrar of this
Court is directed to transmit a copy of this order to the Registrar
of the Magistrates Court of Kuliyapitiya.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

Background of the dispute albeit in brief is as follows:
The 1st Petitioner Company provide Digital Transformation, e-Government,
Workflow Management, Secure Electronic Payment Automation,
Information Systems Security, and Mobil Enterprise Automation Solutions
in Sri Lanka. It provides local support & maintenance services, product
customizations, on-site post implementation technical support,
consumable supply, and logistics services for N Series Travel Document
Printing System to personize and issue N Series Travel Documents to the
citizens of Sri Lanka since the year 2003.
This Writ application pertains to the procurement of a supply of Five(05)
Million e-passports to the Department of Immigration and Emigration, and
the procurement of 750,000/- passports from the 13th and 14th
Respondents.

--- Page 14 ---

The Petitioners contends that they believe and have reason to believe in
the given circumstances, that the bidding process in relation to the
procurement of supply of Five (05) Million e-passports to the Department
of Immigration and Emigration, was compromised and /or tainted with
mala fides and/or subverted to unduly favour and assist certain vendors
and to the undue disadvantage of others. Further, the said procurement
process adopted as well as the process to purchase N-Series Travel
Documents from the 13th and 14th Respondents have been manipulated
and worked in a manner that is unlawful, arbitrary, capricious,
unreasonable, irrational, in violation of the Principles of Natural justice,
without due process, contrary to the legitimate expectations of the
Petitioners and with malice for collateral purposes.
The Petitioners state that the Petitioners are reasonably informed that
following the letter sent by the Petitioners to the National Procurement
Commission dated 18th September 2024 marked X57 and the recent
developments which took place following the Sri Lanka Presidential
Election 2024, the 6th Respondent and/or other interested parties
motivated by collateral purposes best known to such parties, are hurriedly
moving to proceed with the procurement of 750,000 Machine Readable
Passports from the 13th and 14th Respondents, and that plans are afoot to
immediately procure the said Passports at the behest of the 13th and 14th
Respondents.
The Petitioners further state that due to above reasons, grave and
irreparable loss, damage, harm, and severe prejudice, will be caused to the
Petitioners, and continue to be caused to them, and their interests, and
the reliefs claimed herein will be rendered nugatory, unless this Court
grant the interim reliefs sought through this application.

in order to overcome the present crisis faced by the country since
there are only thirteen thousand eighty (13080) blank passports left

Department of Immigration and Emigration is issuing an average of
one thousand (1000) passports per day and the stock which is
available will only be sufficient for 13 working days and thereafter
no single blank passport will be available in order to meet emergency
requirements in Sri Lanka.
2. The Petitioner has suggested by letter dated 30/09/2024 to make
use of Epic Travel Document Personalization System (Epic TDPS)
which is the existing travel document system at the Department of
Immigration and Emigration to personalize any passport
government may decide to procure from any vendor subject to a
license fee not more than 150 US Dollars per a passport until a new
TDPS system is procured by the Government of Sri Lanka.
3. The Hon. Attorney General has received instructions from the
Controller General of Department of Immigration and Emigration
that the proposal submitted by Epic Lanka is not necessary in order
to obtain new passports. However, there is a requirement to do a
changeover to remove two security features installed by the
Petitioners, thus they are in agreement to effect a payment for the
same.
15 | P age

--- Page 16 ---
CA-Writ / 0609-2024
On behalf of the Controller, learned Additional Solicitor General suggests
that both parties discussed about the technical features and the related
payments at a mutually convenient date in order to reach a settlement.
The Acting Controller of Immigration and Emigration undertakes to
appoint a five-member committee to negotiate with the Petitioners officials
and the committee will be appointed on or before 02/10/2024.
The Controller of Immigration and Emigration will take urgent steps to
procure seven hundred and fifty thousand (750,000) normal N-Series
Passports to resolve the existing crisis.
The Learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioners states that the
compromise is agreed to by the Petitioners voluntarily despite being
advised of the sustainability of the guides assorted in terms of the Petition

mentioned in the minute.
The learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioners filed a motion on
03.12.2024 to vary the inquiry date fixed on 09.12.2024. Order was made
accordingly and the matter was re-fixed for inquiry on 23.01.2025. This
date too no mention about the extension of the stay order.
On 09.10.2024 the learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioners filed a
motion and move the Court to call this case on that date. Accordingly, the
matter was called in Court and the learned Presidents Counsel for the
Petitioners moved the Court to extend the interim order until 23.01.2025.
The learned Counsel for the 13th and 14th Respondents had objected to the
said application on the basis that there is no interim order extended after
06.11.2024 up to on that day.
Born out from the Court record the Learned Presidents Counsel for the
Petitioners had not moved to extend the interim order as it is his duty to
make an application for the extension of the interim order. At the same
time the Counsel for the 13th and 14th Respondent filed papers to vacate
the interim order and the inquiry was fixed on 09.12.2024.
This Court has no objection in extending the interim order on the
application of the Petitioners, if there should not be any objection by the
affected parties. In this application the 13th and 14th Respondents are
vehemently objecting for the extension. As such, there must be a legal
basis for the Court to extend the interim order.
17 | P age

--- Page 18 ---
CA-Writ / 0609-2024
In Jayasinghe and Another v Pedris and Another [2005] 1 SLR 29 the
Court held that:
(ii) This is an appeal able order under section 754(2). The defendants
do not disclose exceptional circumstances warranting the exercise of
the reversionary jurisdiction. The only excuse given is that the
defendants attorney-at-law had taken down the wrong date, it is not
an excuse, and his negligence cannot be considered as an exceptional
circumstance.
In Pakiyanathan v Singaraja [1991] 2 SLR 205 the Court held that:
It is necessary to make a distinction between mistake or
inadvertence of an attorney-at-law or party and negligence. A mere
mistake can generally be excused; but not negligence, especially
continuing negligence. The decision will depend on the facts and
circumstances of each case. The Court will in granting relief ensure
that it's order will not condone or in any manner encourage the neglect
of professional duties expected of Attorneys-at-Law.
In light of the above judgments, negligent of a Counsel cannot be condoned
and this Cour under no circumstances will encourage the neglection of
duties of a Counsel. As such, in this case we see no basis to extend the
interim order.
Interim order is a discretionary remedy and the Petitioners cannot ask for
an interim order as a right. In such a situation he must be vigilant in
making application for extension. In this case, no application made for
extension, not once, twice. It shows there is a neglect on the part of the
Petitioners.
It is pertinent to draw the doctrine of  vigilantibus non dormientibus jura
subveniunt. The maxim is relevant as the Court look after the people those
are vigilant and not those who sleep over their rights.
18 | P age

--- Page 19 ---

Hence, considering the nature and the circumstances of the case, I
conclude that the application of the Petitioners to extend the interim order
cannot be considered at this stage.
Therefore, the objections raised by the Counsel for the 13th and 14th
Respondents is hereby accepted.
As agreed by all parties this matter is fixed for inquiry 23.01.2025.

M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J.

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an application for revision in
terms of Article 138 of the Constitution of the
Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka,

Chairman,

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 3 ---
Assemblies of God Ceylon
No.248, Negombo Road,
Ja  Ela.
PETITIONER - RESPONDENT  RESPONDENT
BEFORE : M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J. &
M. Ahsan. R. Marikar J.
COUNSEL : Nalin Ladduwahetty P.C. with Hafeel
Farisz and Ranjith Samarasekara for
the Respondent Petitioner- Petitioner.
Lakshan Dias for the Petitioner -
Respondent - Respondent.
ARGUED ON : 22.10.2024
DECIDED ON : 18.12.2024
M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J.
Introduction
The 1st and 2nd Respondent-Petitioner-Petitioners (hereinafter referred to as the
Petitioners) have filed this revision application against the Petitioner-
Respondent-Respondent (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent), seeking to
revise the judgment delivered by the High Court Judge of Puttalam on 14th
December 2023. The High Court Judge had refused to revise the order made by
the learned Magistrate of Anamaduwa on 13th October 2022 in an application
instituted under Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act No. (hereinafter referred to as the Primary Court Procedure Act).
Additionally, the Petitioners seek to have the aforementioned order of the
Magistrate be set aside.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 4 ---
Factual background
The Respondent initially filed a Petition on 7th February 2022 in the Magistrates
Court of Anamaduwa under Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts Procedure
Act, which was subsequently amended on 8th March 2022. The learned
Presidents Counsel for the Petitioners alleged that the Respondent altered the
scope of the application in the amended Petition. However, as this matter was
not raised by the Petitioners in the original Court, I will not treat it as an issue
for determination by this Court.
Along with the information submitted to the Magistrates Court, the Respondent
also filed several documents to support his contention1.
In response, the 1st Petitioner submitted an affidavit along with several
documents to establish his possession2.
The Respondent filed a counter-affidavit and submitted documents to challenge
the Petitioners claim of possession3.
Analysis
It is undisputed that the subject matter of this application is the Bethel Church
located in Serukale, Siyambalagaswewa, Anamaduwa.
The Respondent claims to be the President, Chief Priest, and Head of the
Administrative Board of Directors of the Assembly of God of Ceylon,
established under Act No. . He asserts that approximately 45 pastors
serve under him, including the 1st and 2nd Petitioners. The 1st Petitioner serves as
a pastor at Bethel Church, located in Serukale, Siyabalagaswewa, Anamaduwa,
which was constructed using funds contributed by the devotees of the said
Chapter. The Respondent further states that the Church was built on land
purchased from its permit holder, Nirosha Priyangani. According to the
Respondent, the Assembly of God of Ceylon is the rightful owner and
custodian of the Church.
1 At pages 184 to 278.
2 At pages 326 to 366.
3 At pages 283 to 319.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 5 ---
According to the Petitioners, the 1st Petitioner obtained membership and a license
to evangelize on behalf of the Assembly of God of Ceylon around 2007, while
the 2nd Petitioner obtained the same around 2015. The Petitioners state that this
occurred after they began serving as priests at Bethel Church, Serukale,
Siyambalagaswewa, Anamaduwa, in 2005. They further assert that they had
already commenced their work as priests in the Siyambalagaswewa area around
the year 2000, well before 2005.
The Respondent stated that the Assembly of God of Ceylon received complaints
from devotees alleging that the 1st Petitioner had committed rape against the
female manager of the Church and that his wife, the 2nd Petitioner, was engaged
in an illicit affair involving undisciplined behaviour. Although the Respondent
made the serious allegation of rape, a grave offense under penal law, no
evidence, such as a police complaint, was produced.
According to the Respondent, these complaints were investigated by a
committee appointed by the Assembly of God of Ceylon. Based on the
investigation, the Petitioners were temporarily suspended from their roles as
pastors and servants of the Church on 21st November 2021. However, the
Petitioners, in a communication dated 23rd November 2021, rejected the
Assemblys decision. Subsequently, they resigned from their membership in the
Assembly of God of Ceylon, effective from 25th November 2021.
The Respondent alleges that, following their resignation, the Petitioners forcibly
occupied the Church premises for their personal use. Furthermore, the
Respondent claims that the Petitioners began using the Churchs address as their
personal address, despite their actual residence being located elsewhere.
The Petitioners agree with the Respondent in acknowledging that
Hettiarachchige Nirosha Priyangani is the rightful owner of the land on which
the Church stands. In support of this, the Petitioners submitted an affidavit sworn
by Nirosha Priyangani4, along with the counter-affidavit. The Grant issued in her
name and the corresponding plan5 were also attached. Additionally, the Register
4 X 1.
5 A 1 and A 2.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 6 ---
of Grants under the Land Development Ordinance6 submitted with the counter
affidavit further establishes Nirosha Priyanganis title to the land.
In her affidavit, Nirosha Priyangani states that, around 2005, she granted
permission to the 1st Petitioner, Dilhan Peiris, and a person named Anton Mee
Kauper Martin to build a Church on her land. She further states that she entered
into an agreement to sell7 the land to Anton Mee Kauper Martin. Nirosha
Priyangani, the landowner, categorically asserts that the Assembly of God of
Ceylon or its Chairman has no legal title to the Church situated on her land.
These well-established facts contradict the Respondents claim that the
Assembly of God of Ceylon owns the property, despite its legal capacity to hold
property.
Affidavits from three priests8 and four Christian devotees confirm that the 1st
Petitioner built the Church and conducted services there from 2005 onwards. The
devotees9, in their affidavits, further confirm that they have assisted Pastor
Manoj Dilhan Peiris, the 1st Petitioner, in his work over the years and that the 1st
Petitioner managed the affairs of the Church. Additionally, the parents of
children who participated in the projects conducted at the Church have also
provided affidavits affirming the 1st Petitioners possession of the Church for the
past seven years10.
The Respondent submitted similar affidavits, allegedly from neighbours and
devotees of the Church, stating that the 1st Petitioner is not in possession of the
Church. The affirmants further assert that the 1st Petitioner was appointed as a
priest of the Church by the Assembly of God of Ceylon, and since he has been
removed, he is no longer entitled to conduct services or stay at the Church11. All
the affidavits state that the 1st Petitioner does not reside at the Church but only
conducts services there. It is also stated that the Church was built with funds
provided by the devotees. According to the Respondent, the electricity and water
6 A 3.
7 A 4.
8 At pages 332 and 334 of the appeal brief.
9 At pages 335, 336 and 338, 339.
10 At page 340 to 344 of the appeal brief.
11 At pages 228 to 273 of the appeal brief.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 7 ---
bills for the Church were paid using funds from the devotees and the Assembly
of God of Ceylon. However, the electricity bills filed in the record are in the
name of the 1st Petitioner.
In support of the fact that the Church was the property of Assembly of God of
Ceylon, the Respondent submitted a letter12. However, the said letter itself refers
to the Church as your church (ඔබගේ ගේවස්ථානය) indicating that the Church
belongs to the 1st Petitioner. In the letter, the Church was accepted as a project
under the Assembly of God of Ceylon. Accordingly, an identification number
was also issued.
The Respondent contended that the Church is not a residential place but a place
where people gather for prayers. The Petitioners have not claimed that they
reside in the Church. However, it is important to note that to possess a building,
one does not necessarily need to reside in it. Conducting religious prayers and
similar activities can constitute physical possession. In the case of Jayasinghe
and others v. Loku Bandara13, His Lordship Samayawardhane J. held that actual
possession does not require uninterrupted physical presence throughout the day.
The Respondents contention is that he had constructive possession of the
Church. However, it is important to note that this possession was through the
Petitioners, the rival party.
His Lordship Samayawardhane J., sitting in the Court of Appeal (as His Lordship
then was) in the aforementioned case of Jayasinghe and others v. Loku
Bandara14, concluded that in an application under Section 66 of the Primary
Courts Procedure Act, if the dispute is between the licensee and the licensor, the
licensees possession cannot be considered as the possession of the licensor.
There is no allegation by the Respondent that he was forcibly evicted from the
Church. His contention is that the Assembly of God of Ceylon had continuous
possession from the inception of the Bethel Church.
12 At page 220 of the appeal brief.
13 [2019]2 Sri L.R. page 202.
14 Ibid.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 8 ---
In the case of Iqbal v. Majedudeen and Others15, it was stated that the law
recognizes two types of possession.
i. When a person has direct physical control over a thing at a given time,
he is said to have actual possession of it.
ii. A person has constructive possession when he, though not in actual
possession, has both the power and the intention at a given time to
exercise dominium or control over a thing either directly or through
another person.
In my view, the Petitioners' involvement in religious activities as members of the
Assembly of God of Ceylon is somewhat akin to an activity carried out under a
license granted by another, acting as an agent. Once the license is revoked, the
right to conduct activities under that license ceases to exist; however, the
possessory rights would not be extinguished.
In an application under Section 66 of the Primary Courts Procedure Act, the
Magistrate is not required to investigate title. However, in the case of
Shanmugasundara Kurukkal Sri Skandarajah Kurukkal v. Ramalingham
Ranarajah and Sixteen Others16 (C.A.), His Lordship A. H. M. D. Nawaz J., (as
His Lordship then was), observed as follows:
The Magistrate is not required to investigate the title of the disputed land or the
rights of the administrative body. In fact, he can use the evidence of title merely
to guide and aid his mind in coming to a decision upon the question of
possession, but he is precluded from deciding questions of title alone.
According to the Grant issued by the State, the subject land belongs to Nirosha
Priyangani, and therefore, she should be considered the owner of the building
standing on it as well. The dominion of a property is naturally vested in its true
owner. In this case, the true owner, Nirosha Priyangani, has affirmed in an
affidavit that she authorized the 1st Petitioner to build on her land and to maintain
the Church within the premises.
15 [1999]3 Sri L.R. 213.
16 [1987] 1 Sri.L.R. 94.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 9 ---
However, as I have already stated above, the primary consideration in an
application of this nature is not the title, but rather the actual physical possession.
Based on the analysis of the facts outlined in this judgment, I am of the view that
the Petitioners were in physical possession of the Bethel Church on the date the
information was filed, and that the Respondent had not been dispossessed within
the two months immediately preceding the filing of the information.
Breach of the peace
One of the arguments advanced by the Petitioners (Respondents in the
Magistrates Court) was that there was no breach of the peace to invoke the
jurisdiction of the Magistrates Court under Section 66(1) of the Primary Courts
Procedure Act. As it was held in the case of Velupillai and others v. Sivanathan17
and followed by several other decisions, including Punchi Nona v. Padumasena
and others18, when information is filed under Section 66(1)(a) of the Act, the
formation of the opinion as to whether a breach of the peace is threatened or
likely is left to the Police Officer inquiring into the dispute. The Magistrate is
not required to inquire whether a breach of peace is threatened or likely, as
jurisdiction is vested in the Magistrate to inquire into and make a determination
on the dispute.
However, when an information is filed under Section 66(1)(b), it is incumbent
upon the Magistrate to first satisfy himself as to whether there is a threat or
likelihood of a breach of the peace.
Nevertheless, in the recent case of Jayasinghe and others v. Loku Bandara19
(C.A.), His Lordship Samayawardhane J., having scrutinized Section 66(1)(a)
and (b) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act, the repealed Section 62 of the
Administration of Justice Law, and the corresponding Section 145 of the Indian
Code of Criminal Procedure, held that: When first information is filed under
Section 66 (1) of the Primary Couts Procedure Act, irrespective of whether the
first information was filed by the Police or a party to the dispute, the Magistrate
17 [1993] 2 Sri L.R., 123.
18 [1994]2 Sri L.R. ,117.
19 Supra note 13.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 10 ---
is automatically vested with jurisdiction under Section 66(2) to inquire into and
determine the matter. There is no further requirement for the Magistrate to
ascertain whether the breach of the peace is threatened or likely.
In any event, I observe that the learned Magistrate, in her impugned order, has
carefully analysed the question of whether there was a threatened breach of the
peace. The learned Magistrate has, inter alia, referred to a letter written to the
Assembly of God of Ceylon by the Petitioner, in which it is stated that the
devotees of the Bethel Church have divided into two factions, thereby creating a
potential breach of the peace.
The Respondent has produced a letter signed by several individuals stating that
the devotees are agitated due to the conduct of the 1st Petitioner, and there is an
imminent threat of a breach of the peace20. Additionally, an agent of the
Respondent has sent a letter to the Officer in Charge of the Pallama Police
Station, seeking police assistance to establish their title21.
Even when the evidence presented to the learned Magistrate is examined, this
Court observes that two factions have submitted affidavits in support of the
Petitioner and the Respondent, which contradict each other.
Consequently, based on the available evidence, I am satisfied that there was a
potential threat of a breach of the peace, as correctly concluded by the learned
Magistrate and upheld by the learned High Court Judge.
The Petitioners raised the following grounds to impugn the order of the learned
High Court Judge.
(i) There were no exceptional grounds
(ii) The learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the principles of law
regarding constructive possession.
20 At page 274 of the appeal brief.
21 At page 277 of the appeal brief.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 11 ---
(iii) The learned High Court Judge erred in law and thereby caused grave
miscarriage of justice on the Petitioners by failing to analyse the purported
dispossession by the Petitioners.
I will begin by considering a judgment delivered by this Court on a similar issue.
In the case of Shanmugasundara Kurukkal Sri Skandarajah Kurukkal v.
Ramalingham Ranarajah and Sixteen others22 (C.A.), His Lordship Nawaz J.
considered a dispute between a Kurukkal (or Poosari) and the administrative
body of a temple. His Lordship examined whether the possession of the Kurukkal
satisfied the requirements of possession under Section 68.
According to the facts of the case, the administrative body of the temple claimed
to have some kind of right to summarily remove a priest. His Lordship
considered what gave them this power? Did they appoint him as a priest? If so,
did it entitle them to oust him in the manner in which he was removed?
It was an admitted fact that the members of the administrative body broke open
the closed door of the temple, to which the Kurukkal had the keys, secured it
with new locks, and took possession from him.
The learned Magistrate ordered that the Kurukkal, who had been dispossessed,
be restored to possession.
In the revision application filed against the said order, the learned High Court
Judge held that since the temple and its properties are always vested in the
administrative body of the temple, the body has the power to remove a priest at
any time. It was further held that merely having custody of the keys did not
amount to possession within the meaning of Section 68(3) of the Primary Courts
Procedure Act. The Kurukkal only held ritual rights to conduct the pooja and
should vindicate those rights through an action in the District Court.
Consequently, the learned High Court Judge overturned the decision of the
learned Magistrate.
22 CA(PHC) No.41/2004, Court of Appeal minutes dated 08.08.2018.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 12 ---
His Lordship observed that the learned High Court Judge overturned the decision
of the learned Primary Court Judge on the grounds that the possession of the
Kurukkal could not be equated to exclusive possession, similar to the possession
of a Bank Manager or a Hotel Manager.
In analysing the judgment of the learned High Court Judge, His Lordship
considered several judgments in which the elements of possession were
discussed. In the case Iqbal v. Majedudeen and others23, His Lordship U.D.Z.
Gunawardana J. observed that the words forcibly dispossessed in Section 68(3)
of the Primary Courts Procedure Act mean that dispossession took place against
the will of the person entitled to possess, and without the authority of the law.
In the course of the judgment, His Lordship Nawaz J. observed as follows:
In fact, there is no evidence, so to speak, to establish that the Respondent has
actual possession of this temple. It was the Appellant who had been in
possession of the temple premises by virtue of the fact that his presence therein
was necessitated by his functions and the fact that the key to the temple had
been in his custody at the relevant time of dispossession connotes actual
possession of the temple premises on the part of the Appellant. (Emphasis
added)
Finally, His Lordship Nawaz J., held that actual possession should be real and
tangible, meaning there should be effective occupation and control of the
property.
His Lordship concluded that the administrative body had ousted the Kurukkal,
who had been in possession of the temple premises, within a period of two
months preceding the date the information was filed.
The facts of the above case are almost identical to the case at hand. The parties
are not at variance that the Petitioners conducted the service of the Bethel Church
as Pastors.
23 [1999]3 Sri L.R. 213.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 13 ---
Consequently, this judicial precedence supports the view that the 1st and 2nd
Petitioners were in possession of the Bethel Church.
Whether there are exceptional circumstances
The primary consideration before examining the merits of a revision application
is whether exceptional circumstances exist that justify the Courts intervention,
as this serves as the gateway to relief.
The Petitioners have sought the exercise of this Courts revisionary jurisdiction
with respect to both the order of the learned High Court Judge and the order of
the learned Magistrate.
In the case of Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd and others v. Mercantile Hotels
Management Ltd24, Sharvananda C.J. observed that:
It is settled law that the exercise of revisionary powers of the Appellate Court
is confined to cases in which exceptional circumstances exist warranting its
intervention.
In the case of Divisional Secretary Kalutara v. Kalupahana Mestrige Jayathissa
and others25, the Supreme Court observed that:
It must be noted that the Respondents had invoked revisionary jurisdiction of
this court, which is discretionary remedy. Thus, if relief to be granted, the party
seeking the relief has to establish that, not only the impugned Order is illegal,
but also the nature of the illegality is such, that it shocks the conscience of the
court.
Based on the reasons outlined above, it is my considered view that the Petitioners
have demonstrated that the impugned orders of the learned Magistrate and the
learned High Court Judge are manifestly erroneous and, therefore, shock the
conscience of this Court, warranting intervention.
24 [1987]1 Sri L.R. at page 05.
25 SC Appeals 246, 247, 249, 250/14.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 14 ---
Conclusion
In light of the above analysis, I hold that the Respondent cannot be considered
as having had constructive possession, and that the Petitioners were in
continuous actual physical possession prior to and at the time of filing the
information in the Magistrates Court. Furthermore, there was no dispossession
of either party within two months of the filing of the information.
For the foregoing reasons, I hold that the learned High Court Judge erred in
upholding the order of the learned Magistrate by misinterpreting the pertinent
statutory provisions and the relevant principles of constructive possession.
After considering all the submitted materials and the arguments of both Counsel,
this Court concludes that both the impugned orders of the learned Magistrate and
the learned High Court Judge cannot stand. Consequently, I allow the application
and, acting in revision, set aside the order of the learned High Court Judge dated
14th December 2023, as well as the order of the learned Magistrate dated 13th
October 2022.
I confirm the Petitioners' possession and direct that they be restored to possession
immediately, if they have been evicted.
Application allowed, subject to a cost of Rs. 50,000/-.
The Registrar of this Court is directed to communicate to the High Court of
Puttalam.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
M. Ahsan. R. Marikar J.
I Agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 4 ---

Dhammika Ganepola, J.
When this matter was taken up for support on 07 October 2024, the
learned Counsel for the Petitioners made submissions in support of the
application. However, the learned Counsel for the 13th Respondent took
up several preliminary objections in relation to maintainability of this
application. The Petitioners in this application are inter alia seeking the
following reliefs:
 Writs of Certiorari quashing the quit notice [P19] issued by the
3rd Respondent;
 the 1st Respondent decision dated 18th March 2024[P11(ii)]
granting a permit to the 9th Respondent to cultivate the land
depicted as CC and A in the Sub Division Plan No.
Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September 2016 and Sub Division Plan
No. KA/DSO/2020/502, and
 Writs of Mandamus directing the 1st Respondent to grant the
possession to the Petitioners of the land depicted in Lot 238 of
Village Plan No.140[P1] and also depicted as CC and A in the
Sub Division Plan No. Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September
2016[P2] and Sub Division Plan No. KA/DSO/2020/502 [P3] and
 grant a long-term lease to the Petitioners in respect of the
property in subject.
The Petitioners state that they have been cultivating rubber and other
crops in Lot No.328 of P1 and Lot CC of P2 for more than 40 years. The
predecessor of the Petitioners, one Ranpati Pathirage Rajapaksha had
come into know that the said property is a State land and had taken steps
to legalize his possession in around 1990 making multiple requests to
various authorities. However, no inquiry has been held in respect of such
requests. The Petitioners state that the 1st Petitioner and the 2nd and 3rd
Petitioners [wife and the children of deceased] inherited the property in
subject after the demise of the said predecessor in 2020.
In support of the position that the Petitioners are in possession of the
subject property, the Petitioners have submitted several receipts
pertaining to payment of acres tax, receipts on payment of the rubber

--- Page 5 ---
replanting project, rubber replanting permits and rubber replanting
payment receipts in respect of the impugned property. Apart from
tendering such documents, the Petitioners also rely upon the permit
P11(ii) issued by 9th Respondent in invoking writ jurisdiction of this Court.
It appears that said permit P11(ii) has been issued by the 9th Respondent
to cultivate the land without conducting a formal inquiry into the requests
made by the Petitioners to obtain leasehold rights to the property.
The Petitioners assert that under the above circumstances, the materials
and evidence to form an opinions formed by the competent authority to
evict the Petitioners from the impugned property are wrongful and that
the decision to evict the Petitioners is unreasonable and irrational.
In the case of Udagedara Waththe Anusha KumarinNikaathagoda vs.
Jayasinghe Mudiyanselage Chamila Indika Jayasinghe, Divisional Secretary
and Others CA/WRIT/293/2017 decided on 18.11.2019 His Lordship Justice
Arjuna Obeyesekere has held;
This Court wishes to emphasize, for the avoidance of any doubt that
the Competent Authority is not required in terms of the Act to carry
out an inquiry of the title of the person who is in unauthorized
possession of such land.
The principle then is that while no inquiry is needed to form an
opinion, there should be a rational basis to form the opinion that the
State is lawfully entitled to the land. The rational basis should satisfy
the Wednesbury test of reasonableness. Thus, a Competent
Authority would be acting reasonably if he were acting on the basis
of a Surveyor Generals plan, even if the occupant is claiming
prescription. The Competent Authority is not expected to, and
indeed is precluded from, carrying out an inquiry
Accordingly, a requirement exists for the Court to consider whether there
was a rational basis for the competent authority to form an opinion that
the State is lawfully entitled to the land. In light of the above, the Court is
of the view that this Court should consider whether the competent
authority had sufficient material to arrive at such opinion and as to
whether the competent authority has taken into consideration relevant
matters when forming such opinions.
The Honorable Attorney General has taken up the stance that the instant
application should not be entertained as the material facts of the case are

--- Page 6 ---
in dispute. The Petitioners state that the 6th Respondent who drew up the
Subdivision Plan No. Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September 2016 [P2] had
demarcated the property as inclusive of private property of the Petitioners.
It is stated that there is an ongoing dispute in respect of the property
between the Petitioners and the 9th Respondent before the District Court
of Matugama bearing No. L/5175/2024. However, it is important to
observe that the Petitioners in their written submissions have stated that
they do not wish to challenge the legality of the said plans in the instant
application and that no such relief has been sought in respect of the
legality of said plans.
Additionally, on behalf of the 13th Respondents, several preliminary
objections such as delay, futility and misrepresentation of material facts
have been taken up. However, the considering the circumstances and the
facts involved in the application, this Court is of the view that it is
appropriate to consider such objections at the stage of hearing.
Based on the above and the circumstances of the application I am inclined
to issue formal notices on the Respondents.
It is observed that unless this Court stay the operation of the quit notice
marked P19 until the final determination of this application, the
application will be rendered nugatory. Accordingly, I issue the stay order
suspending the operation of the quit notice P19 until the final
determination of this application.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
Damith Thotawatta, J.
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC
OF SRI LANKA

in terms of Article 138 of the Constitution of
the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri
Lanka.
Court of Appeal Officer-In-Charge,
Revision Application No: Police Station,
CA (PHC) APN 118/2024 Yatawatta.
COMPLAINANT
High Court of Matale Vs.
Case No: MT REV 155/2019 Ekanayaka Mudiyanselage Pahala
Gedara Ekanayake,

--- Page 2 ---
AND BETWEEN

CLAIMANT-PETITIONER

2. The Hon. Attorney General,

Colombo 12.
RESPONDENTS
AND NOW BETWEEN
Dodamwala Upasaka Gedara Sajeewani
Lalanthi,
Lakshahena C, Udasgiriya,
Matale.
CLAIMANT-PETITIONER-PETITIONER

--- Page 3 ---
Vs.
1. Officer-In-Charge,
Police Station,
Yatawatta.
COMPLAINANT-RESPONDENT-
RESPONDENT
2. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
RESPONDENT-RESPONDENT
Before : Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
: P. Kumararatnam, J.
Counsel : Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku and
Shannon Tillekerathne instructed by Nihara
Randeniya for the Petitioner.
: Osward Perera, S.C. for the State.
Supported on : 182024
Order on : 172024

--- Page 4 ---
Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
This is an application preferred by the claimant-petitioner-petitioner (hereinafter
referred to as the petitioner) seeking to invoke the discretionary remedy of
revision granted to this Court by Article 138 of The Constitution.
This matter was supported for notice on the respondent-respondents mentioned
in the petition, and also for an order staying the operation of the order dated 112024 by the learned High Court Judge of the Provincial High Court of Central
Province Holden in Matale, and also the order dated 052019 by the learned
Magistrate of Matale, until the final conclusion of this application.
The learned State Counsel who represented the Hon. Attorney General as well
as the complainant-respondent-respondent objected to the issuance of formal
notice in this regard and also the stay orders as sought on the basis that there
exist no obvious exceptional grounds for this Court to issue notice.
This is a matter where the accused person mentioned in the petition has been
charged before the Magistrates Court of Matale in Case Number 56190 for
having transported Mahogany and Gini Sapu timber valued at Rs. 62,717.92/=
in the vehicle bearing number 226-9439 without having a valid permit in terms
of the Forest Ordinance, which is an offence punishable in terms of section 25(2)
read with section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended.
The accused mentioned has pleaded guilty to the charge before the learned
Magistrate of Matale, and subsequently, has been sentenced.
Thereafter, the learned Magistrate of Matale has called upon the registered owner
of the vehicle involved in the offence to show cause as to why the vehicle should
not be confiscated in terms of section 40 of the Forest Ordinance.
At the inquiry held in that regard, the petitioner, being the registered owner of
the vehicle, has given evidence and another witness has also been called upon
to give evidence on behalf of the registered owner.

--- Page 5 ---
At the conclusion of the inquiry, the learned Magistrate of Matale, of his order
dated 052019, has decided to confiscate the vehicle involved in the offence
on the basis that the registered owner has failed to establish that she has taken
the necessary precautions to prevent the offence being committed, and also that
she has had the knowledge of the accused committing the offence.
The petitioner has preferred an application in revision seeking to challenge the
said order before the Provincial High Court of Central Province Holden in Matale.
The learned High Court Judge of Matale of his judgment dated 112024 has
dismissed the revision application of the petitioner on the basis that he finds no
reason to interfere with the order of the learned Magistrate of Matale.
The petitioner has preferred the instant application before this Court seeking to
challenge the order of the learned Magistrate of Matale, as well as the judgment
of the learned High Court Judge of the Provincial High Court of Central Province
Holden in Matale.
It is settled law that the Court of Appeal will intervene using its power of granting
the discretionary remedy of revision only under exceptional circumstances.
I would like to quote from the case of Sadi Banda Vs. Officer-In-Charge of
Norton Bridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33, which I find relevant in the
above context.
The revisionary power of Court is a discretionary power. This is an
extraordinary jurisdiction which is exercised by the Court and the grant of
relief is entirely dependent of the Court. The grant of such relief is of course
a matter entirely in the discretion of the Court, and always be dependent on
the circumstances of each case. Existence of exceptional circumstances is
the process by which the extraordinary power of revision should be adopted.
The exceptional circumstances would vary from case to case and their
degree of exceptionality must be correctly assessed and gauged by the Court
taking into consideration all antecedent circumstances using the yardstick

--- Page 6 ---
whether a failure of justice would occur unless revisionary powers are
invoked.
It was held in the case of Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels
Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 that;
It is settled law that the exercise of the revisionary powers of the appellate
Court is confined to cases in which exceptional circumstances exist
warranting its intervention.
In the case of Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report
Volume IV page 47), it was stated that;
Revision is a discretionary remedy and will not be available unless the
application discloses circumstances which shocks the conscience of the Court.
In the case of Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365, it
was observed that;
Revisionary powers should be exercised where a miscarriage of justice has
occasioned due to a fundamental rule of procedure being violated, but only
when a strong case is made out amounting to a positive miscarriage of justice.
It was held in the case of Rustom Vs. Hapangama and Co. 1978/79 2 SLR 225
that;
Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case there are no
such exceptional circumstances disclosed as would cause the Appellate
Court to exercise its discretion and grant relief by way of revision. Unless
there was something illegal about the order made by the trial judge which
has deprived the petitioner of some right, the justice of the case required that
the Court of Appeal would not in the circumstances of this case grant the
petitioner the indulgence of exercising its revisionary powers.

--- Page 7 ---
The proviso of section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Forest
(Amendment) Act No. , under which the learned Magistrate of Matale
has allowed the petitioner to show cause as to why the vehicle involved in this
incident, namely the vehicle numbered 226-9439, should not be confiscated
reads as follows:
Provided that in any case where the owner of such tools, vehicles,
implements and machines used in the commission of such offence is
a third party, no order of confiscation shall be made if such owner
proves to the satisfaction of the Court that he has taken all
precautions to prevent the use of such tools, vehicles, implements,
cattle and machines, as the case may be, for the commission of the
offence.
Our Superior Courts have held the constant view that all precautions stated in
the section does not mean every possible precaution, but precautions that could
have been taken under the given facts and the circumstances. It is well-settled
law that in an inquiry of this nature, it is incumbent upon the owner of the
vehicle to satisfy the Court that he or she took reasonably possible precautions
to prevent the commission of the offence, and also had no knowledge of such an
offence being committed.
As correctly determined by the learned Magistrate of Matale, as well as the
learned High Court Judge of Matale, the petitioner giving evidence before the
Magistrates Court has clearly admitted that she had the knowledge of the timber
being transported in the vehicle belonging to her. The driver of the vehicle,
namely the accused, who was charged before the Magistrates Court has
informed her of the fact of loading timber to the vehicle to be transported
elsewhere.
There is nothing in the evidence to show that the petitioner took any steps to
inquire from the driver whether he is going to transport timber that is permitted

--- Page 8 ---
to be transported without a permit or at least what kind of timber he is
transporting and its destination.
This shows that the petitioner clearly had the knowledge of the offence being
committed and also has failed to take reasonable precautions to prevent the
offence from being committed.
Hence, it is the view of this Court that the learned Magistrate of Matale was
correct in confiscating the vehicle, and the learned High Court Judge of Matale
was correct in determining that he has no reasons to interfere by exercising the
revisionary jurisdiction granted to the said High Court in terms of Article 154P
of The Constitution.
For the reasons as considered above, this Court finds no reason to issue a formal
notice in relation to this application or to grant stay orders as sought by the
petitioner.
Accordingly, the application is dismissed without the formal notice being issued.
The Registrar of the Court is directed to communicate this order to the Provincial
High Court of the Central Province Holden in Matale, and also to the Magistrates
Court of Matale for information.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
P. Kumararatnam, J.
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for Bail
under and in terms of Section 83(2) of
the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance No. as
amended by Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No.
The Officer-in-Charge,
Criminal Intelligence Analysis and
Prevention Division,
Court of Appeal Case No. No. 145, Main Street, Battaramulla.
CA/BAL/0102/2024 Complainant
High Court of Gampaha Vs.
Case No. HC- 206/2021
Samaraweera Arachchige Jeewan
Perera.
Accused
AND NOW BETWEEN
Nandinahewa Mangalika,
No. 299/6,
Gemunu Mawatha,
Kirindiwela.
Petitioner

--- Page 2 ---
Vs.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,
Criminal Intelligence Analysis and
Prevention Division,
No. 145, Main Street, Battaramulla.
Complainant-Respondent
2. Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
Respondent
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL: Sumith Senanayake, PC with Prabodhini Nissanka and
Kavindi Kodithuwakku instructed by Nisali Balachandra
for the Petitioner.
Jehan Gunasekara, SC for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON: 28.11.2024
DECIDED ON: 10.12.2024
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J.
1. The Petitioner had preferred this application for bail under Section 83(2)
of the Poison, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by
Act . The Petitioner is seeking bail for her husband,
Samaraweera Arachchige Jeewan Perera (Accused). Mr. Sumith

--- Page 3 ---
Senanayake, P.C., supporting this application sought bail on the
following grounds which he submits as being exceptional.
i. Delay of all most three and half years,
ii. No previous convictions.
2. Mr. Senanayake, P.C., submitted that the Accused was arrested on
18.04.2019 and is in remand up until now. His main contention is that
the trial has not concluded within a reasonable time and several dates
have been sought and the trial had been postponed at least on 06-07
occasions. The indictment is dated 02.07.2021 and the trial has
commenced on 06.10.2022. It was submitted that upon leading
evidence of witness No. 01, further trial had been postponed until today
and it is now fixed for further trial on 17.02.2025. Accordingly, it is
argued that this delay is excessive and oppressive and moves that the
Accused be granted bail.
3. The learned State Counsel objecting to this application submitted that
indictment has been filed without a delay and the pure quantity of
heroine involved in this offence is 3.749 kilogrammes. Whilst conceding
that the trial commenced on 06.12.2022 and the matter was postponed
for cross-examination of witness No.01. Thereafter upon the matter
being postponed on several occasions, it is now set for further trial for
17.02.2025. The position of the Respondents is that it is the Accused
and the defence that is primarily responsible for the postponements and
the delay. In support of this contention, the learned State Counsel
submitted that initially when it was for further trial, the defence had
moved for several dates in order to tender certain CCTV footages despite
time being obtained the said recordings were not produced and then
has abandoned and withdrawn the said application. Then, on
26.02.2024, a postponement had also been sought due to a personal
ground of a defence Counsel. These facts are confirmed by the certified
copy of the proceeding tendered by the Petitioner to this Court when
the matter is taken up for inquiry.

--- Page 4 ---
4. Accordingly, it is obvious and apparent that the defence is responsible
for a greater part of the postponements and dates obtained between
06.10.2022 and today. There is no way in which one could attribute
this delay to the prosecution or the respondents. An Accused cannot
create an exceptional circumstance by the postponements which the
defence had obtained. Such lapse of time may have caused a delay but
it is not excessive or oppressive.
5. As regards the lapse time, what may be exceptional is not the per se
lapse of time, but the excessive or oppressive delay. As held in Attorney
General v. Ediriweera (S.C. Appeal No. 100/2005), Delay is always a
relative term and the question to be considered is not whether there was
mere explicable delay, as when there is a backlog of cases, but whether
there has been excessive or oppressive delay and this always depends
on the facts and circumstances of the case.
6. According to the provisions of Section 83(2), bail in respect of persons
charged with trafficking or possession of 10 grammes or over may be
considered only if the applicants satisfy Court of exceptional
circumstances. However, the provisions of Section 83 (2) as amended
by Act, No. , decrees that a person accused or suspected of
being in possession of 10 grammes or more, is required to be kept in
remand, unless such person satisfies this Court as to the existence of
circumstances that are exceptional.
7. No doubt, under the normal law during the pre-trial and pre-conviction
stages granting of bail is the rule and the refusal is the exception. This
is in accord with the presumption of innocence which prevails during
the pendency of the trial. However, when exceptional circumstances are
by statute decreed as being a necessary prerequisite, then the
legislature has intended that, persons accused of such offences be held
in remand pending the determination of such trials. Considering
Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance

--- Page 5 ---
(prior to the amendment) in Labukola Ange Wisin Gedera Ashani
Dhanushshika v. OIC Divisional Crimes Investigation Unit
Panadura [CA/PHC/APN/04/2016- CAM 06.10.2016] it was opined
thus;
The Petitioners first point is that the suspect is in remand nearly
for two years. The intention of the Legislature is to keep in remand
any person who is suspected of or accused of possessing or
trafficking heroine until the conclusion of the case. The Section
83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance
express the intention of the Legislature. It is enacted by the
Parliament that No person suspected or accused of an offence
under section 54A or section 54B of this Ordinance shall be
released on bail, except by the High Court in exceptional
circumstances.
8. The provisions of Section 83 have been enacted with the intent and
purpose of containing and curbing the growing drug-related offences.
The Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance being a special
statute could certainly prevail and override the provisions of other more
general statutes. In relation to bail, Section 83 has incorporated
provisions which decrees in the mandatory form that bail should not
ordinarily and as a rule be granted in cases involving serious drug
offences under subsection (1) of Section 54A and Section 54B except in
exceptional circumstances. When a special statute contains specific
provisions for granting of bail such provisions cannot be ignored whilst
considering such bail applications.
9. It is now settled law that the time spent in remand due to the lack of
exceptional circumstance cannot by itself create a circumstance that is
exceptional which otherwise would not have been there. This, in effect,
is that the period of remand due to the absence of exceptional
circumstances, will not, by itself, amount to or be converted to an
exceptional circumstance. This was succinctly expounded by Justice

--- Page 6 ---
Ranjith Silva in CA (PHC) APN 64/2009 (decided on 07.08.2009) as
follows;
If an accused cannot assign exceptional circumstances he
will have to be kept on remand and when an accused had
been on remand for 03 years because he had no exceptional
circumstances will that by itself constitute exceptional
circumstances. If that is treated as an exceptional
circumstance, in my view it would be an anomaly because
the fact that there arent any exceptional circumstances
finally mature into exceptional circumstances. The fact that
he had no exceptional circumstances becomes a qualification
after 03 years. If that was the intention of the legislature,
the section itself would have stated the exceptional
circumstances should not be insisted after 03 years and
there is no such qualification, no such jurisdiction found in
the particular provision dealing with bail.
10. Now to consider if the accused in this matter is entitled to any benefit
or if there be any ground that may be considered in his favour to grant
bail. On the face of it, there is certainly a time lag of three years from
the date of arrest up until now. Is this undue, oppressive or an excessive
delay? Undue, oppressive and excessive delay are not absolute terms
but would be relative depending on the context and circumstances in
which it is considered. The delay in concluding the trial in the present
case is attributable to the defence as the trial was postponed on an
application made on behalf of the accused (as admitted by both
counsel). To my mind when prolonging of a trial or the delay of a trial
is wholly or partly due to the conduct of the accused himself, he cannot
use such delay to his own benefit in seeking bail. It is a delay for which
the accused himself is to blame. Accordingly, the submission of
excessive or oppressive delay in the present context is misconceived and
not acceptable. The trial is now scheduled for 17.02.2025. As such, in

--- Page 7 ---
the absence of any exceptional circumstance we see no lawful basis to
consider this application favourably.
11. In the light of the aforesaid, this Court is of the view the Petitioner
had failed to establish any circumstance that may be considered
exceptional. This Court is left with no option but to refuse and reject
this application. Accordingly, this application is refused and dismissed.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC
OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an application for revision
under and in terms of Article 138 of the
Constitution of the Democratic Socialist
Republic of Sri Lanka.
Court of Appeal The Hon. Attorney General,
Revision Application No: Attorney Generals Department,
CA/CPA/0124/24 Superior Courts Complex,
Hulftsdorp Street,
High Court of Ampara Colombo 12.
Case No: HC/AMP/1976/19 COMPLAINANT
Vs.
Magistrates Court of Ampara 1. Wathuliyadde Gedara Malinda Nuwan
Case No: MC/AMP/B/7494/10 Samarasinghe,
Siriwasa, Ankelipitiya, Thalatu-oya,
Kandy.
2. Sachini Rinosha Wickramarachchi,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.

--- Page 2 ---
3. Kalubowila Arachchilage Gayan
Buddhika,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.
ACCUSED
AND NOW BETWEEN
1. Wathuliyadde Gedara Malinda Nuwan
Samarasinghe,
Siriwasa, Ankelipitiya,
Thalatu-oya,
Kandy.
1st ACCUSED-PETITIONER
Vs.
1. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Superior Courts Complex,
Hulftsdorp Street,
Colombo 12.
COMPLAINANT-RESPONDENT

--- Page 3 ---
2. Sachini Rinosha Wickramarachchi,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.
2nd ACCUSED-RESPONDENT
3. Kalubowila Arachchilage Gayan
Buddhika,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.
3rd ACCUSED-RESPONDENT
Before : Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
: Amal Ranaraja, J.
Counsel : A.M.E.B. Atapattu for the 1st Accused-Petitioner
Supported on : 042024
Order on : 192024
Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
This is an application preferred by the 1st accused-petitioner (hereinafter referred
to as the petitioner) in terms of Article 138 of The Constitution seeking to invoke
the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court.
The petitioner is the 1st accused in the High Court of Ampara Case No.
HC/AMP/1976/19.

--- Page 4 ---
He has been indicted by the Hon. Attorney General along with two others, for
conspiring to cause criminal breach of trust to Seylan Bank of which he was an
employee attached to its Ampara Branch for a sum of Rs. 5019000/- between
the period of 142010 and 172010, and thereby committing an offence
punishable in terms of section 391 read with section 113B and 102 of the Penal
Code.
He has also been indicted for committing the earlier mentioned criminal breach
of trust for the said sum at the same time and at the same transaction, and
thereby committing an offence punishable in terms of section 391 of the Penal
Code.
The trial against the petitioner and the other accused has commenced before the
learned High Court Judge of Ampara and PW-01 has so far partly concluded his
evidence in chief. In the process of the said evidence, PW-01 has produced
several gold jewellery pawn receipts relevant to the action, marked up to P-04.
In the petition before the Court, the petitioner has sought to set aside the orders
given by the learned High Court Judge of Ampara allowing to mark documents
P-01, P-02, P-03, P-04, P-04(1), P-04(2), P-04(3), P04(4), P-04(5), P-04(6), P-
04(7), P-04(8), P-04(9), P-04(10), and the documents marked during the trial on
262023 and 222024, among other reliefs sought in the prayer of the
petition.
When this matter was supported for notice and also for a stay order, the main
reason submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner for initiating this
action was that the documents mentioned in the indictment filed by the Hon.
Attorney General are documents not tendered to Magistrates Court when the
matter was initially reported to the Magistrate of Ampara, and therefore
producing them at the High Court is against the provisions of section 431 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
It was his submission that the learned High Court Judge unfairly overruled his
objection and therefore, his client was denied a fair trial. It was also submitted

--- Page 5 ---
that although the learned High Court Judge ordered the prosecution to hand
over the copies of the items mentioned in the indictment as productions, the
prosecution has failed to hand over them. Another matter taken up by the
learned Counsel was that the pawn receipts so far marked at the trial are not
the originals, but photocopies.
It was on that basis the learned Counsel submitted that the petitioner has
sufficient exceptional grounds to invoke the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court
to seek relief as prayed for.
Having considered the submissions of the learned Counsel, this Court is of the
view that section 431 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act has no direct
application to the matter under consideration.
It is clear from the proceedings of the High Court that the petitioner and the
other accused have been indicted before the High Court of Ampara for conspiracy
to commit criminal breach of trust, committing criminal breach of trust and also
aiding and abetting to commit criminal breach of trust, and thereby, causing a
loss to Seylan Bank of the sum mentioned in the indictment.
The evidence so far led appears to be on the basis that this criminal breach of
trust has been committed by knowingly accepting fake gold jewellery as pawn
articles to the bank. The documents that had been so far marked are the
duplicate copies of the pawn receipts the bank had in possession. Although the
learned Counsel claims that the prosecution has failed to mark the original
documents, obviously the originals of the pawn receipts cannot be in the
possession of the bank as the said originals are meant to be handed over to the
person who pawned the articles. The evidence of PW-01 led so far reveals the fact
that once a person pawned an item, a receipt is prepared in triplicate, where the
original is handed over to the customer, while the pink-coloured copy is kept
with the pawned article, and the green-coloured copy is used for auditing
purposes.

--- Page 6 ---
It is also clear from the proceedings that attempts had been made on behalf of
the accused to prevent the relevant documents being marked on unacceptable
grounds, where the learned High Court Judge has given a clear order in that
regard on 092023, which I find is a correct order made in that regard.
It appears from the proceedings that the questioned items of the fake gold
jewellery and the relevant pink and green coloured receipts issued in that regard
have been kept under the custody of the Seylan bank, being the owner of the
said items for better safekeeping. I find that this is a common practice adopted
by the Court to allow the owners of the items of productions to keep the custody
of the said productions until a conclusion of a trial for obvious reasons.
Although the learned High Court Judge has ordered that the items of jewellery,
which are the productions of the case shall be handed over to the Court, I do
not find any necessity to hand over the said jewellery to the Court as the purpose
is to ensure the safe custody of the same until the conclusion of the trial. In my
view, Seylan Bank is the best place where the said jewellery can be safely kept
for the purposes of this action as they are the owners of the jewellery.
As clearly determined by the learned High Court Judge, if the marked documents
or other productions are not in order or suspicious, it is a matter for the learned
trial Judge to determine on that when relevant. I find no basis to shut out such
documents or items of productions in the manner the petitioner is attempting to
claim.
It is clear from the case record that the learned trial Judge has done all he could
to ensure a fair trial towards the petitioner and the other accused in the case.
If the prosecution has failed to hand over copies of the other documents they
intend to mark at the trial as ordered by the learned High Court Judge, it will
again be a matter that the learned High Court Judge should decide whether to
allow evidence in that regard or what order should be made in that regard.

--- Page 7 ---
Even after the documents had been marked, the defence can again ask for copies
of the same, if they are unable to cross-examine the witnesses straightaway in
that regard, and obtain an order from the Court.
I am of the view that this type of applications should not be encouraged under
any circumstances, unless the decisions made by the trial Court in the process
of a trial are manifestly wrong, which shocks the conscience of the Court as it
would lead to delay in proceedings before a trial Court. In the instant matter, I
find no reasons to come to such a finding,
Having considered the application before the Court, and the relevant facts and
circumstances, I find that this is not a case where notice should be issued to the
named respondents, as I find no merit in any of the grounds urged before the
Court.
Accordingly, the revision application is dismissed without the notice being
issued.
The Registrar of the Court is directed to communicate this order to the High
Court of Ampara for necessary information.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
Amal Ranaraja, J.
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
