--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC
SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for
Bail under and in terms of Section
83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs Ordinance No. as amended by Poisons,
Opium and Dangerous Drugs
(Amendment) Act No. .
The Democratic Socialist Republic of
Sri Lanka.
Complainant
Court of Appeal Case No.
CA/BAL/0231/2024
Magistrate Court of Kaduwela Vs.
Case No. B 59541/22/ODD
Gunethi Damindu Shamnedra
Perera.
Suspect
AND NOW BETWEEN
Gunethi Damindu Shamnedra
Perera,
No.678/19, Wanawatha para,
Thunadahena, Mahawata,
Koratota, Kaduwela.
Suspect-Petitioner

--- Page 2 ---
Vs.
1. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
2. Officer-in-Charge,
Antivice Striking Force,
Valana Central, Panadura.
3. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station,
Athurugiriya.
Respondents
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H. KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL : Eranga Sirisena for the Petitioner.
Malik Azeez, SC for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON : 29.11.2024
DECIDED ON : 18.12.2024
K.M.G.H. KULATUNGA, J.
1. This application for bail is preferred by the Suspect-Petitioner under
the provisions of Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance. According to the Petition and the submissions
made during the inquiry, the suspect had been arrested on
21.05.2022. As stated in the annexed B report the suspect at the
point of arrest had been in possession of 25.6g of heroine. Then

--- Page 3 ---
upon being interrogated a further 144.5g of heroine had been
recovered from a house in Hokandara. It is in respect of these
recoveries that the suspect is now held in remand. According to the
Government Analysts Report the pure quantities of heroine in the
said two recoveries are 13.8g and 89.27g respectively. The
Government Analysts Report is dated 31.08.2022.
2. The main ground urged by Ms. Eranga Sirisena, Attorney-at- Law
for the Petitioner is that no indictment or charges have been
preferred up until the date of this inquiry. Accordingly, for almost
two and half years the Respondents have failed to institute criminal
action and prefer charges in respect of this matter. The learned
Counsel for the Petitioner admits that the suspect has another
pending case for a similar offence involving 79mg of heroine. The
main thrust of the argument advanced is that the delay of almost
two and a half-year without indicting or preferring charges is
excessive and oppressive which can be considered as an exceptional
circumstance.
3. In response and in opposition to this application, the learned State
Counsel Mr. Malik Azeez submitted that the cumulative quantity of
the two recoveries is 106g of pure heroine which according to Mr.
Azeez is substantial and considerable. Further, he submitted that
the IB extracts was received by the Hon. Attorney General almost
one year ago. The indictment is under consideration and it is now
finalized and a decision had been taken to send out two indictments
for each recovery separately. Mr. Azeez was optimistic that the
indictment will be dispatched soon. He also emphasized the fact that
the offence had been committed whilst the suspect was on bail for
another similar offence which is the matter involving 79mg of
heroine. It is the position of learned State Counsel that IBs have

--- Page 4 ---
been forwarded within one year and within another year
preparations have been made to finalized and forward an
indictment. In these circumstances, Mr. Azeez believes and submits
that the delay of two and half years cannot be considered as being
excessive or oppressive.
4. Upon been inquired, the learned State Counsel conceded that apart
from initial recoveries no further investigations were required or
directed by the Attorney General nor done by the Police. Therefore,
what was required to institute legal process was to forward the
Information Book extracts to the Attorney General to consider such
material and draw up the indictment.
5. This process has taken 30 months or a period of two and half years.
There is no convincing or any acceptable reason to explain this lapse
of time and to justify the same.
6. The primary ground of seeking bail is the alleged undue delay which
is referred to as oppressive or excessive delay which according to the
petitioner is an exceptional circumstance. The legislature has in its
wisdom limited the granting of bail in respect of certain offences
under the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance only
upon satisfying Court of exceptional circumstances. Section 83 as
amended by the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs
(Amendment) Act, No. reads thus;
83. (1) Subject to the provisions of sections 84, 85 and
subsection (2) of this section, a person suspected or accused of
an offence under sections 54A and 54B of this Ordinance, shall
not be released on bail by the High Court except in exceptional
circumstances.
(2) Notwithstanding the provisions of sections 84 and 85,
a person suspected or accused of an -

--- Page 5 ---
(a) of which the pure quantity of the dangerous drug,
trafficked, imported, exported or possessed is ten
grammes or above in terms of the report issued by the
Government Analyst under section 77A; and
(b) which is punishable with death or life
imprisoment,[sic] shall not be released on bail except by
the Court of Appeal in exceptional circumstances.
(3) For the purposes of this section dangerous drug means
Morphine, Cocaine, Heroin and Methamphetamine..
7. No doubt, under the normal law at the pre-trial and pre-conviction
stages granting of bail is the rule and the refusal is the exception.
This is in accord with the presumption of innocence that which
prevails during the pendency of the trial. However, when exceptional
circumstances are by statute decreed as being a necessary
prerequisite, then the legislature has intended that, persons
accused of such offences be held in remand pending the
determination of such trials. Considering section 83(1) of the
Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance (prior to the
amendment) in Labukola Ange Wisin Gedera Ashani
Dhanushshika v. OIC Divisional Crimes Investigation Unit
Panadura [CA/PHC/APN/04/2016- CAM 06.10.2016] it was opined
thus;
The Petitioners first point is that the suspect is in remand
nearly for two years. The intention of the Legislature is to keep
in remand any person who is suspected of or accused of
possessing or trafficking heroine until the conclusion of the
case. The Section 83(1) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance express the intention of the Legislature. It is
enacted by the Parliament that No person suspected or
accused of an offence under section 54A or section 54B of this

--- Page 6 ---
Ordinance shall be released on bail, except by the High Court
in exceptional circumstances.
8. No doubt the provisions of section 83 has been enacted with the
intent and purpose of containing and curbing the growing drug
related offences. The Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs
Ordinance being a special statute could certainly prevail and
override the provisions of other more general statutes. In relation to
bail, section 83 has incorporated provisions which decrees in the
mandatory form that bail should not ordinarily and as a rule be
granted in cases involving serious drug offences under subsection
(1) of section 54A and section 54B except in exceptional
circumstances. When a special statute contains specific provisions
for granting of bail such provisions cannot be ignored whilst
considering such bail applications. Considering a similar issue in
the Indian case of Arun v. D. Pakyntein, 2009(7) SCALE 568,
(2009)16 SCC 496 it was opined that, where a statute confers drastic
powers and provides for stringent penal provisions including the
matters relating to grant of bail, the conditions precedent therefore
must be scrupulously complied with.
9. However, to my mind this extremely stringent provision of section 83
on granting of bail certainly cannot become or be allowed to be used
as a means to incarcerate an accused person without instituting
action or concluding the trial for an indefinite and unreasonably long
time without a just cause. Thus, time in remand when considered in
conjunction with the failure to take meaningful steps to institute
action or diligently prosecute to a finality in context may create the
circumstances that can be considered exceptional. The time spent in
remand cannot be considered in the abstract to determine if its
exceptional. Similarly, the normal effluxion of time between the
arrest and trial, cannot by itself amount to an exceptional

--- Page 7 ---
circumstance. If the delay is inordinate and unexplained, it may very
well be.
10. It is very relevant to be conscious and mindful that remanding of a
person denies his freedom and liberty. In reality holding a person in
custody for two and half years virtually and necessarily deprives such
person, two and half years of his life and living. Therefore, those who
are responsible for so denying the freedom and liberty are required
to act consciously and diligently to expeditiously process and
progress with necessary steps to file criminal proceedings. Any
dereliction of this obligation in whatever degree or any lackadaisical
attitude exhibited in this process should necessarily be viewed with
utmost seriousness.
11. In the instant matter, in view of the submissions made by the learned
State Counsel, the police had taken one year to have IB extracts
forwarded to the Attorney General. No acceptable reason is
forthcoming. Similarly, another one and half years has now been
taken to finalize the charges or the indictment. I regret to note that
the persons empowered to take action to institute criminal
proceedings seem to have completely lost sight that a suspect is
languishing in remand somewhere. Further, it is admitted that a
previous application for bail had also been preferred by this suspect
which had been refused and rejected on 04.04.2024. This is deposed
to in paragraph 09 of the affidavit of the 2nd Respondent. The
relevance and what emanates from this fact is that the respondents
have been aware and it has been brought to their conscious attention
of the delay in finalizing criminal action in respect of this matter as
far back as 04.04.202. The said bail application bears No.
CA/BAL/409/2023 according to which in 2023 the Respondents
have had notice of this matter pending without criminal action as at

--- Page 8 ---
that point. No doubt, this Court has on 04.04.2024 dismissed the
said application. Now, at the end of November 2024, the indictment
is yet to be finalized and sent out. From April 2024 up to now the
State has very conveniently and nonchalantly let 07 months pass by
and suddenly when this matter was taken up for inquiry on
29.11.2024 informs that indictment will be sent out in due course.
This sequence of events in no uncertain terms demonstrate an
extreme indifference and disregard of the rights of a person in
remand. To our mind this lackadaisical attitude of those responsible
is serious. End of the day delay remains unexplained.
12. This suspect may have a similar pending matter and the quantities of
heroine is no doubt substantial and considerable. In my mind even
the worst criminal is entitled benefits and rights guaranteed and
protected by the constitution and statute. Where the delay is
unexplained and excessive the combined effect specially as the
Respondents in this instance having had sufficient notice in view of
the previous bail application should necessarily have consciously
acted and expeditiously indicted the suspect, which they have failed
to do.
13. Accordingly, as stated above in the absence of any valid and
acceptable reason the lapse of two and half years necessarily become
excessive and as far as the suspect is concerned it is oppressive. As
regards the lapse of 19 months, what may be exceptional is not the
per se lapse of time, but the excessive or oppressive delay. As held in
Attorney General v. Ediriweera (S.C. Appeal No. 100/2005), Delay
is always a relative term and the question to be considered is not
whether there was mere explicable delay, as when there is a backlog
of cases, but whether there has been excessive or oppressive delay and
this always depends on the facts and circumstances of the case.

--- Page 9 ---
14. Accordingly, I hold that in these circumstances the delay is excessive
and oppressive. And therefore, can be considered as been exceptional.
Accordingly, this Court is inclined to grant bail to the Petitioner-
Suspect to the following conditions.
i. Cash bail of Rs.200,000.00,
ii. Should produce two sureties who should execute bond in a
sum of Two Million Rupees each,
iii. Each surety should tender Grama Sevaka Certificates and
Police Reports from their respective residential area,
iv. The Suspect-Petition should report to the Officer-in-Charge of
the Antivice Striking Force, Walana Central, Panadura on
every 2nd and 4th Sunday of the month before 12 noon,
v. The Suspect-Petitioner is required to surrender his passport
or any travel document if he has any to the Registrar of the
Magistrates Court of Kaduwela.
15. Accordingly, this application is allowed and bail is granted to the Suspect-
Petitioner subject to the above conditions. Application is allowed. The
Registrar of this Court is allowed to send copy of this order to the Registrar
of the Magistrates Court of Kaduwela.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for Bail
under and in terms of Section 83(2) of
the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance No. as
amended by Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No.
The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station,
Baddegama.
Court of Appeal Case No.
CA/BAL/0625/2023 Complainant
Magistrate Court of Baddegama Vs.
Case No. B 174/2023
1. Kadupitiya Arachchige Haritha
Lakshan.
2. Kariyawasam Peradorapage Thisaru
Eranda.
Suspects
AND NOW BETWEEN
Walakada Gamage Shriya jayakanthi,
Athula, Nagoda,
Galle.
Petitione

--- Page 2 ---
Vs.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Narcotic Bureau,
Baddegama.
2. Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
Respondents
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL: Kasun Liyanage for the Petitioner.
Oswald Perera, SC for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON: 19.11.2024
DECIDED ON: 06.12.2024
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J.
1. This application is made under Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs Ordinance seeking bail for the 2nd suspect, Thisaru
Eranda. According to the Petitioner the 2nd suspect was arrested on
18.02.2023 with 100.69g of pure Methamphetamine. The grounds urged
are the relative weakness of the case and the unusual delay in concluding
the pre-trial conference.
2. It is common ground that the indictment has been filed on 12.02.2024,
within one year of the arrest and detection. The main grievance and
complaint of the petitioner is the unusual delay in concluding the pre-trial
proceedings in the Galle High Court. It is argued that provisions of Section

--- Page 3 ---
195A. (5) requires the pre-trial conference to be concluded within 3 months.
Section 195A. (5) reads thus;
195A. (5) Every endeavor shall be made to conclude a pre-trial
conference as expeditiously as possible:
Provided however, a pre-trial conference shall be concluded
within a period not exceeding three months from the date on
which the accused appeared before the court or was
required to appear before the court.
3. Of course, on the face of it the proviso to section 195A. (5) does require the
pre-trial proceeding to be concluded within three months from the date on
which the accused appeared before the court. It is couched in the
mandatory form. However, this matter is now set to be mentioned on
30.01.2025. Two previous scheduled pre-trial conference dates have been
cancelled. The petitioner tendered a certified copy of the journal entries of
HC/5963/23 of the High Court of Galle. According to which the indictment
was served on 12.02.2024 and this matter was set for pre-trial on
25.04.2024and mentioned 19.06.2024 and now it is to be mentioned again
on 30.01.2025. Accordingly, from the point of serving the indictment it has
now taken almost ten months and the trial date is yet to be fixed. The matter
for determination and consideration is, whether this delay in these
circumstances will be exceptional for the purposes of considering bail under
Section 83(2) of the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. The
mere delay or the lapse of time does not amount to being exceptional unless
such delay is excessive or oppressive. Pre-trial conference is a joint exercise
with the participation of the prosecuting counsel, defence counsel and the
aggrieved party or the counsel if any, appearing on behalf of the aggrieved
party, of course presided over by the High Court Judge or the Recorder
Judge. Thus, it is the obligation of all the parties to endeavour to conclude
the same within the prescribed 3 month period though presided over by the
High Court Judge. In the present instance it appears from the journal
entries that the Accused himself has acquiesced and at least passively

--- Page 4 ---
participated in the cancellation of the pre-trial conference and the in the
postponement beyond 3 months without any objection.
4. Of course, the procedure prescribed by section 195A of the Code of Criminal
procedure Act does require a pre-trial conference to be concluded within a
period not exceeding three months from the date on which the accused
appeared before the court and it is primarily the duty of the presiding judge
to ensure the adherence to the said mandatory time frames. However, in
the circumstances of this matter the petitioner is not entitled take
advantage of and cannot be heard to say that the said delay is excessive or
oppressive.
5. The prosecution has expeditiously filed the indictment within a reasonable
time. However, the pre-trial proceedings appear to have taken time initially
due to not providing all the documents. Then, as to the delay in calling and
receiving certain items of productions and the other delay in this instance
cannot entirety or primarily be attributed to conduct of an oppressive or
excessive nature on the part of the prosecution. It may appear to be
excessive in the context of section 195A (5), but it is the Judge who had
granted these dates and certain steps to obtain the productions have taken
some time. Upon the consideration of the totality of the facts and
circumstances it appears that the time taken is not unusual and unique to
this matter alone and this appears to be the usual lapse of time that is
common to all similar cases pending before the said High Court. No doubt,
the 2nd suspect is said to have no previous convictions. However, since the
lapse of time in context cannot be singularly considered as being oppressive
or excessive, this cannot be considered as being exceptional.
6. The next argument advanced is the apparent improbability in the
prosecution version as to the manner of recovery and arrest. It was
submitted that this suspect along with another is alleged to has been
arrested while in room of a hotel at Baddegama. According to the notes of
investigation at pages 16 and 17 of the certified copy annexed, when the
police officers arrived at the hotel two suspects were in the room of which

--- Page 6 ---
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for Bail
under and in terms of Section 83(2) of
the Poisons, Opium and Dangerous
Drugs Ordinance No. as
amended by Poisons, Opium and
Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act No.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,

CA/BAL/0706/2023 2. The Officer-in-Charge,

Kuliyapitiya Pannala.

Vs.

Wikummala,
Thalammahera,
Pannala.
Suspect
AND NOW BETWEEN

--- Page 2 ---
Gamaralalage Indra Kumara,
No. 25/1,
Pamunuwatta,
Meerigama.
Petitioner
Vs.
1. The Officer-in-Charge,
Police Narcotics Bureau,
Colombo 01.

Police Station,
Pannala.
3. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
Complainants-Respondents
BEFORE : MENAKA WIJESUNDERA, J
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J
COUNSEL: M.C.M. Imtiaz instructed by Anuradi Nakandala for the
Petitioner.
Malik Azeez, SC, for the Respondents.
INQUIRY ON: 03.12.2024
DECIDED ON: 19.12.2024

--- Page 3 ---
K.M.G.H KULATUNGA, J.
1. This application for bail is preferred by the Petitioner on behalf of the
Accused Respondent under the provisions of Section 83(2) of the
Poisons, Opium, and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. According to the
Petitioner, the suspect was arrested at her house on 07.10.2023. When
the Police arrived, another person (male) had escaped from the house.
It is common ground that the person who so left the house is Loku
Pathiranage Lahiru Rukshan the husband of the suspect. (vide-the B
report marked X-5) When he so retreated he has left behind his mobile
phone a jeep was also found in the compound of the house which
belongs to him. Therefore, it appears that the suspects husband had
in fact taken to his heels and escaped when the Police team approached
the house.
2. The suspect denies being in possession of any narcotics. However,
according to the Respondents, as depicted in the B Reports, the suspect
was having a parcel of heroin in a plastic bag in her hand when the
raiding team approached the house. It is also common ground that the
husband who escaped had been apprehended several days after whilst
being in possession of heroin. The portion marked X-10 of the B Report
X-5 also states that the said Loku Pathiranage Lahiru Rukshan has
previously been apprehended by several police stations in that area for
similar offences.
3. It was further submitted that the suspect has a child of three years,
who is said to be now cared for and looked after by her aging parents.
4. The learned State Counsel vehemently objected to this application, but
conceded that the indictment is yet to be forwarded as the Attorney
General is awaiting the IB Extracts.
5. The crux of the Petitioners submission is that it is improbable to expect
any ordinary person to hold a parcel containing 310 grammes of heroin
in her hand when a Police team is seen approaching the house. Her

--- Page 4 ---
husband who was there, appears to have taken to his heels just as the
raiding party was approached. In these circumstances, if the suspect
was conscious and knew that the parcel contained narcotics, it is highly
unlikely and improbable for her to have held on to it and keep it in her
hand. Therefore, the suspect was either unaware and ignorant as to the
contents of the bag or the B Reports do not narrate correctly the manner
of arrest and how she possessed the substance.
6. Secondly, the petitioner relies on the delay without instituting criminal
proceedings which is submitted to be excessive and oppressive. The
indictment or charges are yet to be preferred.
7. The arrest has taken place in October 2023. A period of one year and
two months has lapsed as at the date of the inquiry. The State Counsel
concedes the indictment is yet to be considered as the Attorney General
is yet to receive the IB extracts. The learned State Counsel is unable to
inform this Court as the present status of the IB extracts or of any
reason for the delay. This application for bail had been filed on
13.12.2023. The state had appeared on notice on 22.10.2024 on which
day this was fixed for the objections on 04.03.2024. However, in the
interim this was fixed for inquiry on 03.12.2024 and by letter dated
06.11.2024 the Hon. Attorney General was informed by the Registrar of
this Court that this will be taken up for inquiry on 03.12.2024 and has
also informed that objections if any be filed on or before 25.11.2024.
Accordingly, the matter was taken up for inquiry on 03.12.2024 on
which day, the State Counsel was heard. However, there was no
statement of objection filed of record. The State Counsel is unable to
inform as to a date or at least a probable time frame as to when charges
may be filed.
8. As such it is the opinion of this Court that the delay of one year and
two months considered in conjunctions with the said failure to explain
may be considered has been exceptional. It is well to remember that

--- Page 5 ---
when a person is denied of his liberty and held in detention those who
are responsible for the said deprivation should consciously and
diligently take necessary steps to diligently pursue with, finalize and
institute legal action. If a reasonable explanation for any delay is not
forthcoming such delay will be considered as being excessive or
oppressive. As held in Attorney General v. Ediriweera (S.C. Appeal
No. 100/2005), Delay is always a relative term and the question to be
considered is not whether there was mere explicable delay, as when
there is a backlog of cases, but whether there has been excessive or
oppressive delay and this always depends on the facts and
circumstances of the case.
9. Under section 83(2) of the Poisons Opium and Dangerous Drugs
Ordinance bail may be considered only on exceptional circumstances.
However, to my mind this extremely stringent provision of section 83
on granting of bail certainly cannot become or be allowed to be used as
a means to incarcerate an accused person without instituting action or
concluding the trial for an indefinite and unreasonably long time
without a just cause. Thus, time in remand when considered in
conjunction with the failure to take meaningful steps to institute action
and diligently prosecute to a finality in context may create the
circumstances that can be considered exceptional. The time spent in
remand cannot be considered in the abstract to determine if its
exceptional. Similarly, the normal delay which occurs between the
arrest and trial, cannot by itself amount to an exceptional
circumstance. I do not say that delay per se may not amount to an
exceptional circumstance. If there is inordinate and unexplained delay,
it may very well be.
10. It is common ground that the suspects estranged husband was present
and did escape and retreat when the police party was approaching. He
said to be a person with a previous history of drug related offences.
Then, on the other hand, there is an apparent improbability of the

--- Page 6 ---
suspect keeping in her hand a parcel with heroine when the police are
seen approaching and her husband retreats. As stated above, either she
may have been unaware as to the content or the version of the police
may be incorrect. Whatever be the reason this circumstance considered
with the unexplained delay in our view amounts to a circumstance that
can be considered exceptional. Accordingly, we are inclined to grant bail
to the suspect on the following conditions.
1. cash bail in a sum of Rs. 100,000.00;
2. to provide two sureties who should execute bonds to the value of
Rs. 500,000.00 each;
3. the sureties should provide certificates from the Grama Sevaka
and police reports from respective residential areas of such
sureties;
4. to surrender the passport or any travel document of the suspect,
if she has any, to the Registrar of the Magistrates Court of
Kuliyapitiya; and
5. report to the Officer-in-Charge of the Pannala Police Station on
every last Sunday of the month before 12 noon.
This Application is accordingly allowed and the Registrar of this
Court is directed to transmit a copy of this order to the Registrar
of the Magistrates Court of Kuliyapitiya.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
Menaka Wijesundera, J
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

Counsels: Faisz Musthapha, P.C. with Faisza Musthapha, P.C., Keerthi Thilakaratne
and Thushani Machado for the Defendant-Petitioners
Shaheeda Barrie with Nisala Seniya Fernando for the Plaintiff- Respondents
Supported On: 25.11.2024

--- Page 8 ---
Written
Submissions: 13.12.2024 (by the Defendant-Petitioners)
On 13.12.2024 (by the Plaintiff- Respondents)
Order On: 18.12.2024
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
This leave to appeal application emanates from the Order of the Wakf Tribunal dated
06.04.2024 where the Tribunal appointed a receiver, removing the Trustees from the
Management and required the Petitioners who are the Trustees to hand over the possession
of the property at Maharagama to the said receiver.
This application deals with the N.D.H. Abdul Ghaffoor Trust established by the Deed of Trust
No. 2125 dated 21.11.1935 attested by John Wilson, Notary Public of Colombo. This Deed of
Trust involves two properties namely a plantation land (comprising of 3 buildings on one end
thereof and a plantation on the remainder) of a total of 17 Acres in extent, situated at
Maharagama and more fully described in the First Scheule of the said Trust Deed and a
prime commercial land of approximately 386 perches (2  acres) situated in Grandpass,
Colombo 14 and more fully described in the Second Scheule of the said Trust Deed.
The Petitioners state that several old boys of the Gaffooriya Arabic College which is a
property described in the First Scheule of the said Trust Deed have made several applications
against the trustees of the said Trust in the Wakf Tribunal.
The Petitioners state that the Plaintiff- Respondents who are claiming to have interest in the
said Trust, filed a plaint in the Wakf Tribunal in case bearing No. WT/297/2023 inter alia
seeking as one of the prayers to appoint a receiver for the better custody and management of

--- Page 9 ---
the properties described in the Trust. The Tribunal delivered its order dated 06.04.2024
marked as P23 inter alia appointing a receiver by removing the Trustees from the
Management and requiring the Petitioners to hand over the possession of the property at
Maharagama to the said receiver.
The Petitioners have preferred the present leave to appeal application against the said order
of the Wakf Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 marked as P23 to set aside the same and seek an
interim order staying the operations of the said order and the proceedings of the Wakf
Tribunal Case bearing No. WT/297/2023.
We are mindful that a number of cases have been filed against the trustees in the Wakf
Tribunal. Against the orders of the said Wakf Tribunal, several cases have been filed in the
Court of Appeal to quash the said orders.
In LTA/06/2021 connected with the Wakf Tribunal Case No. WT/273/2020 which deals with
the same Trust Deed where the Petitioners in this Case have challenged the order of the
Wakf Tribunal dated 04.02.2021 and sought an interim order on the basis that the said Deed
of Trust bearing No. 2125 is not a Muslim Charitable Trust. For convenience, the said order
of the Court of Appeal is reproduced below.
This application is filed by 1 to 11" Respondent Petitioners among several other
reliefs seeking to impugn the order of the Wakfs Tribunal dated 40 . February 2021
('P9*). The Respondent-Petitioners also sort the interim - and/or stay orders prayed
for in prayer (f), (g), (i), (), (k) and (1) of the Petition. This Court has already issued
the interim order prayed for in prayer (g) of the Petition, on 10" February 2022 and
has been extended from time to time.

--- Page 10 ---
Having carefully considered the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the
Appellant, learned State Counsel for the 1st Respondent and the learned Counsel for
the 3rd to 7th Respondents, we are of the view that, prima facie there is a serious
question of law need to be, gone into by this Court as to whether the Deed of Trust
bearing No. 2125 dated 21st November 1935, attested by John Wilson, Notary Public
(PI') is or not a Muslim Charitable Trust or Wakf.
Consequently, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the new Management
Committee of Ghaffooriya Arabic College is lawful, and also whether the Wakf
Tribunal has jurisdiction to accept, hear and determine the application made by the
applicant respondent and to make the impugned order marked P9
Accordingly, we formally issue notice on the respondent's name in the petition of this
court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs
(f), (g),( i),( j), (k), and (l) until the final determination of this application.
According to the above-said order, the Court of Appeal has decided that there is a serious
question to be looked into whether the particular trust is or is not a Muslim Charitable Trust
and issued a stay order staying the further proceedings of the Tribunal.
We are mindful that the Wakf Tribunal has jurisdiction only if the particular trust comes
under the Muslim Charitable Trust according to Section 9J of the Muslim Mosques and
Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended.
Despite this order, the Tribunal has affirmed that the Trust established by Deed of Trust No.
2125 is a Muslim Charitable Trust and proceeded to appoint a receiver.

--- Page 11 ---
When the matter was supported, the Counsel for the Petitioners brought to the notice of the
Court the following facts.
A) Knowing the fact that the cases are pending before the Court of Appeal regarding whether
the Trust involved is a Muslim Charitable Trust or not which is a jurisdictional issue, the
Tribunal has proceeded to act on the basis that it is a Muslim Charitable Trust. The
jurisdiction of the Tribunal is limited only to the Muslim Trusts. But the main objection
taken by the Petitioner is that the said Trust is a Private Trust, therefore, the Tribunal
has no jurisdiction to hear the matter.
B) According to Section 671 of the Civil Procedure Code, the appointment of the receiver
should be done by the Court and no one else. For the purpose of convenience, the said
Section 671 is reproduced below.
Whenever it appears to the court to be necessary for the restoration, preservation, or
better custody or management of any property, movable or immovable, the subject of
an action, or under sequestration, the court may on the application of any party who
shall establish a prima facie right to or interest in such property, by order
(a) appoint a receiver of such property, and, if need be,
(b) remove the person, in whose possession or custody the property may be,
from the possession or custody thereof;
(c) commit such property to the custody or management of such receiver; and
(d) grant to such receiver such fee or commission on the rents and profits of the
property by way of remuneration as the court thinks fit, and all such powers
as to bringing and defending actions and for the realization, management,
protection, preservation, and improvement of the property, the collection of the

--- Page 12 ---
rents and profits thereof, the application and disposal of such rents and profits,
and the execution of instruments in writing, as the owner himself has, or such
of those powers as the court thinks fit.
We are mindful that the Tribunal has directed the Respondents to recommend a name which
means that the Tribunal has acted in contravention of Section 671 of the Civil Procedure
Code which directs the Court to appoint the receiver of the Trust. An excerpt of the order of
the Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 is reproduced below for easy reference.
We therefore, allow this application for the appointment of a Receiver and make order
removing the trustees, the 1st to the 12th defendants, from the management and
custody of the Gaffooriya Arabic College and the property at Maharagama and appoint
one of the persons named by the plaintiffs as Receiver, in terms of section 671 of the
Civil Procedure Code to manage the said Arabic College, which is the subject matter
of this case.
The Tribunal has delegated its powers to Respondents to nominate a receiver. The power
conferred on the authority (the Tribunal) by statute must be lawfully exercised by the
authority itself. This principle is discussed in Wade and Forsyths Administrative Law,
Twelfth Edition at page 255 - 257;
Delegation
Inalienable Discretionary Power
An element which is essential to the lawful exercise of power is that it should be
exercised by the authority upon whom it is conferred, and by no one else. The principle
is strictly applied, even where it causes administrative inconvenience, except in cases
where it may reasonably be inferred that the power was intended to be delegable.

--- Page 13 ---
Normally the courts are rigorous in requiring the power to be exercised by the precise
person or body stated in the statute, and in condemning as ultra vires action taken by
agents, sub-committees or delegates, however expressly authorised by the authority
endowed with the power.
One aspect of this principle is the rule that the participation of non-members in the
deliberations or decisions of a collective body may invalidate its acts. The decision of a
disciplinary committee, for example, is likely to be invalid if any non-member of the
committee has taken part in its proceedings. It is not clear that the mere presence of a
non-member will be fatal, although in one case Lord Wright MR said:
It would be most improper on general principles of law that extraneous
persons, who may or may not have independent interests of their own, should
be present at the formulation of that judicial decision.
Therefore, the question is whether the Tribunal has the power to delegate.
C) When the receiver was appointed, there was no quorum as required by Section 9D (3) of
the Muslim Mosques and Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended
which reads as follows;
Two members of the Tribunal shall form a quorum. No matter shall be heard
by the Tribunal unless a quorum is present.
We hold that when the receiver was appointed by the Chairman of the Wakf Tribunal, the
quorum required by the statute was not met. Our Courts have considered that failure to meet
the quorum as required by the statute will go to the root of the matter.

--- Page 14 ---
In Anoma S. Polwatte v. Ms. L. Jayawickrama and Others SC WRIT Application No. 01/2011
decided on 27.07.2018, His Lordship Vijith K. Malalgoda PC, J held that;
When looking at the provisions of the above three provisions of the Act it is clear that
by the above provisions, a clear distinction had been made between the powers of the
Commission and functions of the Commission. As identified in section 3 referred to
above, when an offence is disclosed after an Investigation, Commission shall direct
the institution of proceedings and the said conduct of the Commission had been
identified within the Functions of the Commission. The powers of the Commission has
been identified under section 5 of the Act and under section 2 (8), such powers of the
Commission may exercise by its members either sitting together or separately.
Thus it is clear that the members of the Commission can exercise ancillary powers on
his own though the full complement of the Commission is not available at one given
time. But as for the exercise of functions such as the direction to be given to the
Director General, it is crystal clear that the Act has not provided for one member alone
to give such direction. However as already observed by me, R-1 refers to a directive
given by one member and in the said directive, it is not clear as to whether the reports
referred to, had been considered by the full commission before making such directive.
In the said circumstance, I have no hesitation to conclude that there is no valid
directive made under section 11 of the Act to institute criminal proceedings before the
Magistrates Court, with regard to the investigations carried out by the fraud
Investigation Unit of the Commission to Investigate Bribery and Corruption as
against the Petitioner to the present Application. I therefore conclude the directive
produced marked R-1 is patently illegal.

--- Page 15 ---
In Associated Motorways (Pvt) Ltd. v. Consumer Affairs Authority of Sri Lanka and Another
CA/WRIT/430/2015 decided on 16.11.2020, His Lordship Mahinda Samayawardhena, J. (as
he was then) held that;
Before I consider the Petitioners case on its merits, there is a preliminary issue to be
addressed, though technical in nature, which goes to the root of the matter. That is,
the validity of the impugned decision due to lack of quorum.
Item 8(2) of the Schedule to the Consumer Affairs Authority Act (read with section
3(4) of the Act) says The quorum for any meeting of the Authority shall be four
members. Learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioner submits that when the
impugned decision A18B was purportedly made on 27.11.2014, there was no quorum
of the Authority in the eyes of the law to make such a decision.
Further held that;
For the aforesaid reasons I hold that the impugned decision A18B is a nullity, as it
has not been made by a properly constituted panel of inquiry as required by law. In
other words, the decision has no force or avail in law due to the lack of quorum.
Therefore, in this instant case, the question is when the Chairman appointed the receiver
whether there was the quorum required by the statute.
In addition, the allegation made by the Plaintiffs was of mismanagement of the Trust. We
are mindful that before appointing the receiver, the Tribunal should have asked the
Petitioners to submit the accounts relating to the Trust to satisfy themselves of the allegation
made against the Petitioners. Simply appointing a receiver on the allegation made by the
Plaintiffs is not expected from the Tribunal. Before the Tribunal appointed the person, they
should have asked for the proper accounts to be produced.

--- Page 16 ---
Therefore, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the receiver is lawful.
Accordingly, we grant the leave to appeal against the order dated 06.04.2024 made by the
Wakf Tribunal and we issue notice on all the Respondents named in the Petition to this
Court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs (e),
(f), (g) (h) and (i) until the final determination of this application.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
R. Gurusinghe, J.
I AGREE
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

affected parties. In this application the 13th and 14th Respondents are
vehemently objecting for the extension. As such, there must be a legal
basis for the Court to extend the interim order.
17 | P age

--- Page 18 ---
CA-Writ / 0609-2024
In Jayasinghe and Another v Pedris and Another [2005] 1 SLR 29 the
Court held that:
(ii) This is an appeal able order under section 754(2). The defendants
do not disclose exceptional circumstances warranting the exercise of
the reversionary jurisdiction. The only excuse given is that the
defendants attorney-at-law had taken down the wrong date, it is not
an excuse, and his negligence cannot be considered as an exceptional
circumstance.
In Pakiyanathan v Singaraja [1991] 2 SLR 205 the Court held that:
It is necessary to make a distinction between mistake or
inadvertence of an attorney-at-law or party and negligence. A mere
mistake can generally be excused; but not negligence, especially
continuing negligence. The decision will depend on the facts and
circumstances of each case. The Court will in granting relief ensure
that it's order will not condone or in any manner encourage the neglect
of professional duties expected of Attorneys-at-Law.
In light of the above judgments, negligent of a Counsel cannot be condoned
and this Cour under no circumstances will encourage the neglection of
duties of a Counsel. As such, in this case we see no basis to extend the
interim order.
Interim order is a discretionary remedy and the Petitioners cannot ask for
an interim order as a right. In such a situation he must be vigilant in
making application for extension. In this case, no application made for
extension, not once, twice. It shows there is a neglect on the part of the
Petitioners.
It is pertinent to draw the doctrine of  vigilantibus non dormientibus jura
subveniunt. The maxim is relevant as the Court look after the people those
are vigilant and not those who sleep over their rights.
18 | P age

--- Page 19 ---
CA-Writ / 0609-2024
Hence, considering the nature and the circumstances of the case, I
conclude that the application of the Petitioners to extend the interim order
cannot be considered at this stage.
Therefore, the objections raised by the Counsel for the 13th and 14th
Respondents is hereby accepted.
As agreed by all parties this matter is fixed for inquiry 23.01.2025.
JUDGE OF COURT OF APPEAL
M. T. Mohammed Laffar, J.
I Agree
JUDGE OF COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 9 ---
Order On: 18.12.2024
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
This leave to appeal application emanates from the Order of the Wakf Tribunal dated
06.04.2024 where the Tribunal appointed a receiver, removing the Trustees from the
Management and required the Petitioners who are the Trustees to hand over the possession
of the property at Maharagama to the said receiver.
This application deals with the N.D.H. Abdul Ghaffoor Trust established by the Deed of Trust
No. 2125 dated 21.11.1935 attested by John Wilson, Notary Public of Colombo. This Deed of
Trust involves two properties namely a plantation land (comprising of 3 buildings on one end
thereof and a plantation on the remainder) of total of 17 Acres in extent, situated at
Maharagama and more fully described in the First Scheule of the said Trust Deed and a
prime commercial land of approximately 386 perches (2  acres) situated in Grandpass,
Colombo 14 and more fully described in the Second Scheule of the said Trust Deed.
The Petitioners state that several old boys of the Gaffooriya Arabic College which is a
property described in the First Scheule of the said Trust Deed have made several applications
against the trustees of the said Trust in the Wakf Tribunal.
The Petitioners state that the Plaintiff- Respondents who are claiming to have interest in the
said Trust, filed a plaint in the Wakf Tribunal in case bearing No. WT/298/2023 inter alia
seeking as one of the prayers to appoint a receiver for the better custody and management of
the properties described in the Trust. The Tribunal delivered its order dated 06.04.2024
marked as P23 inter alia appointing a receiver by removing the Trustees from the

--- Page 10 ---
Management and requiring the Petitioners to hand over the possession of the property at
Maharagama to the said receiver.
The Petitioners have preferred the present leave to appeal application against the said order
of the Wakf Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 marked as P23 to set aside the same and seek an
interim order staying the operations of the said order and the proceedings of the Wakf
Tribunal Case bearing No. WT/298/2023.
We are mindful that a number of cases have been filed against the trustees in the Wakf
Tribunal. Against the Chairman of the said Wakf Tribunal, several cases have been filed in
the Court of Appeal.
In LTA/06/2021 connected with the Wakf Tribunal Case No. WT/273/2020 which deals with
the same Trust Deed where the Petitioners in this Case have challenged the order of the
Wakf Tribunal dated 04.02.2021 and sought an interim order on the basis that the said Deed
of Trust bearing No. 2125 is or is not a Muslim Charitable Trust. For convenience, the said
order of the Court of Appeal is reproduced below.
This application is filed by 1 to 11" Respondent Petitioners among several other
reliefs seeking to impugn the order of the Wakfs Tribunal dated 40 . February 2021
('P9*). The Respondent-Petitioners also sort the interim - and/or stay orders prayed
for in prayer (f), (g), (i), (), (k) and (1) of the Petition. This Court has already issued
the interim order prayed for in prayer (g) of the Petition, on 10" February 2022 and
has been extended from time to time.
Having carefully considered the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the
Appellant, learned State Counsel for the 1st Respondent and the learned Counsel for
the 3rd to 7th Respondents, we are of the view that, prima facie there is a serious

--- Page 11 ---
question of law need to be, gone into by this Court as to whether the Deed of Trust
bearing No. 2125 dated 21st November 1935, attested by John Wilson, Notary Public
(PI') is or not a Muslim Charitable Trust or Wakf.
Consequently, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the new Management
Committee of Ghaffooriya Arabic College is lawful, and also whether the Wakf
Tribunal has jurisdiction to accept, hear and determine the application made by the
applicant respondent and to make the impugned order marked P9
Accordingly, we formally issue notice on the respondent's name in the petition of this
court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs
(f), (g),( i),( j) , (k), and (l) until the final determination of this application.
According to the above-said order, the Court of Appeal has decided that there is a serious
question to be looked into whether the particular trust is or is not a Muslim Charitable Trust
and issued a stay order staying the further proceedings of the Tribunal.
We are mindful that the Wakf Tribunal has jurisdiction only if the particular trust comes
under the Muslim Charitable Trust according to Section 9J of the Muslim Mosques and
Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended.
Despite this order, the Tribunal has affirmed that the Trust established by Deed of Trust No.
2125 is a Muslim Charitable Trust and proceeded to appoint a receiver.
When the matter was supported, the Counsel for the Petitioners brought to the notice of the
Court the following facts.

--- Page 12 ---
A) Knowing the fact that the cases are pending before the Court of Appeal regarding whether
the Trust involved is a Muslim Charitable Trust or not which is a jurisdictional issue, the
Tribunal has proceeded to act on the basis that it is a Muslim Charitable Trust. The
jurisdiction of the Tribunal is limited only to the Muslim Trusts. But the main objection
taken by the Petitioners is that the said Trust is a Private Trust, therefore, the Tribunal
has no jurisdiction to hear the matter.
B) According to Section 671 of the Civil Procedure Code, the appointment of the receiver
should be done by the Court and no one else. For the purpose of convenience, the said
Section 671 is reproduced below.
Whenever it appears to the court to be necessary for the restoration, preservation, or
better custody or management of any property, movable or immovable, the subject of
an action, or under sequestration, the court may on the application of any party who
shall establish a prima facie right to or interest in such property, by order
(a) appoint a receiver of such property, and, if need be,
(b) remove the person, in whose possession or custody the property may be,
from the possession or custody thereof;
(c) commit such property to the custody or management of such receiver; and
(d) grant to such receiver such fee or commission on the rents and profits of the
property by way of remuneration as the court thinks fit, and all such powers
as to bringing and defending actions and for the realization, management,
protection, preservation, and improvement of the property, the collection of the
rents and profits thereof, the application and disposal of such rents and profits,

--- Page 13 ---
and the execution of instruments in writing, as the owner himself has, or such
of those powers as the court thinks fit.
We are mindful that the Tribunal has directed the Respondents to recommend a name which
means that the Tribunal has acted in contravention of Section 671 of the Civil Procedure
Code which directs the Court to appoint the receiver of the Trust. An excerpt of the order of
the Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 is reproduced below for easy reference.
We therefore, allow this application for the appointment of a Receiver and make order
removing the trustees, the 1st to the 12th defendants, from the management and
custody of the Gaffooriya Arabic College and the property at Maharagama and appoint
one of the persons named by the plaintiffs as Receiver, in terms of section 671 of the
Civil Procedure Code to manage the said Arabic College, which is the subject matter
of this case.
The Tribunal has delegated its powers to Respondents to nominate a receiver. The power
conferred on the authority (the Tribunal) by statute must be lawfully exercised by the
authority itself. This principle is discussed in Wade and Forsyths Administrative Law,
Twelfth Edition at page 255 - 257;
Delegation
Inalienable Discretionary Power
An element which is essential to the lawful exercise of power is that it should be
exercised by the authority upon whom it is conferred, and by no one else. The principle
is strictly applied, even where it causes administrative inconvenience, except in cases
where it may reasonably be inferred that the power was intended to be delegable.
Normally the courts are rigorous in requiring the power to be exercised by the precise

--- Page 14 ---
person or body stated in the statute, and in condemning as ultra vires action taken by
agents, sub-committees or delegates, however expressly authorised by the authority
endowed with the power.
One aspect of this principle is the rule that the participation of non-members in the
deliberations or decisions of a collective body may invalidate its acts. The decision of
a disciplinary committee, for example, is likely to be invalid if any non-member of the
committee has taken part in its proceedings. It is not clear that the mere presence of
a non-member will be fatal, although in one case Lord Wright MR said:
It would be most improper on general principles of law that extraneous
persons, who may or may not have independent interests of their own, should
be present at the formulation of that judicial decision.
Therefore, the question is whether the Tribunal has the power to delegate.
C) When the receiver was appointed, there was no quorum as required by Section 9D (3) of
the Muslim Mosques and Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended
which reads as follows;
Two members of the Tribunal shall form a quorum. No matter shall be heard
by the Tribunal unless a quorum is present.
This Court notes that when the receiver was appointed by the Chairman of the Wakf
Tribunal, the quorum required by the statute was not met.
Our Courts have considered that failure to meet the quorum as required by the statute will
go to the root of the matter.

--- Page 15 ---
In Anoma S. Polwatte v. Ms. L. Jayawickrama and Others SC WRIT Application No. 01/2011
decided on 27.07.2018, His Lordship Vijith K. Malalgoda PC, J held that;
When looking at the provisions of the above three provisions of the Act it is clear that
by the above provisions, a clear distinction had been made between the powers of the
Commission and functions of the Commission. As identified in section 3 referred to
above, when an offence is disclosed after an Investigation, Commission shall direct
the institution of proceedings and the said conduct of the Commission had been
identified within the Functions of the Commission. The powers of the Commission has
been identified under section 5 of the Act and under section 2 (8), such powers of the
Commission may exercise by its members either sitting together or separately.
Thus it is clear that the members of the Commission can exercise ancillary powers on
his own though the full complement of the Commission is not available at one given
time. But as for the exercise of functions such as the direction to be given to the
Director General, it is crystal clear that the Act has not provided for one member alone
to give such direction. However as already observed by me, R-1 refers to a directive
given by one member and in the said directive, it is not clear as to whether the reports
referred to, had been considered by the full commission before making such directive.
In the said circumstance, I have no hesitation to conclude that there is no valid
directive made under section 11 of the Act to institute criminal proceedings before the
Magistrates Court, with regard to the investigations carried out by the fraud
Investigation Unit of the Commission to Investigate Bribery and Corruption as
against the Petitioner to the present Application. I therefore conclude the directive
produced marked R-1 is patently illegal.

--- Page 16 ---
In Associated Motorways (Pvt) Ltd. v. Consumer Affairs Authority of Sri Lanka and Another
CA/WRIT/430/2015 decided on 16.11.2020, His Lordship Mahinda Samayawardhena, J. (as
he was then) held that;
Before I consider the Petitioners case on its merits, there is a preliminary issue to be
addressed, though technical in nature, which goes to the root of the matter. That is,
the validity of the impugned decision due to lack of quorum.
Item 8(2) of the Schedule to the Consumer Affairs Authority Act (read with section
3(4) of the Act) says The quorum for any meeting of the Authority shall be four
members. Learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioner submits that when the
impugned decision A18B was purportedly made on 27.11.2014, there was no quorum
of the Authority in the eyes of the law to make such a decision.
Further held that;
For the aforesaid reasons I hold that the impugned decision A18B is a nullity, as it
has not been made by a properly constituted panel of inquiry as required by law. In
other words, the decision has no force or avail in law due to the lack of quorum.
Therefore, in this instant case, the question is when the Chairman appointed the receiver
whether there was the quorum required by the statute.
In addition, the allegation made by the Plaintiffs was of mismanagement of the Trust. We
are mindful that before appointing the receiver, the Tribunal should have asked the
Petitioners to submit the accounts relating to the Trust to satisfy themselves of the allegation
made against the Petitioners. Simply appointing a receiver on the allegation made by the
Respondents is not expected from the Tribunal. Before the Tribunal appointed the person,
they should have asked for the proper accounts to be produced.

--- Page 17 ---
Therefore, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the receiver is lawful.
Accordingly, we grant the leave to appeal against the order dated 06.04.2024 made by the
Wakf Tribunal and we issue notice on all the Respondents named in the Petition to this
Court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs (e),
(f), (g) (h) and (i) until the final determination of this application.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
R. Gurusinghe, J.
I AGREE
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST
REPUBLIC OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an application for revision in
terms of Article 138 of the Constitution of the
Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka,
read with the High Court of the Provinces

Reverend Erol Chrissokumar Handy
C.A./ CPA No. 16/2024 Chairman,
