Chairman,

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 3 ---
Assemblies of God Ceylon
No.248, Negombo Road,
Ja  Ela.
PETITIONER - RESPONDENT  RESPONDENT
BEFORE : M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J. &
M. Ahsan. R. Marikar J.
COUNSEL : Nalin Ladduwahetty P.C. with Hafeel
Farisz and Ranjith Samarasekara for
the Respondent Petitioner- Petitioner.
Lakshan Dias for the Petitioner -
Respondent - Respondent.
ARGUED ON : 22.10.2024
DECIDED ON : 18.12.2024
M. Sampath K. B. Wijeratne J.
Introduction
The 1st and 2nd Respondent-Petitioner-Petitioners (hereinafter referred to as the
Petitioners) have filed this revision application against the Petitioner-
Respondent-Respondent (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent), seeking to
revise the judgment delivered by the High Court Judge of Puttalam on 14th
December 2023. The High Court Judge had refused to revise the order made by
the learned Magistrate of Anamaduwa on 13th October 2022 in an application
instituted under Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act No. (hereinafter referred to as the Primary Court Procedure Act).
Additionally, the Petitioners seek to have the aforementioned order of the
Magistrate be set aside.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 4 ---
Factual background
The Respondent initially filed a Petition on 7th February 2022 in the Magistrates
Court of Anamaduwa under Section 66(1)(b) of the Primary Courts Procedure
Act, which was subsequently amended on 8th March 2022. The learned
Presidents Counsel for the Petitioners alleged that the Respondent altered the
scope of the application in the amended Petition. However, as this matter was
not raised by the Petitioners in the original Court, I will not treat it as an issue
for determination by this Court.
Along with the information submitted to the Magistrates Court, the Respondent
also filed several documents to support his contention1.
In response, the 1st Petitioner submitted an affidavit along with several
documents to establish his possession2.
The Respondent filed a counter-affidavit and submitted documents to challenge
the Petitioners claim of possession3.
Analysis
It is undisputed that the subject matter of this application is the Bethel Church
located in Serukale, Siyambalagaswewa, Anamaduwa.
The Respondent claims to be the President, Chief Priest, and Head of the
Administrative Board of Directors of the Assembly of God of Ceylon,
established under Act No. . He asserts that approximately 45 pastors
serve under him, including the 1st and 2nd Petitioners. The 1st Petitioner serves as
a pastor at Bethel Church, located in Serukale, Siyabalagaswewa, Anamaduwa,
which was constructed using funds contributed by the devotees of the said
Chapter. The Respondent further states that the Church was built on land
purchased from its permit holder, Nirosha Priyangani. According to the
Respondent, the Assembly of God of Ceylon is the rightful owner and
custodian of the Church.
1 At pages 184 to 278.
2 At pages 326 to 366.
3 At pages 283 to 319.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 5 ---
According to the Petitioners, the 1st Petitioner obtained membership and a license
to evangelize on behalf of the Assembly of God of Ceylon around 2007, while
the 2nd Petitioner obtained the same around 2015. The Petitioners state that this
occurred after they began serving as priests at Bethel Church, Serukale,
Siyambalagaswewa, Anamaduwa, in 2005. They further assert that they had
already commenced their work as priests in the Siyambalagaswewa area around
the year 2000, well before 2005.
The Respondent stated that the Assembly of God of Ceylon received complaints
from devotees alleging that the 1st Petitioner had committed rape against the
female manager of the Church and that his wife, the 2nd Petitioner, was engaged
in an illicit affair involving undisciplined behaviour. Although the Respondent
made the serious allegation of rape, a grave offense under penal law, no
evidence, such as a police complaint, was produced.
According to the Respondent, these complaints were investigated by a
committee appointed by the Assembly of God of Ceylon. Based on the
investigation, the Petitioners were temporarily suspended from their roles as
pastors and servants of the Church on 21st November 2021. However, the
Petitioners, in a communication dated 23rd November 2021, rejected the
Assemblys decision. Subsequently, they resigned from their membership in the
Assembly of God of Ceylon, effective from 25th November 2021.
The Respondent alleges that, following their resignation, the Petitioners forcibly
occupied the Church premises for their personal use. Furthermore, the
Respondent claims that the Petitioners began using the Churchs address as their
personal address, despite their actual residence being located elsewhere.
The Petitioners agree with the Respondent in acknowledging that
Hettiarachchige Nirosha Priyangani is the rightful owner of the land on which
the Church stands. In support of this, the Petitioners submitted an affidavit sworn
by Nirosha Priyangani4, along with the counter-affidavit. The Grant issued in her
name and the corresponding plan5 were also attached. Additionally, the Register
4 X 1.
5 A 1 and A 2.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 6 ---
of Grants under the Land Development Ordinance6 submitted with the counter
affidavit further establishes Nirosha Priyanganis title to the land.
In her affidavit, Nirosha Priyangani states that, around 2005, she granted
permission to the 1st Petitioner, Dilhan Peiris, and a person named Anton Mee
Kauper Martin to build a Church on her land. She further states that she entered
into an agreement to sell7 the land to Anton Mee Kauper Martin. Nirosha
Priyangani, the landowner, categorically asserts that the Assembly of God of
Ceylon or its Chairman has no legal title to the Church situated on her land.
These well-established facts contradict the Respondents claim that the
Assembly of God of Ceylon owns the property, despite its legal capacity to hold
property.
Affidavits from three priests8 and four Christian devotees confirm that the 1st
Petitioner built the Church and conducted services there from 2005 onwards. The
devotees9, in their affidavits, further confirm that they have assisted Pastor
Manoj Dilhan Peiris, the 1st Petitioner, in his work over the years and that the 1st
Petitioner managed the affairs of the Church. Additionally, the parents of
children who participated in the projects conducted at the Church have also
provided affidavits affirming the 1st Petitioners possession of the Church for the
past seven years10.
The Respondent submitted similar affidavits, allegedly from neighbours and
devotees of the Church, stating that the 1st Petitioner is not in possession of the
Church. The affirmants further assert that the 1st Petitioner was appointed as a
priest of the Church by the Assembly of God of Ceylon, and since he has been
removed, he is no longer entitled to conduct services or stay at the Church11. All
the affidavits state that the 1st Petitioner does not reside at the Church but only
conducts services there. It is also stated that the Church was built with funds
provided by the devotees. According to the Respondent, the electricity and water
6 A 3.
7 A 4.
8 At pages 332 and 334 of the appeal brief.
9 At pages 335, 336 and 338, 339.
10 At page 340 to 344 of the appeal brief.
11 At pages 228 to 273 of the appeal brief.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 7 ---
bills for the Church were paid using funds from the devotees and the Assembly
of God of Ceylon. However, the electricity bills filed in the record are in the
name of the 1st Petitioner.
In support of the fact that the Church was the property of Assembly of God of
Ceylon, the Respondent submitted a letter12. However, the said letter itself refers
to the Church as your church (ඔබගේ ගේවස්ථානය) indicating that the Church
belongs to the 1st Petitioner. In the letter, the Church was accepted as a project
under the Assembly of God of Ceylon. Accordingly, an identification number
was also issued.
The Respondent contended that the Church is not a residential place but a place
where people gather for prayers. The Petitioners have not claimed that they
reside in the Church. However, it is important to note that to possess a building,
one does not necessarily need to reside in it. Conducting religious prayers and
similar activities can constitute physical possession. In the case of Jayasinghe
and others v. Loku Bandara13, His Lordship Samayawardhane J. held that actual
possession does not require uninterrupted physical presence throughout the day.
The Respondents contention is that he had constructive possession of the
Church. However, it is important to note that this possession was through the
Petitioners, the rival party.
His Lordship Samayawardhane J., sitting in the Court of Appeal (as His Lordship
then was) in the aforementioned case of Jayasinghe and others v. Loku
Bandara14, concluded that in an application under Section 66 of the Primary
Courts Procedure Act, if the dispute is between the licensee and the licensor, the
licensees possession cannot be considered as the possession of the licensor.
There is no allegation by the Respondent that he was forcibly evicted from the
Church. His contention is that the Assembly of God of Ceylon had continuous
possession from the inception of the Bethel Church.
12 At page 220 of the appeal brief.
13 [2019]2 Sri L.R. page 202.
14 Ibid.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 8 ---
In the case of Iqbal v. Majedudeen and Others15, it was stated that the law
recognizes two types of possession.
i. When a person has direct physical control over a thing at a given time,
he is said to have actual possession of it.
ii. A person has constructive possession when he, though not in actual
possession, has both the power and the intention at a given time to
exercise dominium or control over a thing either directly or through
another person.
In my view, the Petitioners' involvement in religious activities as members of the
Assembly of God of Ceylon is somewhat akin to an activity carried out under a
license granted by another, acting as an agent. Once the license is revoked, the
right to conduct activities under that license ceases to exist; however, the
possessory rights would not be extinguished.
In an application under Section 66 of the Primary Courts Procedure Act, the
Magistrate is not required to investigate title. However, in the case of
Shanmugasundara Kurukkal Sri Skandarajah Kurukkal v. Ramalingham
Ranarajah and Sixteen Others16 (C.A.), His Lordship A. H. M. D. Nawaz J., (as
His Lordship then was), observed as follows:
The Magistrate is not required to investigate the title of the disputed land or the
rights of the administrative body. In fact, he can use the evidence of title merely
to guide and aid his mind in coming to a decision upon the question of
possession, but he is precluded from deciding questions of title alone.
According to the Grant issued by the State, the subject land belongs to Nirosha
Priyangani, and therefore, she should be considered the owner of the building
standing on it as well. The dominion of a property is naturally vested in its true
owner. In this case, the true owner, Nirosha Priyangani, has affirmed in an
affidavit that she authorized the 1st Petitioner to build on her land and to maintain
the Church within the premises.
15 [1999]3 Sri L.R. 213.
16 [1987] 1 Sri.L.R. 94.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 9 ---
However, as I have already stated above, the primary consideration in an
application of this nature is not the title, but rather the actual physical possession.
Based on the analysis of the facts outlined in this judgment, I am of the view that
the Petitioners were in physical possession of the Bethel Church on the date the
information was filed, and that the Respondent had not been dispossessed within
the two months immediately preceding the filing of the information.
Breach of the peace
One of the arguments advanced by the Petitioners (Respondents in the
Magistrates Court) was that there was no breach of the peace to invoke the
jurisdiction of the Magistrates Court under Section 66(1) of the Primary Courts
Procedure Act. As it was held in the case of Velupillai and others v. Sivanathan17
and followed by several other decisions, including Punchi Nona v. Padumasena
and others18, when information is filed under Section 66(1)(a) of the Act, the
formation of the opinion as to whether a breach of the peace is threatened or
likely is left to the Police Officer inquiring into the dispute. The Magistrate is
not required to inquire whether a breach of peace is threatened or likely, as
jurisdiction is vested in the Magistrate to inquire into and make a determination
on the dispute.
However, when an information is filed under Section 66(1)(b), it is incumbent
upon the Magistrate to first satisfy himself as to whether there is a threat or
likelihood of a breach of the peace.
Nevertheless, in the recent case of Jayasinghe and others v. Loku Bandara19
(C.A.), His Lordship Samayawardhane J., having scrutinized Section 66(1)(a)
and (b) of the Primary Courts Procedure Act, the repealed Section 62 of the
Administration of Justice Law, and the corresponding Section 145 of the Indian
Code of Criminal Procedure, held that: When first information is filed under
Section 66 (1) of the Primary Couts Procedure Act, irrespective of whether the
first information was filed by the Police or a party to the dispute, the Magistrate
17 [1993] 2 Sri L.R., 123.
18 [1994]2 Sri L.R. ,117.
19 Supra note 13.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 10 ---
is automatically vested with jurisdiction under Section 66(2) to inquire into and
determine the matter. There is no further requirement for the Magistrate to
ascertain whether the breach of the peace is threatened or likely.
In any event, I observe that the learned Magistrate, in her impugned order, has
carefully analysed the question of whether there was a threatened breach of the
peace. The learned Magistrate has, inter alia, referred to a letter written to the
Assembly of God of Ceylon by the Petitioner, in which it is stated that the
devotees of the Bethel Church have divided into two factions, thereby creating a
potential breach of the peace.
The Respondent has produced a letter signed by several individuals stating that
the devotees are agitated due to the conduct of the 1st Petitioner, and there is an
imminent threat of a breach of the peace20. Additionally, an agent of the
Respondent has sent a letter to the Officer in Charge of the Pallama Police
Station, seeking police assistance to establish their title21.
Even when the evidence presented to the learned Magistrate is examined, this
Court observes that two factions have submitted affidavits in support of the
Petitioner and the Respondent, which contradict each other.
Consequently, based on the available evidence, I am satisfied that there was a
potential threat of a breach of the peace, as correctly concluded by the learned
Magistrate and upheld by the learned High Court Judge.
The Petitioners raised the following grounds to impugn the order of the learned
High Court Judge.
(i) There were no exceptional grounds
(ii) The learned High Court Judge failed to evaluate the principles of law
regarding constructive possession.
20 At page 274 of the appeal brief.
21 At page 277 of the appeal brief.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 11 ---
(iii) The learned High Court Judge erred in law and thereby caused grave
miscarriage of justice on the Petitioners by failing to analyse the purported
dispossession by the Petitioners.
I will begin by considering a judgment delivered by this Court on a similar issue.
In the case of Shanmugasundara Kurukkal Sri Skandarajah Kurukkal v.
Ramalingham Ranarajah and Sixteen others22 (C.A.), His Lordship Nawaz J.
considered a dispute between a Kurukkal (or Poosari) and the administrative
body of a temple. His Lordship examined whether the possession of the Kurukkal
satisfied the requirements of possession under Section 68.
According to the facts of the case, the administrative body of the temple claimed
to have some kind of right to summarily remove a priest. His Lordship
considered what gave them this power? Did they appoint him as a priest? If so,
did it entitle them to oust him in the manner in which he was removed?
It was an admitted fact that the members of the administrative body broke open
the closed door of the temple, to which the Kurukkal had the keys, secured it
with new locks, and took possession from him.
The learned Magistrate ordered that the Kurukkal, who had been dispossessed,
be restored to possession.
In the revision application filed against the said order, the learned High Court
Judge held that since the temple and its properties are always vested in the
administrative body of the temple, the body has the power to remove a priest at
any time. It was further held that merely having custody of the keys did not
amount to possession within the meaning of Section 68(3) of the Primary Courts
Procedure Act. The Kurukkal only held ritual rights to conduct the pooja and
should vindicate those rights through an action in the District Court.
Consequently, the learned High Court Judge overturned the decision of the
learned Magistrate.
22 CA(PHC) No.41/2004, Court of Appeal minutes dated 08.08.2018.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 12 ---
His Lordship observed that the learned High Court Judge overturned the decision
of the learned Primary Court Judge on the grounds that the possession of the
Kurukkal could not be equated to exclusive possession, similar to the possession
of a Bank Manager or a Hotel Manager.
In analysing the judgment of the learned High Court Judge, His Lordship
considered several judgments in which the elements of possession were
discussed. In the case Iqbal v. Majedudeen and others23, His Lordship U.D.Z.
Gunawardana J. observed that the words forcibly dispossessed in Section 68(3)
of the Primary Courts Procedure Act mean that dispossession took place against
the will of the person entitled to possess, and without the authority of the law.
In the course of the judgment, His Lordship Nawaz J. observed as follows:
In fact, there is no evidence, so to speak, to establish that the Respondent has
actual possession of this temple. It was the Appellant who had been in
possession of the temple premises by virtue of the fact that his presence therein
was necessitated by his functions and the fact that the key to the temple had
been in his custody at the relevant time of dispossession connotes actual
possession of the temple premises on the part of the Appellant. (Emphasis
added)
Finally, His Lordship Nawaz J., held that actual possession should be real and
tangible, meaning there should be effective occupation and control of the
property.
His Lordship concluded that the administrative body had ousted the Kurukkal,
who had been in possession of the temple premises, within a period of two
months preceding the date the information was filed.
The facts of the above case are almost identical to the case at hand. The parties
are not at variance that the Petitioners conducted the service of the Bethel Church
as Pastors.
23 [1999]3 Sri L.R. 213.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 13 ---
Consequently, this judicial precedence supports the view that the 1st and 2nd
Petitioners were in possession of the Bethel Church.
Whether there are exceptional circumstances
The primary consideration before examining the merits of a revision application
is whether exceptional circumstances exist that justify the Courts intervention,
as this serves as the gateway to relief.
The Petitioners have sought the exercise of this Courts revisionary jurisdiction
with respect to both the order of the learned High Court Judge and the order of
the learned Magistrate.
In the case of Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd and others v. Mercantile Hotels
Management Ltd24, Sharvananda C.J. observed that:
It is settled law that the exercise of revisionary powers of the Appellate Court
is confined to cases in which exceptional circumstances exist warranting its
intervention.
In the case of Divisional Secretary Kalutara v. Kalupahana Mestrige Jayathissa
and others25, the Supreme Court observed that:
It must be noted that the Respondents had invoked revisionary jurisdiction of
this court, which is discretionary remedy. Thus, if relief to be granted, the party
seeking the relief has to establish that, not only the impugned Order is illegal,
but also the nature of the illegality is such, that it shocks the conscience of the
court.
Based on the reasons outlined above, it is my considered view that the Petitioners
have demonstrated that the impugned orders of the learned Magistrate and the
learned High Court Judge are manifestly erroneous and, therefore, shock the
conscience of this Court, warranting intervention.
24 [1987]1 Sri L.R. at page 05.
25 SC Appeals 246, 247, 249, 250/14.

CA/CPA/0016/2024

--- Page 14 ---
Conclusion
In light of the above analysis, I hold that the Respondent cannot be considered
as having had constructive possession, and that the Petitioners were in
continuous actual physical possession prior to and at the time of filing the
information in the Magistrates Court. Furthermore, there was no dispossession
of either party within two months of the filing of the information.
For the foregoing reasons, I hold that the learned High Court Judge erred in
upholding the order of the learned Magistrate by misinterpreting the pertinent
statutory provisions and the relevant principles of constructive possession.
After considering all the submitted materials and the arguments of both Counsel,
this Court concludes that both the impugned orders of the learned Magistrate and
the learned High Court Judge cannot stand. Consequently, I allow the application
and, acting in revision, set aside the order of the learned High Court Judge dated
14th December 2023, as well as the order of the learned Magistrate dated 13th
October 2022.
I confirm the Petitioners' possession and direct that they be restored to possession
immediately, if they have been evicted.
Application allowed, subject to a cost of Rs. 50,000/-.
The Registrar of this Court is directed to communicate to the High Court of
Puttalam.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
M. Ahsan. R. Marikar J.
I Agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

Before : Hon. M Sampath K. B Wijeratne,J.(CA)

--- Page 3 ---
CPA 0039-2024
Counsels : AAL Vijith Singh with AAL A. Shihaara Shafeeq
Khan for the Respondents-Petitioner-Petitioner.
. AAL Anuruddha Dharmaratne with AAL Indika
Jayaweera for the Complainant-Respondent-
Respondent.
Supported on : 16.10.2024
Decided on : 06.12.2024
M. Ahsan R. Marikar, J. (CA)
Introduction
1) The Respondent-Petitioner-Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as the
Petitioner) had made this revision application against the Complainant-
Respondent-Respondent (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent) to
seek the reliefs prayed for in the petition dated 22nd April 2024.
2) The said reliefs sought in the Petitioners petition are reproduced as
follows;
a) Accept and maintain this application exonerating the Petitioner from
the delay in filing this application,
b) Issue notice on the Respondent,
c) Stay the further proceeding in the case No 1722 (නෙරපීම) before the
Honourable Magistrate Court until judgment or Order delivered in
the appeal case No CA (PHC)46/2002 and the case is terminated,
d) The appeal case No CA (PHC) 46/2022 and this revision application
to be taken together,
e) Set aside the Order dated 10th September 2019 of the Honourable
Magistrate of Bandarawela in case No 1722 (නෙරපීම),
f) Set aside the Order dated 18th January 2022 of his Lordship the
High Court Judge of Badulla in case No 94/2019,

--- Page 4 ---
CPA 0039-2024
g) For costs,
h) For such other and further reliefs.
Facts of this case
3) The Petitioner had sought in the prayer of the petition to set aside the
Learned Magistrates Order dated 10th September 2019 and to set aside the
Learned High Court Judges Order dated 18th January 2022.
4) This action pertains to the recovery of possession of state land, filed by the
Competent Authority in the Magistrates Court of Bandarawela.
5) The Magistrate had reviewed the facts, documents and granted the
Respondent-Competent Authority, permission to evict the Petitioner and his
occupants who were in possession of the quarters on the state land.
6) Aggrieved by the aforesaid Order, the Petitioner had filed a revision
application in the Provincial High Court of Badulla. The Learned High Court
Judge, having considered the relevant facts, had dismissed the Petitioners
revision application and had affirmed the Order of the Learned Magistrate.
7) Aggrieved by the aforementioned High Court Order, the Petitioner had filed
this revision application to invoke the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court,
on the grounds that the Learned High Court Judge had failed to consider
the quit notice under Section 3 of the State Lands (Recovery of Possession)
Act No. , which had not been served on the Petitioner.
8) Furthermore, the Petitioner had asserted that the identification of the land
was ambiguous in the application submitted by the Respondent to the
Magistrates Court.
9) As per the Petitioner, the aforementioned grounds had not been considered
by the Learned High Court Judge in the revision application filed by the
Petitioner in the High Court of Badulla.
10) In light of this, the Petitioner had sought the reliefs prayed for in the
petition.

--- Page 5 ---
CPA 0039-2024
Disputed facts
11) When this petition was supported by the Counsel for the Petitioner on 16th
October 2024, the Learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent objected
to the application and argued that there was no merit in proceeding with the
matter. After hearing the arguments on the application, the matter was
adjourned for an Order.
12) Considering the facts pertinent to this case and the arguments presented by
the Counsels, I am of the view that the following disputed points should be
examined to determine whether the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court
can be invoked;
I. Was the Learned Magistrate's Order dated 10th September 2019
properly evaluated by the Learned High Court Judge, taking into
account the disputes raised by the Petitioner in the High Court?
II. If so, can the application filed by the Petitioner to invoke the
revisionary jurisdiction be sustained?
I. Was the Learned Magistrate's Order dated 10th September 2019
properly evaluated by the Learned High Court Judge, taking into
account the disputes raised by the Petitioner in the High Court?
13) On perusal of the Learned High Court Judges Order dated 10th
September 2019, it is evident that the Learned High Court Judge had
considered the facts pertinent to the Magistrates Order in detail.
14) The Petitioner had filed the revision application against the Order of the
Magistrate by way of a petition dated 28th February 2020. In the said
petition, the Petitioner had raised three grounds for seeking a revision of
the Order issued by the Learned Magistrate;

--- Page 6 ---
CPA 0039-2024
i. The quit notice under Section 3 of the State Land (Recovery of
Possession) had not been served on the Petitioner.
ii. The Respondent is not the Competent Authority.
iii. The identity of the land from which the Petitioner is to be evicted is
ambiguous.
15) The Learned High Court Judge correctly articulated his position
regarding the Petitioners ground that the Respondent is not the
Competent Authority. His decision was based on the principles
established in the case of Divisional Secretary Manikhinna v
Jenudeen Buhurdeen 1
The scope of the inquiry before the Magistrate is circumscribed
strictly to two matters, and he has no jurisdiction to a beyond what
has been mandated by the Act. The Act particularly states that the
Magistrate shall not call for any evidence in support of the
Application, which shall be made in the Form prescribed by the Act.
Hence, in my view, it is unfair by the Magistrate, to set aside by the
Appellate Court the order of the Magistrate as an erroneous one on
totally different grounds. Then the Act shall be amended to widen the
scope of the inquiry before the Magistrate. In my view, if the
Respondent wants to challenge the decision of the Petitioner
(Competent Authority), that shall be done in a properly constituted
writ application, and not by way of an appeal filed against the
decision of the Magistrate. Merely because the word "inquiry" is used
in those sections, it is clear by reading those sections contextually
that conducting a full trial was never the intention of the legislature. If
that was the intention, as stated in section 8, the Magistrate cannot
proceed to hear and determine the matter forthwith. it is not
mandatory that the Magistrate shall fix the matter for the inquiry for
oral evidence to be led. What the Magistrate shall do is to give the
person summoned a fair opportunity to satisfy the Court that he has
a valid permit or other written authority of the State granted in
accordance with any written law. The person so summoned cannot
be allowed to convert it into a full-fledged trial, which will defeat the
intention of the legislature.
1 CA (PHC) 140/2013

--- Page 7 ---
CPA 0039-2024
16) It should be noted that the Learned High Court Judge explicitly
referenced the position taken by the Learned Magistrate in the Order,
wherein it was stated that the Petitioner had failed to produce a valid
permit to substantiate their claim of lawful possession of the disputed
land.
17) The Learned High Court Judge had drawn his attention to the decided
cases of Muhandiram v Chairman, No 111 Janatha Estate
Development Board 2 And M.C Magrate Perera v Divisional
Sectretary, Naula and another 3.
18) As per the aforementioned decided cases, it was determined that, under
Section 9 of the State Lands (Recovery of Possession) Act No. ,
the scope of the inquiry before the Magistrate is circumscribed by
determining whether the person notified can establish that they are not
in unauthorized occupation. To establish lawful possession, the
individual must produce a valid permit or any other written authorization
granted by the State in accordance with applicable law, provided that
such permit or authorization is valid, active, and has not been revoked or
rendered void.
19) In these circumstances, the Learned High Court Judge correctly
concluded that there is no requirement for the Competent Authority to
establish its status as the legitimate authority before the Magistrate.
20) The next issue raised by the Petitioner is that the aforementioned
eviction notice was issued for a land that was not properly identified. The
Learned High Court Judge, on page 10 of the Order, correctly identified
the boundaries of the disputed portion of the quarters and the land on
which it is situated. This fact had been established before the Magistrate.
2 (1992) 1 SLR 110
3 (CA/PHC/41/2010)

--- Page 8 ---
CPA 0039-2024
21) On the said grounds, when this matter was taken up to support the
argument was narrowed down as to whether the eviction notice had been
issued, as the eviction notice was not available in the docket.
22) Consequently, the Court requested the original case record from the
Magistrates Court of Bandarawela, in which the quit notice was
available. Therefore, the argument raised by the Petitioner cannot be
accepted.
23) Upon reviewing the Learned Magistrate's Order, it is clear that the
Learned Magistrate properly considered the provisions under Section
5(a), (b), and (c) of the State Lands (Recovery of Possession) Act No. , and, as prescribed, the eviction notice had been issued.
24) The High Court Judge had considered the aforementioned facts relevant
to the Magistrates Order and concluded that there was no basis to
invoke the Revisionary Jurisdiction of the High Court, as the Learned
Magistrate had correctly determined the facts.
25) At this juncture, I am of the opinion that there is no merit in issuing any
notice or proceeding with the application filed by the Petitioner.
II. If so, can the application made by the Petitioner to invoke the
revisionary jurisdiction be sustained?
26) In consideration of the foregoing facts and documents, I find no
substantive grounds presented by the Petitioner to justify setting aside
the Order made by the Learned High Court Judge, as a revision
application is a discretionary remedy. Moreover, the Learned High Court
Judge has fully addressed and examined the disputes raised by the
Petitioner before the High Court.

--- Page 9 ---
CPA 0039-2024
27) Further, I draw my attention to the decision of Divisional Secretary
Kalutara v Kalupahana Mestrige Jayatissa4;
It must be noted that the Respondents had invoked
revisionary jurisdiction of this court, which is
discretionary remedy. Thus, if relief to be granted, the
party seeking the relief has to establish that, not only
the impugned order is illegal, but also the nature of the
illegality is such, that it shocks the conscience of the
court
28) In the aforementioned decision, it was held that an impugned Order in a
revision application must not only be illegal but must also shock the
conscience of the court. In the present appeal, I do not find any
argument from the Petitioner addressing the grounds referenced in the
case of Divisional Secretary Kalutara v Kalupahana Mestrige
Jayatissa.
29) Upon careful review, it is apparent that the Learned High Court Judge
did not violate any legal provisions in rendering the decision. The Judge
thoroughly considered all relevant facts, including the proper service of
the quit notice, the Petitioners failure to produce a valid permit, and the
accurate identification of the boundaries of the disputed land. In this
regard, the Judges decision appears sound and in accordance with the
law.
30) Given these findings, and after considering all relevant arguments and
legal precedents, I am of the view that the Petitioner's appeal is devoid of
merit. The Petitioner had failed to provide any valid grounds to warrant
interference with the decision of the Learned High Court Judge.
31) Therefore, I do not consider that the Petitioner can seek any reliefs
prayed for in the petition of appeal dated 22nd April 2024.
4 SC Appeals 246,247,249,250/14

--- Page 10 ---
CPA 0039-2024
CONCLUSION
32) For the reasons set out above, I dismiss the Petition of Appeal dated 22nd
April 2024 subject to payment of Rs. 25 000/- cost to the Respondent.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
M Sampath K. B. Wijeratne, J. (CA)
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal

Before : Dhammika Ganepola, J.

Counsel : Padmasiri Bandara with R. Herath for the
Petitioner.

Respondents.

Respondent.
Supported On : 07.10.2024
Written Submissions : Petitioners : 21.10.2024
tendered On

--- Page 4 ---
Decided On : 19.12.2024
Dhammika Ganepola, J.
When this matter was taken up for support on 07 October 2024, the
learned Counsel for the Petitioners made submissions in support of the
application. However, the learned Counsel for the 13th Respondent took
up several preliminary objections in relation to maintainability of this
application. The Petitioners in this application are inter alia seeking the
following reliefs:
 Writs of Certiorari quashing the quit notice [P19] issued by the
3rd Respondent;
 the 1st Respondent decision dated 18th March 2024[P11(ii)]
granting a permit to the 9th Respondent to cultivate the land
depicted as CC and A in the Sub Division Plan No.
Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September 2016 and Sub Division Plan
No. KA/DSO/2020/502, and
 Writs of Mandamus directing the 1st Respondent to grant the
possession to the Petitioners of the land depicted in Lot 238 of
Village Plan No.140[P1] and also depicted as CC and A in the
Sub Division Plan No. Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September
2016[P2] and Sub Division Plan No. KA/DSO/2020/502 [P3] and
 grant a long-term lease to the Petitioners in respect of the
property in subject.
The Petitioners state that they have been cultivating rubber and other
crops in Lot No.328 of P1 and Lot CC of P2 for more than 40 years. The
predecessor of the Petitioners, one Ranpati Pathirage Rajapaksha had
come into know that the said property is a State land and had taken steps
to legalize his possession in around 1990 making multiple requests to
various authorities. However, no inquiry has been held in respect of such
requests. The Petitioners state that the 1st Petitioner and the 2nd and 3rd
Petitioners [wife and the children of deceased] inherited the property in
subject after the demise of the said predecessor in 2020.
In support of the position that the Petitioners are in possession of the
subject property, the Petitioners have submitted several receipts
pertaining to payment of acres tax, receipts on payment of the rubber

--- Page 5 ---
replanting project, rubber replanting permits and rubber replanting
payment receipts in respect of the impugned property. Apart from
tendering such documents, the Petitioners also rely upon the permit
P11(ii) issued by 9th Respondent in invoking writ jurisdiction of this Court.
It appears that said permit P11(ii) has been issued by the 9th Respondent
to cultivate the land without conducting a formal inquiry into the requests
made by the Petitioners to obtain leasehold rights to the property.
The Petitioners assert that under the above circumstances, the materials
and evidence to form an opinions formed by the competent authority to
evict the Petitioners from the impugned property are wrongful and that
the decision to evict the Petitioners is unreasonable and irrational.
In the case of Udagedara Waththe Anusha KumarinNikaathagoda vs.
Jayasinghe Mudiyanselage Chamila Indika Jayasinghe, Divisional Secretary
and Others CA/WRIT/293/2017 decided on 18.11.2019 His Lordship Justice
Arjuna Obeyesekere has held;
This Court wishes to emphasize, for the avoidance of any doubt that
the Competent Authority is not required in terms of the Act to carry
out an inquiry of the title of the person who is in unauthorized
possession of such land.
The principle then is that while no inquiry is needed to form an
opinion, there should be a rational basis to form the opinion that the
State is lawfully entitled to the land. The rational basis should satisfy
the Wednesbury test of reasonableness. Thus, a Competent
Authority would be acting reasonably if he were acting on the basis
of a Surveyor Generals plan, even if the occupant is claiming
prescription. The Competent Authority is not expected to, and
indeed is precluded from, carrying out an inquiry
Accordingly, a requirement exists for the Court to consider whether there
was a rational basis for the competent authority to form an opinion that
the State is lawfully entitled to the land. In light of the above, the Court is
of the view that this Court should consider whether the competent
authority had sufficient material to arrive at such opinion and as to
whether the competent authority has taken into consideration relevant
matters when forming such opinions.
The Honorable Attorney General has taken up the stance that the instant
application should not be entertained as the material facts of the case are

--- Page 6 ---
in dispute. The Petitioners state that the 6th Respondent who drew up the
Subdivision Plan No. Ka/BLT/14/521 dated 6th September 2016 [P2] had
demarcated the property as inclusive of private property of the Petitioners.
It is stated that there is an ongoing dispute in respect of the property
between the Petitioners and the 9th Respondent before the District Court
of Matugama bearing No. L/5175/2024. However, it is important to
observe that the Petitioners in their written submissions have stated that
they do not wish to challenge the legality of the said plans in the instant
application and that no such relief has been sought in respect of the
legality of said plans.
Additionally, on behalf of the 13th Respondents, several preliminary
objections such as delay, futility and misrepresentation of material facts
have been taken up. However, the considering the circumstances and the
facts involved in the application, this Court is of the view that it is
appropriate to consider such objections at the stage of hearing.
Based on the above and the circumstances of the application I am inclined
to issue formal notices on the Respondents.
It is observed that unless this Court stay the operation of the quit notice
marked P19 until the final determination of this application, the
application will be rendered nugatory. Accordingly, I issue the stay order
suspending the operation of the quit notice P19 until the final
determination of this application.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
Damith Thotawatta, J.

P. Kumararatnam, J.
This is an application in Revision preferred by the 1st Accused-
Petitioner (Hereinafter referred to as the Petitioner) challenging the
conviction and the sentence imposed by the Learned High Court Judge
of Badulla on 04.01.2024 against him.
2 | P age

--- Page 3 ---
CA (PHC)APN 115/2024
The Petitioner was indicted in the High Court of Badulla along with 2nd
Accused for criminal offences allegedly to have been committed on
10.08.2003. The charges in the indictment are re-produced bellow:
1. For committing robbery of a van bearing No. UP HF 4800 which
was worth about Rs.1,100,000/- and belonging to one Mahinda
Wijesinghe Gunawardena constitute an offence punishable under
Section 380 read with Section 32 of the Penal Code.
2. For committing the murder of Mahinda Wijesinghe Gunawardena
which constitute an offence punishable under Section 296 read
with Section 32 of the Penal Code.
The indictment was read over to the Petitioner and the 2nd Accused on
26.07.2010 and trial commenced subsequently. During the trial, the
prosecution had called 16 witnesses and marked productions P1 to
P18.
The learned High Court Judge had called for the defence having
satisfied that the prosecution had established a prima facie case
against the Petitioner and the 2nd Accused. The Petitioner and the 2nd
Accused made dock statements and closed their case.
After the submissions by the prosecution and the defence, the Learned
High Court Judge had convicted the Petitioner and the 2nd Accused for
the 1st Count and acquitted them from the 2nd Count. Thereafter, the
learned High Court Judge had sentenced them as follows:
Count 1
10 years rigorous imprisonment with fine of Rs. 15000/-. In default
12 months simple imprisonment.
Being aggrieved by the conviction and the sentence the Petitioner had
filed this revision application to this Court.
3 | P age

--- Page 4 ---
CA (PHC)APN 115/2024
The Petitioner had urged following reasons for filing this application
before this Court.
A. The Learned Trial Judge has erred in law by failing to consider
that the Prosecution had not proved the ingredients of the
offence of robbery which is described in section 379 of the Penal
Code.
B. The Learned Trial Judge has erred in law by failing to consider
Section 114 (a) of the Evidence Ordinance in the correct
perspective that a man who is in possession of stolen goods soon
after the theft is either the thief or has received the goods
knowing them to be stolen unless he can account for his
possession.
C. The Learned Trial Judge has erred in law by arriving at the
conclusion that the accused committed of offence of robbery due
to the fact that the van was in the possession of the Accused.
D. In any event, the sentence imposed on the accused is excessive
in the light of the facts and the circumstances of the case.
The Petitioner was acquitted from the charge of murder. As there was
no explanation with regard to the possession of stolen property, the
Petitioner argue that the prosecution should have amended the
indictment and convicted the Petitioner for the offence of theft or a
lesser offence. Further, the Petitioner had no previous conviction or
pending cases when he was convicted for charge of robbery. Hence, the
Petitioner submits, due to this, a serious miscarriage of justice has
occasioned and seek this Courts intervention in the exercise of the
extraordinary jurisdiction by way of revision.
4 | P age

--- Page 5 ---
CA (PHC)APN 115/2024
It is well settled law that the revision is a discretionary remedy that can
be granted only upon exceptional circumstances. The Petitioner
submits that items set out in paragraph 9 and 11 of the petition
constitute exceptional circumstances. The main complaint is that that
the Petitioner should have been convicted for a lesser offence.
In Wijesinghe v Tharmaratnam (Sri kantha Law Report Vol-IV 47), the
court held that:
Revision is a discretionary remedy and will not be available
unless the application discloses circumstances which shocks the
conscience of the Court.
In Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd. V Mercantile Hotels Management Ltd.
1987 1 SLR 5 the Court held that:
It is settled law that the exercise of the revisionary powers of the
appellate Court is confined to cases in which exceptional
circumstances exist warranting its intervention.
The reasons adduced for delay of 08 months to file this revision
application cannot be accepted by this Court. Further, the Petitioner
had not taken any endeavour to file an appeal against the conviction
and the sentence. Had he really wanted to lodge an appeal against
judgment of the learned High Court Judge of Badulla, he could have
done it through the prison.
Hence, considering the seriousness of the offence and the punishment
imposed on the Petitioner by the Learned High Court Judge, I consider
this is not an appropriate case to issue notice to the Respondent.
5 | P age

--- Page 6 ---
CA (PHC)APN 115/2024
Considering all the factors mentioned above, I conclude this is not an
appropriate case to issue notice to the Hon. Attorney General
(Respondent.)
Hence, I refuse notice in this case.
The Registrar of this Court is directed to send this Order to the High
Court of Badulla for information.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
SAMPATH B. ABAYAKOON, J.
I agree.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC
OF SRI LANKA
In the matter of an Application for Revision
in terms of Article 138 of the Constitution of
the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri
Lanka.
Court of Appeal Officer-In-Charge,
Revision Application No: Police Station,
CA (PHC) APN 118/2024 Yatawatta.
COMPLAINANT
High Court of Matale Vs.
Case No: MT REV 155/2019 Ekanayaka Mudiyanselage Pahala
Gedara Ekanayake,
Magistrates Court of Matale No.133/07, Lakshahena B, Udasgiriya,
Case No: 56190 Matale.
ACCUSED
Dodamwala Upasaka Gedara Sajeewani
Lalanthi,
Lakshahena C, Udasgiriya,
Matale.
CLAIMANT

--- Page 2 ---
AND BETWEEN
Dodamwala Upasaka Gedara Sajeewani
Lalanthi,
Lakshahena C, Udasgiriya,
Matale.
CLAIMANT-PETITIONER
Vs.
1. Officer-In-Charge,
Police Station,
Yatawatta.
2. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
RESPONDENTS
AND NOW BETWEEN
Dodamwala Upasaka Gedara Sajeewani
Lalanthi,
Lakshahena C, Udasgiriya,
Matale.
CLAIMANT-PETITIONER-PETITIONER

--- Page 3 ---
Vs.
1. Officer-In-Charge,
Police Station,
Yatawatta.
COMPLAINANT-RESPONDENT-
RESPONDENT
2. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Colombo 12.
RESPONDENT-RESPONDENT
Before : Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
: P. Kumararatnam, J.
Counsel : Hafeel Farisz with Sanjeewa Kodithuwakku and
Shannon Tillekerathne instructed by Nihara
Randeniya for the Petitioner.
: Osward Perera, S.C. for the State.
Supported on : 182024
Order on : 172024

--- Page 4 ---
Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
This is an application preferred by the claimant-petitioner-petitioner (hereinafter
referred to as the petitioner) seeking to invoke the discretionary remedy of
revision granted to this Court by Article 138 of The Constitution.
This matter was supported for notice on the respondent-respondents mentioned
in the petition, and also for an order staying the operation of the order dated 112024 by the learned High Court Judge of the Provincial High Court of Central
Province Holden in Matale, and also the order dated 052019 by the learned
Magistrate of Matale, until the final conclusion of this application.
The learned State Counsel who represented the Hon. Attorney General as well
as the complainant-respondent-respondent objected to the issuance of formal
notice in this regard and also the stay orders as sought on the basis that there
exist no obvious exceptional grounds for this Court to issue notice.
This is a matter where the accused person mentioned in the petition has been
charged before the Magistrates Court of Matale in Case Number 56190 for
having transported Mahogany and Gini Sapu timber valued at Rs. 62,717.92/=
in the vehicle bearing number 226-9439 without having a valid permit in terms
of the Forest Ordinance, which is an offence punishable in terms of section 25(2)
read with section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended.
The accused mentioned has pleaded guilty to the charge before the learned
Magistrate of Matale, and subsequently, has been sentenced.
Thereafter, the learned Magistrate of Matale has called upon the registered owner
of the vehicle involved in the offence to show cause as to why the vehicle should
not be confiscated in terms of section 40 of the Forest Ordinance.
At the inquiry held in that regard, the petitioner, being the registered owner of
the vehicle, has given evidence and another witness has also been called upon
to give evidence on behalf of the registered owner.

--- Page 5 ---
At the conclusion of the inquiry, the learned Magistrate of Matale, of his order
dated 052019, has decided to confiscate the vehicle involved in the offence
on the basis that the registered owner has failed to establish that she has taken
the necessary precautions to prevent the offence being committed, and also that
she has had the knowledge of the accused committing the offence.
The petitioner has preferred an application in revision seeking to challenge the
said order before the Provincial High Court of Central Province Holden in Matale.
The learned High Court Judge of Matale of his judgment dated 112024 has
dismissed the revision application of the petitioner on the basis that he finds no
reason to interfere with the order of the learned Magistrate of Matale.
The petitioner has preferred the instant application before this Court seeking to
challenge the order of the learned Magistrate of Matale, as well as the judgment
of the learned High Court Judge of the Provincial High Court of Central Province
Holden in Matale.
It is settled law that the Court of Appeal will intervene using its power of granting
the discretionary remedy of revision only under exceptional circumstances.
I would like to quote from the case of Sadi Banda Vs. Officer-In-Charge of
Norton Bridge Police Station (2014) 1 SLR 33, which I find relevant in the
above context.
The revisionary power of Court is a discretionary power. This is an
extraordinary jurisdiction which is exercised by the Court and the grant of
relief is entirely dependent of the Court. The grant of such relief is of course
a matter entirely in the discretion of the Court, and always be dependent on
the circumstances of each case. Existence of exceptional circumstances is
the process by which the extraordinary power of revision should be adopted.
The exceptional circumstances would vary from case to case and their
degree of exceptionality must be correctly assessed and gauged by the Court
taking into consideration all antecedent circumstances using the yardstick

--- Page 6 ---
whether a failure of justice would occur unless revisionary powers are
invoked.
It was held in the case of Hotel Galaxy (Pvt) Ltd Vs. Mercantile Hotels
Management Ltd (1987) 1 SLR 5 that;
It is settled law that the exercise of the revisionary powers of the appellate
Court is confined to cases in which exceptional circumstances exist
warranting its intervention.
In the case of Wijesinghe Vs. Thamararatnam (Sriskantha Law Report
Volume IV page 47), it was stated that;
Revision is a discretionary remedy and will not be available unless the
application discloses circumstances which shocks the conscience of the Court.
In the case of Vanik Incorporation Ltd Vs. Jayasekare (1997) 2 SLR 365, it
was observed that;
Revisionary powers should be exercised where a miscarriage of justice has
occasioned due to a fundamental rule of procedure being violated, but only
when a strong case is made out amounting to a positive miscarriage of justice.
It was held in the case of Rustom Vs. Hapangama and Co. 1978/79 2 SLR 225
that;
Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case there are no
such exceptional circumstances disclosed as would cause the Appellate
Court to exercise its discretion and grant relief by way of revision. Unless
there was something illegal about the order made by the trial judge which
has deprived the petitioner of some right, the justice of the case required that
the Court of Appeal would not in the circumstances of this case grant the
petitioner the indulgence of exercising its revisionary powers.

--- Page 7 ---
The proviso of section 40 of the Forest Ordinance as amended by Forest
(Amendment) Act No. , under which the learned Magistrate of Matale
has allowed the petitioner to show cause as to why the vehicle involved in this
incident, namely the vehicle numbered 226-9439, should not be confiscated
reads as follows:
Provided that in any case where the owner of such tools, vehicles,
implements and machines used in the commission of such offence is
a third party, no order of confiscation shall be made if such owner
proves to the satisfaction of the Court that he has taken all
precautions to prevent the use of such tools, vehicles, implements,
cattle and machines, as the case may be, for the commission of the
offence.
Our Superior Courts have held the constant view that all precautions stated in
the section does not mean every possible precaution, but precautions that could
have been taken under the given facts and the circumstances. It is well-settled
law that in an inquiry of this nature, it is incumbent upon the owner of the
vehicle to satisfy the Court that he or she took reasonably possible precautions
to prevent the commission of the offence, and also had no knowledge of such an
offence being committed.
As correctly determined by the learned Magistrate of Matale, as well as the
learned High Court Judge of Matale, the petitioner giving evidence before the
Magistrates Court has clearly admitted that she had the knowledge of the timber
being transported in the vehicle belonging to her. The driver of the vehicle,
namely the accused, who was charged before the Magistrates Court has
informed her of the fact of loading timber to the vehicle to be transported
elsewhere.
There is nothing in the evidence to show that the petitioner took any steps to
inquire from the driver whether he is going to transport timber that is permitted

--- Page 8 ---
to be transported without a permit or at least what kind of timber he is
transporting and its destination.
This shows that the petitioner clearly had the knowledge of the offence being
committed and also has failed to take reasonable precautions to prevent the
offence from being committed.
Hence, it is the view of this Court that the learned Magistrate of Matale was
correct in confiscating the vehicle, and the learned High Court Judge of Matale
was correct in determining that he has no reasons to interfere by exercising the
revisionary jurisdiction granted to the said High Court in terms of Article 154P
of The Constitution.
For the reasons as considered above, this Court finds no reason to issue a formal
notice in relation to this application or to grant stay orders as sought by the
petitioner.
Accordingly, the application is dismissed without the formal notice being issued.
The Registrar of the Court is directed to communicate this order to the Provincial
High Court of the Central Province Holden in Matale, and also to the Magistrates
Court of Matale for information.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
P. Kumararatnam, J.
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF SRI
LANKA
In the matter of an application under and in
terms of Section 46 of the Judicature Act No (as amended) for transfer of the
Magistrates Court of Colombo Court 3 case
Nos 15366/3/14.
CA-TRF-24/23
Ronald Michael Stanely
Permanently Residing at 4 Natalie Court
Cranbourne
Victoria 3977 Australia
Temporarily at 49 Lionel Edirisinghe Mw
Colombo 05.
Petitioner
Vs.
1. Officer in Charge
Police Station
Kirulapone
2. Hon. Attorney General
Attorney Generals Department
Colombo 12.
Respondents

--- Page 2 ---
Before : N. Bandula Karunarathna, P/CA, J.
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
Counsel: The petitioner is appearing in Person
Maheshika Silva, DSG for the Respondents.
Supported On: 18.11.2024
Written
Submissions : 05.12.2024 (by the Petitioner)
Order On: 19.12.2024
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
The Petitioner has preferred this application under section 46 (1) of Judicature Act No. seeking inter alia an order for the transfer of the action pending in the Colombo
Magistrates Court No. 3 case bearing No. 15366/03/14 to any other appropriate
Magistrates Court that this Court deems fit.
The Petitioner, a resident of Australia had entered into a legal agreement with one Mr.
Maithree Fernando to purchase a vehicle bearing No. NW KO 8841 and within three
weeks agreed to purchase the 2nd vehicle bearing No. NW KO 8836. However, the
documentation required for the 2nd vehicle was not completed. The Petitioner states that
since 2013, Mr. Fernando was paid a sum totaling Rs. 6.75 Million. In 2014, the Petitioner
sent several emails to the said Mr. Fernando to issue a receipt for Rs. 6.75 Million for
which no response was availed. The Petitioner states that thereafter, the Petitioner
received a letter from Mr. Fernando stating that two vehicles were given on rent
contradicting the agreement. The Fraud Bureau has initiated a case bearing No.
B83723/2/23 due to the said letter containing false and misleading information.

--- Page 3 ---
The Petitioner has stated that on 21.09.2014, Mr. Fernando and a mob had smashed the
windows of vehicle KO 8841, assaulted the Petitioner, and forcefully took possession of
the said vehicle. At the Police inquiry, Mr. Fernando provided a written guarantee
admitting that the vehicle was taken arbitrarily, that the damages would be paid and the
vehicle would be returned. Since the agreement was violated, the Police filed the case
bearing No. 15366/3/14. The Petitioner states that during the proceedings, the Counsel of
the Accused has used derogatory language against him and due to continuous verbal
abuse by the said Counsel, no Counsel was willing to represent the Petitioner. Further,
though several orders were issued by the Court to produce the said vehicles which were
claimed to be stolen, the Accused has failed to do so. The Petitioner further states that on
22.03.2022 the Petitioners Counsel was humiliated by the Counsels of the other parties
in the open court and the Honorable Magistrate had rejected the corrections made by the
Counsel of the Petitioner ridiculing him. Further, the Petitioner states that when the
Petitioners Counsel submitted a genuine medical, it was also rejected by the Court.
The Petitioner contends that the Learned Magistrate in connivance with the Legal
Counsels of the other parties is acting vindictively and maliciously against the Petitioner.
The Petitioners grievance is that the Learned Magistrates behavior will cause grave
injustice denying him of a fair trial.
This Court is mindful of Section 46 (1) of the Judicature Act No. that regulates
the transfer of a case or proceeding which lays down the following;
Whenever it appears to the Court of Appeal,
a. that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had in any particular court or place;
b. that some questions of law of unusual difficulties are like to arise; or

--- Page 4 ---
c. that a view of the place in or near which any offence is alleged to have been
committed may be required for the satisfactory inquiry into or trial of the same;
d. that it is so expedient on any other ground,
the court may order upon such terms as to the payment of costs or otherwise as
the said court thinks fit, for the transfer of any action, prosecution, proceeding or
matter pending before any court to any other court and accordingly in every such
case, the court to which any such action, prosecution, proceeding or matter is so
transferred shall, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this or any other
law, take cognizance of and have the power and jurisdiction to hear, try and
determine such action, prosecution, proceeding or matter, as fully and effectually
to all intents and purposes as if such court had an original power and jurisdiction.
If this Court has to consider the grounds on which the present application is in favour of
the Petitioner, there should be materials or valid reasons for this Court to come to a
conclusion that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had. We note that, none of the
Counsels who represented the Petitioner have given any affidavits that they were abused
or humiliated in the said Magistrates Court.
Our Courts have held that the Petitioner has to satisfy the Court if an allegation of bias
is made against the judicial officer. The reason is that the judicial officers are trained
officers and there is no reason for them to be biased.
In Abdul Hasheeb vs Mendis Perera and others (1991) 1 SLR 243 at 254, His Lordship
Justice G. P. S. De Silva (as he then was) held that;
In the subsequent authorities cited before us, two tests for disqualifying bias have
been formulated:-
(a) The test of real likelihood of bias; and

--- Page 5 ---
(b) The test of reasonable suspicion of bias.
Further referring to the judgment of Lord Denning in Metropolitan Properties Co (F.G.C)
Limited v. Lannon (1968) 3 All ER 304, His Lordship held that;
It would appear that Lord Denning was inclined to adopt the 'real likelihood' test
but said that it was satisfied if there were circumstances "from which a reasonable
man would think it likely or probable that the justice or the chairman, as the case
may be, would, or did, favour one side unfairly at the expense of the other". Lord
Denning emphasized that "the court looks at the impression which would be given
to other people". "The reason" he said "is plain enough, Justice must be rooted in
confidence; and confidence is destroyed when right minded people go away
thinking; the Judge was biased.
The dictum of His Lordship Justice G. P. S. De Silva was followed by His Lordship Arjuna
Obeyesekere J (as he then was) in Anurudhdha Lihinikaduwa v. Sinnaiya Sooriyakumar
CA (Transfer) Application No: 12/2018 decided on 21.09.2018, where it was held that;
In these circumstances, can it be said that a reasonable right thinking man would
think the learned Magistrate has favoured the prosecution at the expense of the
Petitioner or that the Petitioner would not receive a fair and impartial trial? This
Court does not think so. The accusation made against the learned Magistrate, with
a view to demonstrating bias on his part, is therefore unfounded. Thus, even if the
less stringent of the test is applied, the Petitioner has failed to establish a
reasonable suspicion of bias on the part of the learned Magistrate. In these
circumstances, this Court rejects the argument of the Petitioner that he would not
receive a fair and impartial trial, before the Magistrate's Court of Jaffna.
I am mindful of the following sentiments of His Lordship Justice G. P. S. De Silva (as he
then was) in the above said case;

--- Page 6 ---
In this view of the matter, it seems to me that the facts set out in the petition are
too remote and too tenuous in character to found an allegation of bias on the part
of a judicial officer, who it must be remembered, is one with a trained legal mind.
As submitted by Mr. Pullenayagam, it is a serious matter to allege bias against a
judicial officer and this court would not lightly entertain such an allegation The
totality of the circumstances relied on by the petitioners, do not show that the
Judge has extended favours to one side "unfairly at the expense of the other" and
I accordingly hold that the allegation of bias has not been established.
In the instant case, even if we apply the test of reasonable suspicion of bias, the Petitioner
has failed to produce any material before this Court that the Learned Magistrate was
biased against the Petitioner. The fact remains that most of the allegations made by the
Petitioner are based on the cross-talks between the lawyers.
In view of the reasoning above, we dismiss the application.
No Order for cost.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. Bandula Karunarathna (P/CA), J.
I AGREE
PRESIDENT OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

ORDER
This Order pertains to whether notice is to be issued and interim reliefs are to be granted.
The Petitioner instituted this application by petition dated 31.03.2023 praying for the
following reliefs:
a. Issue notice to the Respondents
b. Issue a mandate in the nature of a writ of certiorari to quash the decision contained
in document marked as P7 Ampara Land Registry Volume/Folio LDO H 24/83 to

The facts of this case are briefly as follows:
According to the petition, the Petitioner claims to be the eldest son of the one Rankoth Gedara
Nandasena who received two Grants for two lots of land by Grant bearing Nos. Am/Pra/3273
and Am/Pra/3265. The Petitioner states that for the said Grant No. 3273, the Petitioners
father had nominated the Petitioners two brothers namely Rankoth Gedara Somarathne and
Rankoth Gedara Ariyawansa as the successors to the said land and such nomination had
been registered in 1991. The Petitioner further avers that he has been cultivating two acres
of the said land since 1972 with his father. The Petitioner states that, the said original
grantee passed away on 04.07.1994.
According to the petition, the 1st and 2nd Respondents had made an application under Section
49 of Land Development Ordinance No. as amended (hereinafter referred to as the
Ordinance) to the 3rd Respondent on 06.03.2020 requesting to be the successors of the said
land in question on the basis they were nominated by the original grantee. Accordingly, steps
were taken. The Petitioner states that after considering the application, the 3rd Respondent
has taken steps under Section 58 of the Ordinance to effect their succession and sent it for
registration to the Registrar of Land which was accordingly effected by registering it in the
Land registry on 10.06.2021.
The Petitioner states that by letter 23.08.2022, the Petitioner informed the 3rd Respondent
that the Petitioner has been in possession of the land in question for the last 40 years and
that the decision of the 3rd Respondent is contrary to Section 68 of the Ordinance, thereby
requesting to cancel the said decision to register said land and act under Section 72 of the
Ordinance on the premise he is the eldest son of the original grantee.

--- Page 4 ---
Further, the Petitioner averred that the 1st and 2nd Respondents have filed a case against the
Petitioner in the District Court of Ampara bearing No. 873/L for a declaration of title to the
land in question and to eject the Petitioner from the land in question.
The main contention of the Petitioner is that the decision of the 3rd Respondent marked as
P7, to accept and register the 1st and 2nd Respondents as successors or owners of the said land
is contrary to Section 68 of the Ordinance as they have failed to make an application within
the stipulated time.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court seeking a writ of
Certiorari to quash the decision marked P7.
One of the main objections taken by the Respondents is that though the Petitioner claims to
be the eldest son of the deceased original grantee, he has failed to provide any evidence before
this Court to establish his rights. Further, the Respondents aver that the document marked
P7 that is sought to be quashed by the Petitioner is not a decision but an extract from the
folio of the Ampara Land Registry, involving a ministerial act done by the Land Registrar on
the direction of the 3rd Respondent. However, the Petitioner has failed to challenge and place
the decision of the 3rd Respondent accepting the 1st and 2nd Respondents as the successors to
the land in dispute before this Court.
In this context, the question is whether this Court is inclined to issue a Writ of Certiorari as
sought by the Petitioner. The concept of availability of Certiorari is considered in the
following scholarly authority.
Sunil F.A.Coorey, Principles of Administrative Law in Sri Lanka, Fourth Edition Volume II-
Page 911, states;
The circumstances in which certiorari and prohibition will be available have been
summed up by Lord Justice Atkin, an English judge, in the following famous words
which on numerous occasions have been cited and followed by our courts:

--- Page 5 ---
" Whenever any body of persons having legal authority to determine questions
affecting the rights of subjects, and having the duty to act judicially, act in excess of
their legal authority they are subject to the controlling jurisdiction of the King's Bench
Division exercised in these Writs."
This dictum has been analyzed as follows as laying down four conditions which must
be satisfied for certiorari or prohibition to issue:-
" Whenever any body of persons, (firstly) having legal authority, (secondly) to
determine questions affecting the rights of subjects, (thirdly) having the duty to act
judicially, (fourthly) act in excess of their legal authority, they are subject to the
controlling jurisdiction exercised by these writs."
In the instant case, the non-availability of the decision made by the 3rd Respondent is fatal.
Be that as it may, the Petitioner has failed to establish that he is the eldest son of the
deceased original grantee. To be eligible under Section 72 of the Ordinance, the Petitioner in
this case needs to prove that the nominated successors failed to succeed.
For easy reference, Section 72 is reproduced thus:
If no successor has been nominated, or if the nominated successor fails to succeed, or
if the nomination of a successor contravenes the provisions of this Ordinance, the title
to the land alienated on a permit to a permit-holder who at the time of his or her death
was paying an annual instalment by virtue of the provisions of section 19 or to the
holding of an owner shall, upon the death of such permit-holder or owner without
leaving behind his or her spouse, or, where such permit-holder or owner died leaving
behind his or her spouse, upon the failure of such spouse to succeed to that land or
holding, or upon the death of such spouse, devolve as prescribed in rule 1 of the Third
Schedule."

--- Page 6 ---
In the instant case, upon the application of the 1st and 2nd Respondents to the 3rd Respondent,
the 3rd Respondent has alienated the land in suit under Section 84 (b) of the Ordinance for
due registration of their nomination which reads as follows:
If the permit-holder is not survived by his or her spouse or if the spouse does not
succeed to the land, any other person who is a duly nominated successor of the
deceased permit-holder shall be entitled to succeed to that land on such person
obtaining a permit from the Government Agent under the provisions of this Ordinance
to occupy that land.
Application of the above Sections in conjunction shows that the 1st and 2nd Respondents who
are the nominated successors to the land in dispute have lawfully succeeded to the land.
Thus, the Petitioners claim does not stand.
This Court is also mindful that the Petitioner was given the land described in Grant No. 3265
on the basis that he was the nominee of the said original grantee namely Rankoth Gedara
Nandasena on 12.05.1995.
For the above said reasons, we dismiss the application with costs of Rs. 100,000/-
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. BandulaKarunarathna (P/CA), J.
I AGREE
PRESIDENT OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
