ORDER
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
This order pertains to whether to issue notice to the Respondents and grant interim
orders.
The Petitioner instituted this action by petition dated 18.08.2020 seeking inter alia writs
of Certiorari to quash the orders made by the minister pertaining to registration and
issuance of licences to tuskers and elephants 1991 contained in extraordinary gazette
notification bearing No. 662/4 dated 14.05.1991 marked "P-5" and the amended
indictment dated 02.12.2019 marked "p-3" in the case bearing No. HC (TAB) 504/19 of the
High Court-at-bar holden in Colombo.
The relevant facts of this case are as follows:
According to the petition, the Petitioner owns tamed/domesticated elephants and provides
such elephants to temples for Perehara and to government departments for their
functions. The Petitioner states that the Petitioner and 6 others were indicted before the
Permanent High Court-at-Bar holden in Colombo under the case bearing No.
HC/PTB/1/3/2018 by the indictment dated 08.10.2018 where the said indictment was
dismissed and the Accused were discharged by the Court.
The Petitioner further states that the Petitioner and 7 others were again indicted before
the High Court-at-Bar holden in Colombo by the indictment dated 22.07.2019 containing
36 charges in the case bearing No. HC (TAB) 504/19. As per the petition, the said

--- Page 5 ---
indictment was amended on 02.12.2019 where 28 charges levelled against all the Accused
pertaining to 5 elephants bearing registration Nos. 163, 164, 202, 303, and 350 which
were in the custody of the Petitioner at the time the said elephants were taken into the
custody of the Department of Wildlife Conservation.
The Petitioner further avers that during the prosecution trial on 16.12.2019, through the
witnessed marked PW 01, the prosecution marked an extraordinary gazette notification
bearing No. 662/4 dated 14.05.1991 marked as P5 which contains orders/regulation made
by the Minister in charge of the subject regarding registration and issuance of licences to
tuskers and elephants known as Order pertaining to registration and issuance of licences
to tuskers and elephants 1991. The Petitioner states that during the cross-examination,
no witness testified that the order in the said gazette notification had been presented to
the Parliament and approved by the Parliament. The Petitioner further states that the
witness marked PW 02 admitted that orders made under the provisions of the Fauna and
Flora Protection Ordinance as amended by Act No. and Act No.
(hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance) need to be approved by the Parliament in order
for the said orders to be valid and forceful.
The Petitioner states that however, the Learned Judges of the High Court-at-Bar
delivered its order dated 22.06.2020 marked as P8 inter alia holding that it is established
that the orders made by the Minister contained in the said gazette notification have been
approved by Parliament and that in any event when considering the provisions of the
Ordinance, the regulations contained in the said gazette notification are not material to
this case. This Court notes that this particular order was not challenged in this
application.
The Petitioner further states that the Learned Judges of the High Court-at-Bar delivered
another order on the same day acquitting the 3rd, 4th, 6th and 8th Accused and deciding to

--- Page 6 ---
call defense in relation to the 1st, 2nd, 5th and 7th Accused. Thereafter, the Accused appealed
against the said orders of the Learned Judges of the High Court-at-Bar. The Petitioner
further states that the 6th Respondent made an application under the Right to Information
Act No. to the Information Officer of the Parliament to ascertain whether the
orders made by the Minister contained in the said gazette notification have in fact been
approved by the Parliament.
The Petitioner further states that as per the charges contained in the said indictment, the
Petitioner has been charged under Section 22A (1) and 22A(7) of the Ordinance for having
in his custody elephants that have not been duly registered and in respect of which
licences have not been issued under the provisions of Ordinance and under Section 5 (3)
of the Public Property Act.
The main contention of the Petitioner is that the amended indictment dated 02.12.2019
marked P3 cannot be maintained against the Petitioner on the basis that the orders made
by the Minister in relation to registration and issuance to tuskers and elephants marked
P5 have not been presented to and approved by the Parliament, therefore are void ab
initio.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Court seeking inter
alia writs of Certiorari to quash the order made by the Minister marked P5 and the
amended indictment dated 02.12.2019 marked P3.
At this juncture where a public document and its force in law is challenged, this Court is
mindful of Section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance and Illustration (d) to the said Section
which read as follows:
The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have
happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human

--- Page 8 ---
Further, this Court is mindful of the prosecutorial discretion that the Attorney General is
conferred with to institute criminal proceedings by filing an indictment. Our Courts have
extensively discussed this principle in the following judgment;
In Mohamed Imad Ibthisam Fakhir v. Hon. Attorney General CA (Writ) Application No:
74/2021 decided on 26.03.2021, His Lordship Arjuna Obeyesekere, J (as he then was) held
that;
While the Attorney General has the discretion to institute criminal proceedings,
such discretion is generally referred to as the prosecutorial discretion in the
Common law jurisdictions, with the Attorney General or the Director of Public
Prosecution, as the case may be, being conferred with the prosecutorial powers to
institute criminal proceedings. It would therefore be appropriate to consider at the
outset whether the power of the Attorney General to forward indictment against
persons who are suspected to have committed an offence is amendable to the Writ
jurisdiction conferred on this Court by Article 140 of the Constitution, and if so,
the circumstances in which a Court will interfere with that power by way of judicial
review.
Further held;
A review of the English cases in this area show that while judicial review is
available in respect of the prosecutorial discretion in order to prevent any abuse
by the prosecuting authorities, the English Courts are mindful of its impact on the
criminal justice system, and has therefore clearly indicated its extreme reluctance
to intervene by way of judicial review.
A similar approach has been taken by the Supreme Court of our country in respect
of decisions of the Attorney General.

--- Page 9 ---
In light of the above judicial pronouncement, it is evident that the Honourable Attorney
General has the discretion to file indictments based on the law and the evidence available.
In the instant case, the main argument brought forward by the Petitioner is that the
amended indictment dated 02.12.2019 is not valid as the law on which such indictment
was based, has no force of law. Nevertheless, this Court accedes to the presumption laid
down in Section 114 of the Evidence Ordinance unless it is proven otherwise. When the
Honourable Attorney General decided to send the indictment, he relied on the particular
gazette which is in force. Therefore, the amended inditement filed by the Honourable
Attorney General exercising the prosecutorial discretion is in accordance with the law.
In view of the above reasoning, we dismiss the application.
No order for costs.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. Bandula Karunarathna (P/CA), J.

This order pertains to whether to issue notice and to grant interim reliefs.
The Petitioner instituted this action by petition dated 08.04.2024 seeking the following

The factual matrix concerned in this case is as follows:
According to the petition, the Petitioner is a company with limited liability and registered
under the Companies Act No. . The Petitioner states that the Petitioner and the 6th
Respondent Union entered into Collective Agreements from time to time and last of which
was signed on 12.12.2014 effective for a period of 3 years from 01.06.2014 to 31.05.2017 which

productivity pay in the United States Dollars and pay in Sri Lankan Rupees to the members
of the 6th Respondent Union and that such exchange rate to be determined at the prevalent
exchange of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. According to the Petitioner, the said productivity
pay was made available to the members of the 6th Respondent as set out in the said
repudiated Collective Agreement and according to such Agreement, the exchange rate on
which the said productivity pay was to be calculated on Internal exchange rates published
by the Company each month.
The Petitioner states that in or around 20.07.2022, the 6th Respondent lodged a complaint
marked as P5 against the Petitioner to the Commissioner of Labour (Industrial Relations)
alleging inter alia that the productivity pay of the members of the 6th Respondent had been
reduced contrary to Annexure A of the Agreement marked P2. Further, by letter dated
24.11.2021 marked as P6, the 6th Respondent raised the same issue to the former Minister of
Labour. The Petitioner further states that as a result of the pandemic and the consequent
grounding of all aircrafts, the Petitioner was compelled to take steps to mitigate its losses
and as such a decision was reached under the auspices of the then Minister of Skills and
Development and Employment and Labour Relations on 04.05.2020 to permit inter alia the
reduction of salaries etc.
The Petitioner states that after several rounds of discussions pertaining to the 6th
Respondents complaint, an inquiry was held on 03.03.2022 chaired by the Commissioner of
Labour (Industrial Relations). Further, the Petitioner states that the Employers Federation
of Ceylon on behalf of the Petitioner set out the position of the Petitioner as a response to the
documents marked P5 and P6 and requested the 3rd Respondent to conclude the matter.
According to the Petitioner, the 6th Respondent by letter dated 15.02.2023 marked as P11
moved the Commissioner of Labour (Industrial Relations) to refer the purported dispute to
arbitration. Thereafter, the 3rd Respondent by letter dated 07.07.2023 marked as P12
informed the Petitioner that in the absence of a resolution to the purported dispute, the said
matter has been referred to arbitration under Section 4 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act No.

--- Page 5 ---
as amended (hereinafter referred to as the Act). As per the Notice dated 20.10.2023
marked as P13, the dispute sough to be referred to arbitration was;
Whether the Flight Attendants of Sri Lankan Airlines Limited has been caused
injustice in the receipt of productivity pay in Sri Lankan rupees by an exchange rate
lesser than the rate determined by the Central bank of Sri Lanka for USA Dollars
being used and if so, to what relief they are entitled.
The Petitioner received a Notice dated 17.11.2023 signed by the 2nd Respondent informing
that as per the powers vested in the 1st Respondent, the Minister under Section 4(1) of the
Act, the 4th Respondent was appointed as the Arbitrator and a further Notice was received
by the Petitioner dated 30.11.2023 signed by the 1st Respondent appointing the 4th
Respondent as the Arbitrator.
The Notice dated 11.12.2023 marked as P16 informed the Petitioner that the purported
Arbitration has been commenced by the 1st Respondent under No. A/87/2023.
The main contention of the Petitioner is that the decision of the 1st Respondent to refer the
purported dispute to Arbitration is unlawful and ultra vires.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Court seeking inter
alia a writ of Certiorari quashing the Notifications marked P13, P14, P15 and P16.
This Court notes that the primary gravamen of the Petitioner is that the 1st Respondent has
failed to act in terms of Section 4 (1) of the Act when referring the dispute for arbitration.
For easy reference, Section 4 (1) of the Act is reproduced below.
The Minister may, if he is of the opinion that an industrial dispute is a minor dispute,
refer it, by an order in writing, for settlement by arbitration to an arbitrator appointed
by the Minister or to a labour tribunal, notwithstanding that the parties to such
dispute or their representatives do not consent to such reference.
According to the above Section, the Minister should form the opinion that the dispute
involved is a minor industrial dispute before referring such a dispute for arbitration.
This Court is mindful of the context in which this dispute arose. When the country was facing
the financial crisis, the exchange rate for dollars was beyond Rs. 400. In that context, the 6th

--- Page 6 ---
Respondent referred the matter to 3rd Respondent informing that there is a dispute. The fact
remains that the Petitioner was paying the particular productivity pay based on the internal
exchange rate of the Company. We are mindful that once the industrial dispute was referred
to the Arbitrator under Section 4 (1), he has to hear the evidence to the dispute and then
make an award. The Arbitrator has to act judicially in making the ultimate award which is
binding on the parties. Therefore, the opinion of the Minister with regard to whether there
is a minor industrial dispute is important. There is no indication in the Act as to what
constitutes a minor dispute. Thus, the Minister needs to form the opinion that the dispute is
a minor dispute. If not, the Minister can forward such dispute to Labour Court for settlement.
We are mindful that there was a Collective Agreement between the parties before the dispute
arose.
We are mindful that the 1st Respondent has failed to file any written submission or
Statements of Objection as to how the opinion was formed for this dispute by Minister.
Our Courts have considered Section 4(1) of the Act and broadly discussed the aspect of
forming the opinion by the Minister when referring a matter for arbitration.
In Volanka Ltd V. Seneviratne Minister Of Labour And Others (2000) 2 SLR 19 at 23  24,
His Lordship De Silva J held that;
Section 4 of the Act confers powers on the Minister to refer by an order in writing an
industrial dispute if he is of the opinion that the industrial dispute is a minor dispute
for settlement by an arbitrator appointed by him. The order of reference is an
administrative act of the Minister who has to form an opinion as to the factual
existence or apprehension of an industrial dispute (Aislaby Estate Ltd. Vs.
Weerasekara(1)). Justice Pathirana in the same case at page 253 stated that "I go still
further and take the view that section 4(1) of the Act vests the Minister with an
amplitude of power (subject only to the fetter that he is referring an industrial dispute
within the meaning of the Act) to order in writing once he is of the opinion that the
industrial dispute is a minor dispute for settlement by arbitration to the Labour
Tribunal . as the Minister is acting solely in an administrators capacity and not
judicially or quasi judicially. The concluding words in section 4(1) "notwithstanding
that the parties to such dispute or their representatives do not consent to such a

--- Page 7 ---
reference", in fact highlight the amplitude of power vested by section 4 in the
Minister".
In Standard Chartered Bank v. The Minister of Labour Relations and Manpower and Others
CA (Writ) Application No. 231/2009 decided on 17.07.2019, His Lordship Arjuna Obeyesekere
J held that;
Page 19,
It is the view of this Court that in terms of Section 4(1}, the Minister must form the
opinion that there exists an industrial dispute, prior to making any reference of such
dispute for resolution by arbitration. This Court is further of the view that where such
a reference is challenged, as in this application, the Minister must explain the matters
that were considered by him in forming such an opinion, or, as submitted by the
learned President's Counsel for the Petitioner, that the "Minister had applied a
judicial mind or even an objective mind, or with all due deference a sensible mind to
the matter".
Page 22,
This Court is of the view that in terms of Section 4(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act,
the Minister is not obliged to refer for arbitration, each and every dispute that he or
she is presented with. The Minister must look at each request objectively and exercise
his discretion judiciously. The fact that the Minister has a discretion is clearly
established when one considers that the Minister may refer for arbitration only if, "he
is of the opinion that an industrial dispute is a minor dispute". How does he form an
opinion that there exists an industrial dispute and that such dispute is a minor
dispute? Is it only by considering the argument advanced by the employee or should
the Minister also consider the position of the employer, as well as any other matters
that the Minister may consider relevant? This Court, whilst not subscribing to the
view that it is mandatory for the Minister to obtain the views of all parties prior to
making a reference under Section 4(1), takes the view that in this application, given
the background circumstances such as the inquiry under the TEW Act, and the
litigation challenging the findings of the Inquiry Officer, the Minister was under a
duty to consider the documents 'X10', 'XU' and 'X12' prior to forming an opinion that

--- Page 8 ---
there exists an industrial dispute. Unfortunately, the Minister has not done so, and
therefore it is the view of this Court that the Minister has failed to take into
consideration relevant matters, prior to arriving at a decision. The learned Senior
Deputy Solicitor General for the 1st and 2nd Respondents had submitted that in terms
of Section 4(1), the consent of the parties is not required for a reference and that this
is an indication that the Minister does not have to consult the other party, prior to
making the reference to arbitration. Whilst agreeing that the consent of the parties is
not required, this Court is of the view that this is not an indication that the Minister
is not required to address his mind in a judicial manner. If this Court may borrow the
language used by the Supreme Court in Municipal Council Colombo vs Munasinghe
with reference to the power of an arbitrator appointed under the Industrial Disputes
Act, the Minister or for that matter, no public official 'has the freedom of the wild
horse' to do whatever he or she wants to. All exercise of statutory duties and functions
must be within the four corners of the statute that confers such duties and functions,
and any transgression will be dealt with in terms of the law.
This was followed in Lanka Electricity Company (Private) Limited v. T. Piyasoma and
Others, CA (Writ) Application No: 310/2017, decided on 11.09.2020 at page 13, His Lordship
Arjuna Obeyesekere J held that;
There is one matter that I wish to advert to, even though the Petitioner has not
challenged the reference to arbitration. In terms of Section 4(1), the Minister must
form the opinion that there exists an industrial dispute, prior to making any reference
of such dispute for resolution by arbitration. The Minister would be guided in this
regard by the Commissioner General of Labour who therefore has the duty to carefully
consider if an industrial dispute has been made out by the complainant.
In the instant case, the 1st Respondent has failed to present any evidence before this Court
that he addressed his mind in a judicial manner to properly form the opinion that there is a
minor dispute existing before referring such dispute for arbitration.

--- Page 9 ---
In view of this, we hold that the Petitioner has made a prima facie case that the Ministers
reference in the instant case is subject to judicial review on the ground that such reference is
ultra vires the Section 4(1) of the Act.
Thus, we issue notice to the Respondents and allow the interim order prayed in prayer ( c) of
the petition dated 08.04.2023 until the conclusion of this application.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. BandulaKarunarathna (P/CA), J.
I AGREE
PRESIDENT OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

--- Page 1 ---
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF SRI
LANKA
In the matter f an application for mandates in
the nature of Writs of Certiorari, Prohibition
and mandamus under and in terms of Article
140 of the Constitution of the Democratic
Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.
CA-WRT23
Transmec Engineering (PV) Ltd,
No. 24/1, Dudley Senanayake Mawatha,
Colombo 8
Petitioner
Vs.
1. B.K. Prabhath Chandrakeerthi
Commissioner General of Labour
Department of Labour
Labour Secretariat
Colombo 05.
2. Y.A.B.S. Yahalawala
Assistant Commissioner of Labour
Department of Labour
Department of Labour Office- Colombo
Central
18th Floor
Labour Secretariat
Colombo 05.
3. K.A.P. Nawaratne
Department of Labour

--- Page 2 ---
Department of Labour Office- Colombo
Central
18th Floor
Labour Secretariat
Colombo 05.
4. G.M. Sabri Wahid
1/8/6, Sunset East Tower
Trillium Residencies
Colombo 8
Respondents
Before : N. Bandula Karunarathna, P/CA, J.
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
Counsels: Kushan De Alwis, P.C. with Prasanna de Silva and R. Ariyawansa for the
Petitioner
Mihiri de Alwis, S.S.C. for the 1st to 3rd Respondents .
Bhagya Herath with Sajeevi for the 4th Respondent
Supported On: 23.10.2024
Written 11.11.2024 (by the Petitioner)
Submissions: 12.11.2024 (by the 1st to 3rd Respondents)
On 13.11.2024 (by the 4th Respondent)
Order On: 17.12.2024
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
This order pertains to whether to issue notice to the Respondents and interim reliefs are
to be granted.

--- Page 3 ---
The Petitioner has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court by the petition dated 17.05.2023
seeking the following reliefs:
a) Issue notice on the Is to 4th Respondents;
b) Direct the 1st Respondent and/or the 2nd Respondent and/or the 3rd Respondent
to produce the File no. CC/C/G/7/486/2020 maintained at the Department of
Labour;
c) Issue a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Certiorari quashing the determination
and/or decision of the 2nd Respondent that there is a surcharge in a sum of Rs.
1,580,250/- on the gratuity to be paid to the 4th Respondent from the Petitioner as
contained in the document marked P6 above;
d) Issue a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Certiorari quashing the determination
and/or decision of the 2nd Respondent that there is a sum of Rs. 6,847,750/-
consisting of a sum of Rs. 5,267,500/- as gratuity and a sum of Rs. 1,580,250/- as
the surcharge thereon due to be paid to the 4th Respondent from the Petitioner as
contained in the document marked P6 above;
e) Issue a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Certiorari quashing the determination
and/or decision of the 2" Respondent directing the Petitioner to deposit a sum of
Rs. 6,847,750/- with the Department of Labour for payment to the 4th Respondent
as gratuity and surcharge due to the 4th Respondent from the Petitioner as
contained in the document marked P6 and P8 above;
f) Issue a mandate in the nature of Writ of Prohibition preventing the 1st Respondent
and/or the 2 Respondent and/or any other person acting under the authority and/or
direction of the 1 st Respondent from demanding and/or claiming from the
Petitioner the payment of the sum of Rs. 6,847,750/- or any part thereof as gratuity
and surcharge due to the 4 Respondent from the Petitioner and/or taking or

--- Page 4 ---
causing to be taken any steps whatsoever to make such demand and/or claim from
the Petitioner;
g) Issue a mandate in the nature of a Writ of Mandamus directing the 1st Respondent
and/or the 2nd Respondent to release the Petitioner from making any payment of
gratuity to the 4th Respondent;
h) i) Issue an Interim Order staying the issuance of a certificate and institution of an
action in the Magistrates Court against the Petitioner under and in terms of the
provisions Section 8(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act for the recovery of the
gratuity allegedly outstanding to the 4th Respondent from the Petitioner, until the
hearing and the final determination of this Application;
Or in the alternative, in the event that the Certificate is issued and action has been
instituted in the Magistrates Court 
ii) Issue an Interim Order staying the proceedings in the Magistrates Court
instituted based on the Certificate against the Petitioner in terms of the provisions
Section 8(1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act for the recovery of the gratuity
allegedly outstanding to the 4th Respondent from the Petitioner, until the hearing
and the final determination of this Application;
i) Grant costs;
j) Grant such other and further relief as Your Lordships Court may seem meet;
The facts of this case are briefly as follows:
According to the petition, the Petitioner is a company duly incorporated under the
Companies Act No. . The Petitioner states that, on or about 31.07.2020, the 4th
Respondent who was a former employee of the Petitioner had made a complaint to the
Department of Labour alleging that a sum of Rs. 34,080,000/- was not paid by the
Petitioner to the 4th Respondent as gratuity. The Petitioner was notified by letter dated

--- Page 5 ---
03.09.2020 of an inquiry to be held by the 3rd Respondent in respect of the said complaint.
In the said inquiry, parties were directed to file their written submissions.
The Petitioner states that the 4th Respondent filing an undated written submission put
forward the position that the 4th Respondent having worked for the Petitioner for 16 years
was drawing a final salary of Rs. 2,130,000/-. Therefore, he is entitled for a sum of Rs.
34,080,000/- with a surcharge of Rs. 10,224,000/- which in total amounts to Rs.
44,304,000/- out of which the 4th Respondent has obtained a loan for a sum of Rs.
31,235,000/- and accordingly a sum of Rs. 13,069,000/- is payable as gratuity to the 4th
Respondent from the Petitioner. The Petitioner states that by the written submission
dated 10.11.2020, he informed that, since the 4th Respondent had a break of service, the
4th Respondent is only entitled to a sum of Rs. 5,262,000/-. The Petitioner further states
that, however, as the 4th Respondent had obtained a loan amounting to a sum of Rs.
31,235,000/- from the Petitioner against the gratuity payable to the 4th Respondent to be
settled, there was no gratuity payable or due to the 4th Respondent by the Petitioner.
The Petitioner avers that, by a letter dated 06.09.2022, the 2nd Respondent informed the
Petitioner that a sum of Rs. 6,847,750/- is payable to the 4th Respondent as unpaid gratuity
and surcharge and further that if the Petitioner has already paid the said sum to the 4th
Respondent, the Petitioner should inform the same with proof thereof to the 2nd
Respondent. In response, the Petitioner by letter 14.09.2022 informed the 2nd Respondent
that, on the request of the 4th Respondent, the Petitioner has already paid the gratuity
and therefore, no surcharge or outstanding amount is payable to the 4th Respondent by
the Petitioner. Further, through this letter, the Petitioner sought a written directive from
the 2nd Respondent that the Petitioner has already paid the gratuity to the 4th Respondent.

--- Page 6 ---
The 2nd Respondent by letter dated 04.10.2022 refused the Petitioners application on the
basis that the gratuity cannot be deducted from a loan as there is no provision for such
effect provided by law.
The main contention of the Petitioner is that the determination of the 2nd Respondent
directing the Petitioner to make the payment of gratuity to the 4th Respondent together
with the surcharge is unlawful and unreasonable.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Court seeking inter
alia writs of Certiorari quashing the determination of the 2nd Respondent marked P6.
On the other hand, the 1st to 3rd Respondents state in their written submission dated
12.11.2024 that according to Section 5 (1) of the Payment of Gratuity Act No.
as amended (hereinafter referred to as the Act), an employee is entitled to gratuity in the
instances of termination, retirement, death or operation of law or otherwise. It is their
submission, therefore, an employee who is in service is unable to obtain a loan against his
gratuity as such employee is entitled to such gratuity only upon ceasing to be an employee.
In this context, this Court focuses on Section 5 (1) of the Act which reads thus;
Every employer who employs or has employed fifteen or more workmen on any
day during the period of twelve months immediately preceding the termination of
the services of a workman in any industry shall, on termination (whether by the
employer or workman, or on retirement or by the death of the workman, or by
operation of law, or otherwise) of the services at any time after the coming into
operation of this Act, of a workman who has a period of service of not less than five
completed years under that employer, pay to that workman in respect of such
services, and where the termination is by the death of that workman, to his heirs,
a gratuity computed in accordance with the provisions of this Part within a period
of thirty days of such termination.

--- Page 7 ---
The above Section clearly depicts that gratuity is to be paid to the workman by the
employer immediately preceding the termination of the services of a workman.
Accordingly, in the instant application, the Petitioners contention that the 4th Respondent
has obtained a loan against his gratuity prior to his termination does not stand.
The question before this Court is how gratuity should be calculated. According to Section
6(2)(b) of the Act, when computing the gratuity, the last drawn salary is the basis on
which such gratuity is calculated.
A workman referred to in subsection. (1) of section 5 shall be entitled to receive
as gratuity, a sum equivalent to-
(a) half a month's, wage or salary for each year of completed service
computed at the rate of wage or salary last drawn by the workman, in the
case of a monthly rated workman; and
In the instant case, the 4th Respondent retired from his work on 30.11.2016. The
contention of the Petitioner is that the Petitioner has paid the gratuity by way of a loan
while the 4th Respondent was in service.
It should be noted that there is no provision in the Act that a loan can be granted against
the gratuity due to him. In fact, gratuity is available on retirement based on his last drawn
salary.
The only provision available in the said Act that estop paying such gratuity is under
Section 13 of the Act which reads thus:
Any workman, to whom a gratuity is payable under Part II of this Act and, whose
services have been terminated for reasons of fraud, misappropriation of funds of
the employer, willful damage to property of the employer, or causing the loss of

--- Page 8 ---
goods, articles or property of the employer, shall forfeit such gratuity to the extent
of the damage or loss caused by him.
In the instant application, the Petitioner has disclosed that an action was filed in the
Magistrate Court of Colombo Case No. 85512/2/22 under Section 136 (1) (a) of the
Criminal Procedure Code against the 4th Respondent for the abetment of offences under
Section 391 (Criminal Breach of Trust) and Section 467 (Falsification of Accounts) of the
Penal Code on the basis of the actions of the 4th Respondent in obtaining the advance
payment of gratuity in a sum that is excessively over and above the sum actually payable
as gratuity to the 4th Respondent.
Nevertheless, it should be noted that the 4th Respondent was not terminated from his
service on this ground. In the instant case, thus, the Petitioner has not indicated that
there is any forfeiture of gratuity as such which comes within the scope of Section 13 of
the Act.
Furthermore, this Court notes that the 4th Respondent has indicated to the Court that the
Petitioner has failed to disclose that the Petitioners Sister Company, Micro Cars (Pvt)
Ltd has instituted an action in the District Court of Mahara case bearing No.
165/2023/DMR against the 4th Respondent to recover the loan granted to the 4th
Respondent.
The 1st and 2nd Respondents have taken steps under Section 8 (1) of the Act to recover the
sum due as gratuity from the Petitioner by filing a certificate after the inquiry.
The main ground urged by the Petitioner is that the determination of the 2nd Respondent
in the document marked P6, directing for the petitioner to make a payment of Rs.
6,847,750/- as gratuity and surcharge to the 4th Respondent and by filing the certificate
instituting action in the Magistrates Court are illegal and ultra vires.

--- Page 9 ---
I hold that by virtue of Sections 5 and 8 of the Gratuity Act, the Commissioner of Labour
is vested with the jurisdiction to recover the gratuity payment.
We further hold that gratuity will be applicable only after the termination of service of a
workman or death of a workman.
The Petitioner has failed to establish a prima facie case to issue writs of Certiorari in
terms of the Atkinian formula.
For the above-mentioned reasons, we dismiss the action with costs of Rs. 50,000/-.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. BandulaKarunarathna (P/CA), J.
I AGREE
PRESIDENT OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC
OF SRI LANKA

under and in terms of Article 138 of the
Constitution of the Democratic Socialist
Republic of Sri Lanka.
Court of Appeal The Hon. Attorney General,
Revision Application No: Attorney Generals Department,
CA/CPA/0124/24 Superior Courts Complex,
Hulftsdorp Street,
High Court of Ampara Colombo 12.
Case No: HC/AMP/1976/19 COMPLAINANT
Vs.
Magistrates Court of Ampara 1. Wathuliyadde Gedara Malinda Nuwan
Case No: MC/AMP/B/7494/10 Samarasinghe,
Siriwasa, Ankelipitiya, Thalatu-oya,
Kandy.
2. Sachini Rinosha Wickramarachchi,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,

--- Page 2 ---
3. Kalubowila Arachchilage Gayan

ACCUSED
AND NOW BETWEEN
1. Wathuliyadde Gedara Malinda Nuwan
Samarasinghe,
Siriwasa, Ankelipitiya,
Thalatu-oya,
Kandy.
1st ACCUSED-PETITIONER
Vs.
1. The Hon. Attorney General,
Attorney Generals Department,
Superior Courts Complex,
Hulftsdorp Street,
Colombo 12.
COMPLAINANT-RESPONDENT

--- Page 3 ---
2. Sachini Rinosha Wickramarachchi,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.
2nd ACCUSED-RESPONDENT
3. Kalubowila Arachchilage Gayan
Buddhika,
No. C 382/1, Mihindupura,
Ampara.
3rd ACCUSED-RESPONDENT
Before : Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
: Amal Ranaraja, J.
Counsel : A.M.E.B. Atapattu for the 1st Accused-Petitioner
Supported on : 042024
Order on : 192024
Sampath B. Abayakoon, J.
This is an application preferred by the 1st accused-petitioner (hereinafter referred
to as the petitioner) in terms of Article 138 of The Constitution seeking to invoke
the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court.
The petitioner is the 1st accused in the High Court of Ampara Case No.
HC/AMP/1976/19.

--- Page 4 ---
He has been indicted by the Hon. Attorney General along with two others, for
conspiring to cause criminal breach of trust to Seylan Bank of which he was an
employee attached to its Ampara Branch for a sum of Rs. 5019000/- between
the period of 142010 and 172010, and thereby committing an offence
punishable in terms of section 391 read with section 113B and 102 of the Penal
Code.
He has also been indicted for committing the earlier mentioned criminal breach
of trust for the said sum at the same time and at the same transaction, and
thereby committing an offence punishable in terms of section 391 of the Penal
Code.
The trial against the petitioner and the other accused has commenced before the
learned High Court Judge of Ampara and PW-01 has so far partly concluded his
evidence in chief. In the process of the said evidence, PW-01 has produced
several gold jewellery pawn receipts relevant to the action, marked up to P-04.
In the petition before the Court, the petitioner has sought to set aside the orders
given by the learned High Court Judge of Ampara allowing to mark documents
P-01, P-02, P-03, P-04, P-04(1), P-04(2), P-04(3), P04(4), P-04(5), P-04(6), P-
04(7), P-04(8), P-04(9), P-04(10), and the documents marked during the trial on
262023 and 222024, among other reliefs sought in the prayer of the
petition.
When this matter was supported for notice and also for a stay order, the main
reason submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner for initiating this
action was that the documents mentioned in the indictment filed by the Hon.
Attorney General are documents not tendered to Magistrates Court when the
matter was initially reported to the Magistrate of Ampara, and therefore
producing them at the High Court is against the provisions of section 431 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure Act.
It was his submission that the learned High Court Judge unfairly overruled his
objection and therefore, his client was denied a fair trial. It was also submitted

--- Page 5 ---
that although the learned High Court Judge ordered the prosecution to hand
over the copies of the items mentioned in the indictment as productions, the
prosecution has failed to hand over them. Another matter taken up by the
learned Counsel was that the pawn receipts so far marked at the trial are not
the originals, but photocopies.
It was on that basis the learned Counsel submitted that the petitioner has
sufficient exceptional grounds to invoke the revisionary jurisdiction of this Court
to seek relief as prayed for.
Having considered the submissions of the learned Counsel, this Court is of the
view that section 431 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act has no direct
application to the matter under consideration.
It is clear from the proceedings of the High Court that the petitioner and the
other accused have been indicted before the High Court of Ampara for conspiracy
to commit criminal breach of trust, committing criminal breach of trust and also
aiding and abetting to commit criminal breach of trust, and thereby, causing a
loss to Seylan Bank of the sum mentioned in the indictment.
The evidence so far led appears to be on the basis that this criminal breach of
trust has been committed by knowingly accepting fake gold jewellery as pawn
articles to the bank. The documents that had been so far marked are the
duplicate copies of the pawn receipts the bank had in possession. Although the
learned Counsel claims that the prosecution has failed to mark the original
documents, obviously the originals of the pawn receipts cannot be in the
possession of the bank as the said originals are meant to be handed over to the
person who pawned the articles. The evidence of PW-01 led so far reveals the fact
that once a person pawned an item, a receipt is prepared in triplicate, where the
original is handed over to the customer, while the pink-coloured copy is kept
with the pawned article, and the green-coloured copy is used for auditing
purposes.

--- Page 6 ---
It is also clear from the proceedings that attempts had been made on behalf of
the accused to prevent the relevant documents being marked on unacceptable
grounds, where the learned High Court Judge has given a clear order in that
regard on 092023, which I find is a correct order made in that regard.
It appears from the proceedings that the questioned items of the fake gold
jewellery and the relevant pink and green coloured receipts issued in that regard
have been kept under the custody of the Seylan bank, being the owner of the
said items for better safekeeping. I find that this is a common practice adopted
by the Court to allow the owners of the items of productions to keep the custody
of the said productions until a conclusion of a trial for obvious reasons.
Although the learned High Court Judge has ordered that the items of jewellery,
which are the productions of the case shall be handed over to the Court, I do
not find any necessity to hand over the said jewellery to the Court as the purpose
is to ensure the safe custody of the same until the conclusion of the trial. In my
view, Seylan Bank is the best place where the said jewellery can be safely kept
for the purposes of this action as they are the owners of the jewellery.
As clearly determined by the learned High Court Judge, if the marked documents
or other productions are not in order or suspicious, it is a matter for the learned
trial Judge to determine on that when relevant. I find no basis to shut out such
documents or items of productions in the manner the petitioner is attempting to
claim.
It is clear from the case record that the learned trial Judge has done all he could
to ensure a fair trial towards the petitioner and the other accused in the case.
If the prosecution has failed to hand over copies of the other documents they
intend to mark at the trial as ordered by the learned High Court Judge, it will
again be a matter that the learned High Court Judge should decide whether to
allow evidence in that regard or what order should be made in that regard.

--- Page 7 ---
Even after the documents had been marked, the defence can again ask for copies
of the same, if they are unable to cross-examine the witnesses straightaway in
that regard, and obtain an order from the Court.
I am of the view that this type of applications should not be encouraged under
any circumstances, unless the decisions made by the trial Court in the process
of a trial are manifestly wrong, which shocks the conscience of the Court as it
would lead to delay in proceedings before a trial Court. In the instant matter, I
find no reasons to come to such a finding,
Having considered the application before the Court, and the relevant facts and
circumstances, I find that this is not a case where notice should be issued to the
named respondents, as I find no merit in any of the grounds urged before the
Court.
Accordingly, the revision application is dismissed without the notice being
issued.
The Registrar of the Court is directed to communicate this order to the High
Court of Ampara for necessary information.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
Amal Ranaraja, J.
I agree.
Judge of the Court of Appeal

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF SRI

MAG AUTO SPRING (PVT) LTD.,

-Vs-

RESPONDENTS

--- Page 4 ---
Before : N. Bandula Karunarathna, P/CA, J.
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
Counsel : Maithree Pitawela with W.P. Sittampalam for the Petitioner
Shemanthi Dunuwille, SC for the Respondents
Supported On: 05.11.2024
Order On: 19.12.2024
B. Sasi Mahendran, J.
ORDER
This order pertains to whether the notice and interim reliefs are to be issued.
The Petitioner instituted this action by way of a petition dated 06.07.2023 seeking the
following reliefs:
a. Issue Notice on the IS to 17th Respondents above named;
b. Issue a Mandate in the nature of a Writ of Certiorari, quashing the said notice or
certificate of the 1st and 2nd Respondents and issue certified copies of the inquiry
held before the 2nd Respondent;
c. Make a direction the 2nd and 3rd Respondents to issue certified copies of the all
documents contained in the inquiry file
d. Issue an Interim Order, staying the operation of the said notice or certificate and/or
restraining the 1st and 2nd Respondents from compelling the Petitioner to pay
default EPF payment or any part thereof, as per and/or in terms of the said notice
or certificate, subject to such terms and/or conditions and or limitations and/or
qualifications as to Your Lordships' Court may seem meet, pending the hearing
and final determination of the above styled Application;
e. Grant Costs;
f. Grant such other and further relief as to Your Lordships' Court may seem meet.
The facts of this case are briefly as follows:

--- Page 5 ---
According to the petition, the Petitioner is a duly incorporated company engaged in the
business of manufacturing and distribution of springs. The Petitioner states that the 4th
to 17th Respondents have made a complaint to the 2nd Respondent that they were deprived
of the Employee Provident Fund contribution (hereinafter referred to as EPF) for the
period commencing from January 2010 to April 2013 which was denied by the Petitioner
that the said Respondents were not employed by the Petitioner during the said period.
After an inquiry, the 2nd Respondent directed the Petitioner to pay a sum of Rs.
2,142,008.47/- as the defaulted EPF contribution. The 2nd Respondent has filed a
certificate dated 28.10.2014 before the Magistrates Court of Kandy to recover the same.
The Petitioner avers that the Petitioner requested certified copies of the inquiry led before
the 2nd Respondent by letter dated 12.01.2021 which was denied by the 2nd Respondent
informing to direct such request to Additional Commissioner General of Labour (Admin).
The Additional Commissioner thereafter informed that such information cannot be
provided directly but can only be accommodated on an order of the Magistrates Court of
Kandy.
Consequent to such denial, the Petitioner again requested the information to invoke the
jurisdiction of this Court by letter dated 13.02.2022 marked as P6 to which the 3rd
Respondent replied that since the Magistrates Court of Kandy has already delivered an
order on the said Certificate, the Petitioner has no legal entitlement to invoke the
jurisdiction of this Court, thus refusing such information. The Petitioner being aggrieved
by the said response of the 3rd Respondent appealed to the High Court of Kandy against
the said order of the Magistrate Court.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Court seeking inter
alia a writ of Certiorari to quash the said notice or certificate of the 1st and 2nd
Respondents.
It should be noted that this application was filed on 20.07.2023 after the order of the
Learned Magistrate was delivered against the Petitioner directing him to pay the due
sum. But, the Petitioner has failed to move this Court to quash the said decision. The only
ground urged by the Petitioner is to quash the certificate issued by the 1st and 2nd
Respondents and direct the 1st and 2nd to issue certified copies of the inquiry held.
Once the Commissioner of Labour files the certificate under Section 38 (2) of the
Employees Provident Fund Act No. as amended (hereinafter referred to as the
Act) to recover the EPF contribution that the employer has failed to pay to the Fund, then

--- Page 6 ---
the Magistrate has the power to recover the arrears of the said contribution. In the instant
case, before filing this action, the Learned Magistrate has issued summons to the
Petitioner asking him to show cause with regard to the recovery of the said sum. We are
mindful that the certificate issued to the Magistrate is the last resort. The Act provides
the employer the final opportunity to show cause before the magistrate that the sum is
not lawfully due. The Petitioner has failed to inform in the petition, that the Magistrate
has not given him an opportunity to show cause. I am of the view that the Petitioner has
suppressed material facts before this Court. Further, we note that the Petitioner has
failed to aver the details of the order made by the Learned Magistrate.
In the particular inquiry before the Learned Magistrate, he should have established that
the Petitioner is not a defaulter. By delivering the order under Section 38(2) of the said
Act, the particular sum shall be deemed to be a fine imposed as a sentence of the
Magistrate. In other words, the Court has declared the Petitioner to be a defaulter. The
said order is not before this Court and is not challenged in this application.
We are mindful that even if the main relief sought by the Petitioner which is to quash the
certificate made by the 1st and 2nd Respondents is to be granted, such would be futile as
the Learned Magistrate of Kandy has already decided on the said Certificate that the
Petitioner is a defaulter.
This Court has followed that writs which are a discretionary remedy will not be issued if
the Court is of the opinion granting such writs is futile.
In Sethu Ramasamy v. A.E.G. Moregoda, 63 NLR 115 at page 117, Gunasekara, J held
that;
 This view of the matter, however, cannot conclude the question whether the
application should be granted; for, as has been pointed out by Mr. Jayararatne, a
mandamus will not be granted when it appears that it would be futile in its result.
In M.M. Shamsudeen, v. The Minister of Defence and External Affairs, 63 NLR 430 at
page 432, L.B. De Silva, J held that;
 The issue of a writ of mandamus is within the discretion of Court and will not be
issued if it will be futile to do so. In this case I am satisfied that the petitioner has
failed to prove that his mother was a citizen of Ceylon by descent.

--- Page 7 ---
The above judgments were considered by His Lordship Sisira de Abrew, J in Selvamani
v. Dr. Kumaraveluppillai and Others, ( 2002) (1) SLR 99 at page 103 where it was held
that;
The petitioner has now vacated post. This is evident from letter dated 25.08.2004
(3R9A). The petitioner has been sent on vacation of post after the decision in P4A.
At the hearing of this application the learned Counsel for the petitioner admitted
that no application for writ of certiorari has been filed to quash the said order
whereby the petitioner was sent on vacation of post.
The petitioner by this application also moves for a writ of mandamus on the first
respondent directing that the petitioner be restored to his earlier position i. e. to
the post of Project Operator. Even if this application of the petitioner is granted,
he is not entitled to resume his earlier office in view of the order of vacation of post
(3R9A). Therefore, issuing a writ of mandamus in this case would be futile.
We hold that, therefore, quashing the certificate filed by the 1st and 2nd Respondents is
futile in view of the order of the learned Magistrate of Kandy.
Application dismissed with costs of Rs. 50,000/-
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
N. Bandula Karunarathna (P/CA), J.
I AGREE
PRESIDENT OF THE COURT OF APPEAL

This order pertains to whether to issue notice and to grant interim reliefs.
The Petitioner instituted this application by petition dated 28.11.2022 praying for the
following reliefs:

--- Page 5 ---
a. Issue notice to the Respondents.
b. Issue a direction to the 23rd Respondent to submit to Your Lordships' Court
certified copy of Individual marking sheets used by the members of the Selection
Committee based on which the Evaluation Sheet marked P6c was prepared.
c. Issue a mandate in the nature of Writ of certiorari quashing:
i. the Evaluation process and assessment of candidates as depicted in
document marked as P6c adopted by the Selection Committee consisting
of the 02nd, 03rd, 11th, 12th, 18th and 22nd Respondents, and
ii. the decision made by the Council of the O1st Respondent on 27.11.2021
at its 251st meeting as stated in document marked as P6e to appoint the
24th, 25th, 26th and 27th Respondents to the Post of Lecturer
Probationary\ in Information and Communication Technology in the
Department of the Information and Communication Technology of the
Faculty of Technology in the O1st Respondent based on the
recommendation of the Selection Committee.
d. Direct the Chairman, University Grants Commission to conduct an appropriate
inquiry and take suitable disciplinary action against the members of the
Selection Committee and Council of the 01st Respondent who are responsible for
the process adopted in the evaluation of candidates in the interview and
unethical conduct in decision making process to make appointment to the Post
of Lecturer [Probationary] in Information and Communication Technology in the
Department of the Information and Communication Technology of the Faculty of
Technology in the 01st Respondent.
e. For Costs and,
f. For such further and other reliefs as to Your Lordships' Court shall seem meet.
The facts of this case are briefly as follows:

--- Page 6 ---
According to the Petition, the Petitioner has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court to quash
the evaluation process and assessment of candidates as depicted in the document marked
P6c adopted by the Selection Committee and quash the decision made by the Council on
27.11.2021 at its 251st Meeting to appoint the 24th to 27th Respondents for the post of
lecturer marked as P6e based on the recommendation of the Selection Committee.
According to the Petitioner, the 1st Respondent published a notice in the newspaper on
19.11.2020 marked as P3 calling for applications inter alia for the post of Lecturer
(Probationary) from suitable candidates. The Petitioner has made an application dated
14.12.2020 for the said post and was asked to be present for an interview on 24.11.2021
where she appeared before the Selection Committee.
The Petitioner further avers that she unofficially became aware that the Council of the 1st
Respondent had decided to recruit and appoint the 24th, 25th, 26th, and 27th Respondents
for the said post based on the recommendations of the Selection Committee on the basis
of the overall assessment of marks scored in the interview.
Since the Petitioner was not selected for the said post, she sought details of marks for
candidates and overall by her application dated 28.11.2021 from the Information Officer
of the 1st Respondent under the Right to Information Act No. which is marked
as P6a. The Petitioner was given a certified copy of the Evaluation Sheet marked as P6c
by the Information Officer by letter dated 29.11.2021. Further, for another application by
the Petitioner, a letter dated 29.12.2021 was received informing that as decided by the
Council in its 251st meeting, letters of appointment were issued to the 24th and 27th
Respondents and that the 24th, 26th, and 27th Respondents have assumed duties with effect
from 13.12.2021 with a copy of the Council Memo: SEU/C/2021/251/Addl/01.
The Petitioner further states that she became aware of the headings under which the
evaluation of the candidates when perusing the said Council Memo. The Petitioner avers

--- Page 7 ---
that when she requested further information by letter dated 13.12.2021, it was denied by
letter dated 23.12.2021 under Part II, Section 5 (1) (a) of the said Act. When the Petitioner
appealed to the 2nd Respondent about the said denial, by letter dated 30.12.2021 the
Petitioner was informed that the said request was denied under Part II, Section 5 (1) (a)
and (g) of the said Act. Further, the Petitioner states that, although several requests were
made to the Information Officer and the 2nd Respondent, she did not receive a satisfactory
response.
The Petitioner contends that, when the Evaluation Sheet marked P6c is carefully perused,
it becomes obvious that the Petitioner should have been given more scores based on her
graduate, postgraduate, and research qualifications and also for her experience working
as a Temporary Demonstrator. The Petitioner avers that, upon an appeal by the
Petitioner on 16.02.2022, the Right to Information Commission delivered its decision on
29.08.2022 holding that the 1st Respondent should release the information requested by
the Petitioner before 30.09.2022.
The Petitioner further avers that the Petitioner received a letter dated 29.09.2022 marked
as P10a from the 1st Respondent with the information requested by the Petitioner. The
Petitioner states that the annexures of P10a demonstrate that some of the selected
candidates were allocated marks in violation of the marking scheme disclosed by the 1st
Respondent. The Petitioner further contends that the 1st Respondent University has also
failed to adhere to the Sri Lanka Qualifications Framework (SLQF) to which the
University Grants Commission has given effect by Circular No. 05/2013(i) dated
25.08.2017 thereby advising the universities to follow the said SLQF in assessing the
qualification of candidates in providing employment in universities.

--- Page 8 ---
According to the Petitioner, the 1st Respondent also had breached Circular No. 721 which
contains Schemes of Recruitment in connection with employment of academic staff by
selecting and appointing the 26th Respondent in the said Post.
The Petitioner further avers that the 24th and 25th Respondents were selected and
appointed based on the personal relationships they have with the 2nd, 11th, and 12th
Respondents who evaluated, selected and recommended the said appointments.
The main gravamen of the Petitioner is that the selection process of the Selection
Committee and the decision process of the 1st Respondent to employ the 24th to 27th
Respondents are unlawful and unfair.
In this context, the Petitioner has invoked the writ jurisdiction of this Court seeking inter
alia writs of Certiorari to quash the documents marked P6c and P6e on the basis that the
marks there was bias towards certain candidates.
2nd Respondent on 01.03.2023 filed the objection marking documents R1 to R11.
When the matter was supported on 23.10.2024 the Counsel of the Petitioner brought to
the notice of the Court that documents marked as R2A, R2A(a), (b), and (c) which were
filed by the 2nd Respondent, the said documents were prepared by the Selection
Committee for the interview held on 24.11.2022 indicating the marks obtained by the said
candidates. On the other hand, the documents received by the Petitioner through the
Information Officer is totally different. That is to say, the documents marked as R2A,
R2A(a), (b), and (c) have interpolations that were not authorized. The question arises as
to whether those were done at the interview or later. Even, no one has certified when
these alterations were done.
When perusing the documents, a doubt is created as to whether these corrections were
done by the Interview Panel or subsequently by any other person as alleged by the
Petitioner.

--- Page 9 ---
Considering the documents, the Petitioner has established a prima facie case to be
considered by this Court.
Therefore, we issue notice to the Respondents.

06.04.2024 where the Tribunal appointed a receiver, removing the Trustees from the
Management and required the Petitioners who are the Trustees to hand over the possession

This application deals with the N.D.H. Abdul Ghaffoor Trust established by the Deed of Trust
No. 2125 dated 21.11.1935 attested by John Wilson, Notary Public of Colombo. This Deed of
Trust involves two properties namely a plantation land (comprising of 3 buildings on one end

property described in the First Scheule of the said Trust Deed have made several applications
against the trustees of the said Trust in the Wakf Tribunal.

of the Wakf Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 marked as P23 to set aside the same and seek an
interim order staying the operations of the said order and the proceedings of the Wakf
Tribunal Case bearing No. WT/297/2023.
We are mindful that a number of cases have been filed against the trustees in the Wakf
Tribunal. Against the orders of the said Wakf Tribunal, several cases have been filed in the
Court of Appeal to quash the said orders.
In LTA/06/2021 connected with the Wakf Tribunal Case No. WT/273/2020 which deals with

Wakf Tribunal dated 04.02.2021 and sought an interim order on the basis that the said Deed

of the Court of Appeal is reproduced below.

reliefs seeking to impugn the order of the Wakfs Tribunal dated 40 . February 2021
('P9*). The Respondent-Petitioners also sort the interim - and/or stay orders prayed
for in prayer (f), (g), (i), (), (k) and (1) of the Petition. This Court has already issued

has been extended from time to time.

--- Page 10 ---
Having carefully considered the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the
Appellant, learned State Counsel for the 1st Respondent and the learned Counsel for
the 3rd to 7th Respondents, we are of the view that, prima facie there is a serious
question of law need to be, gone into by this Court as to whether the Deed of Trust
bearing No. 2125 dated 21st November 1935, attested by John Wilson, Notary Public
(PI') is or not a Muslim Charitable Trust or Wakf.
Consequently, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the new Management
Committee of Ghaffooriya Arabic College is lawful, and also whether the Wakf
Tribunal has jurisdiction to accept, hear and determine the application made by the
applicant respondent and to make the impugned order marked P9
Accordingly, we formally issue notice on the respondent's name in the petition of this
court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs
(f), (g),( i),( j), (k), and (l) until the final determination of this application.
According to the above-said order, the Court of Appeal has decided that there is a serious
question to be looked into whether the particular trust is or is not a Muslim Charitable Trust
and issued a stay order staying the further proceedings of the Tribunal.
We are mindful that the Wakf Tribunal has jurisdiction only if the particular trust comes
under the Muslim Charitable Trust according to Section 9J of the Muslim Mosques and
Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended.
Despite this order, the Tribunal has affirmed that the Trust established by Deed of Trust No.
2125 is a Muslim Charitable Trust and proceeded to appoint a receiver.

--- Page 11 ---
When the matter was supported, the Counsel for the Petitioners brought to the notice of the
Court the following facts.
A) Knowing the fact that the cases are pending before the Court of Appeal regarding whether
the Trust involved is a Muslim Charitable Trust or not which is a jurisdictional issue, the
Tribunal has proceeded to act on the basis that it is a Muslim Charitable Trust. The
jurisdiction of the Tribunal is limited only to the Muslim Trusts. But the main objection
taken by the Petitioner is that the said Trust is a Private Trust, therefore, the Tribunal
has no jurisdiction to hear the matter.
B) According to Section 671 of the Civil Procedure Code, the appointment of the receiver
should be done by the Court and no one else. For the purpose of convenience, the said
Section 671 is reproduced below.
Whenever it appears to the court to be necessary for the restoration, preservation, or
better custody or management of any property, movable or immovable, the subject of
an action, or under sequestration, the court may on the application of any party who
shall establish a prima facie right to or interest in such property, by order
(a) appoint a receiver of such property, and, if need be,
(b) remove the person, in whose possession or custody the property may be,
from the possession or custody thereof;
(c) commit such property to the custody or management of such receiver; and
(d) grant to such receiver such fee or commission on the rents and profits of the
property by way of remuneration as the court thinks fit, and all such powers
as to bringing and defending actions and for the realization, management,
protection, preservation, and improvement of the property, the collection of the

--- Page 12 ---
rents and profits thereof, the application and disposal of such rents and profits,
and the execution of instruments in writing, as the owner himself has, or such
of those powers as the court thinks fit.
We are mindful that the Tribunal has directed the Respondents to recommend a name which
means that the Tribunal has acted in contravention of Section 671 of the Civil Procedure
Code which directs the Court to appoint the receiver of the Trust. An excerpt of the order of
the Tribunal dated 06.04.2024 is reproduced below for easy reference.
We therefore, allow this application for the appointment of a Receiver and make order
removing the trustees, the 1st to the 12th defendants, from the management and
custody of the Gaffooriya Arabic College and the property at Maharagama and appoint
one of the persons named by the plaintiffs as Receiver, in terms of section 671 of the
Civil Procedure Code to manage the said Arabic College, which is the subject matter
of this case.
The Tribunal has delegated its powers to Respondents to nominate a receiver. The power
conferred on the authority (the Tribunal) by statute must be lawfully exercised by the
authority itself. This principle is discussed in Wade and Forsyths Administrative Law,
Twelfth Edition at page 255 - 257;
Delegation
Inalienable Discretionary Power
An element which is essential to the lawful exercise of power is that it should be
exercised by the authority upon whom it is conferred, and by no one else. The principle
is strictly applied, even where it causes administrative inconvenience, except in cases
where it may reasonably be inferred that the power was intended to be delegable.

--- Page 13 ---
Normally the courts are rigorous in requiring the power to be exercised by the precise
person or body stated in the statute, and in condemning as ultra vires action taken by
agents, sub-committees or delegates, however expressly authorised by the authority
endowed with the power.
One aspect of this principle is the rule that the participation of non-members in the
deliberations or decisions of a collective body may invalidate its acts. The decision of a
disciplinary committee, for example, is likely to be invalid if any non-member of the
committee has taken part in its proceedings. It is not clear that the mere presence of a
non-member will be fatal, although in one case Lord Wright MR said:
It would be most improper on general principles of law that extraneous
persons, who may or may not have independent interests of their own, should
be present at the formulation of that judicial decision.
Therefore, the question is whether the Tribunal has the power to delegate.
C) When the receiver was appointed, there was no quorum as required by Section 9D (3) of
the Muslim Mosques and Charitable Trusts or Wakfs Act No. as amended
which reads as follows;
Two members of the Tribunal shall form a quorum. No matter shall be heard
by the Tribunal unless a quorum is present.
We hold that when the receiver was appointed by the Chairman of the Wakf Tribunal, the
quorum required by the statute was not met. Our Courts have considered that failure to meet
the quorum as required by the statute will go to the root of the matter.

--- Page 14 ---
In Anoma S. Polwatte v. Ms. L. Jayawickrama and Others SC WRIT Application No. 01/2011
decided on 27.07.2018, His Lordship Vijith K. Malalgoda PC, J held that;
When looking at the provisions of the above three provisions of the Act it is clear that
by the above provisions, a clear distinction had been made between the powers of the
Commission and functions of the Commission. As identified in section 3 referred to
above, when an offence is disclosed after an Investigation, Commission shall direct
the institution of proceedings and the said conduct of the Commission had been
identified within the Functions of the Commission. The powers of the Commission has
been identified under section 5 of the Act and under section 2 (8), such powers of the
Commission may exercise by its members either sitting together or separately.
Thus it is clear that the members of the Commission can exercise ancillary powers on
his own though the full complement of the Commission is not available at one given
time. But as for the exercise of functions such as the direction to be given to the
Director General, it is crystal clear that the Act has not provided for one member alone
to give such direction. However as already observed by me, R-1 refers to a directive
given by one member and in the said directive, it is not clear as to whether the reports
referred to, had been considered by the full commission before making such directive.
In the said circumstance, I have no hesitation to conclude that there is no valid
directive made under section 11 of the Act to institute criminal proceedings before the
Magistrates Court, with regard to the investigations carried out by the fraud
Investigation Unit of the Commission to Investigate Bribery and Corruption as
against the Petitioner to the present Application. I therefore conclude the directive
produced marked R-1 is patently illegal.

--- Page 15 ---
In Associated Motorways (Pvt) Ltd. v. Consumer Affairs Authority of Sri Lanka and Another
CA/WRIT/430/2015 decided on 16.11.2020, His Lordship Mahinda Samayawardhena, J. (as
he was then) held that;
Before I consider the Petitioners case on its merits, there is a preliminary issue to be
addressed, though technical in nature, which goes to the root of the matter. That is,
the validity of the impugned decision due to lack of quorum.
Item 8(2) of the Schedule to the Consumer Affairs Authority Act (read with section
3(4) of the Act) says The quorum for any meeting of the Authority shall be four
members. Learned Presidents Counsel for the Petitioner submits that when the
impugned decision A18B was purportedly made on 27.11.2014, there was no quorum
of the Authority in the eyes of the law to make such a decision.
Further held that;
For the aforesaid reasons I hold that the impugned decision A18B is a nullity, as it
has not been made by a properly constituted panel of inquiry as required by law. In
other words, the decision has no force or avail in law due to the lack of quorum.
Therefore, in this instant case, the question is when the Chairman appointed the receiver
whether there was the quorum required by the statute.
In addition, the allegation made by the Plaintiffs was of mismanagement of the Trust. We
are mindful that before appointing the receiver, the Tribunal should have asked the
Petitioners to submit the accounts relating to the Trust to satisfy themselves of the allegation
made against the Petitioners. Simply appointing a receiver on the allegation made by the
Plaintiffs is not expected from the Tribunal. Before the Tribunal appointed the person, they
should have asked for the proper accounts to be produced.

--- Page 16 ---
Therefore, the issue arises as to whether the appointment of the receiver is lawful.
Accordingly, we grant the leave to appeal against the order dated 06.04.2024 made by the
Wakf Tribunal and we issue notice on all the Respondents named in the Petition to this
Court.
Further, in order to maintain the status quo, we issue orders prayed for in paragraphs (e),
(f), (g) (h) and (i) until the final determination of this application.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
R. Gurusinghe, J.
I AGREE
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
